title: john hughes III

pages.html:
When I speak to him on the telephone, I give the street address of the café where I'd like to meet. I am trying to pick somewhere discreet, dark during daylight, somewhere where a tape recorder will not provoke eavesdropping attention. When he walks in the whole staff greets him; they already know what kind of coffee he likes. “Hey, John,” says the girl behind the counter. I offer to pay for his drink, but the waitress assures me he won't be charged. His coffee is not on the house because he is John Hughes III, founder of Hefty Records. His coffee is not on the house because he happens to be the son of a famous 80's teenage cult-film director. His coffee is on the house because he's a regular. “I somehow always end up here,” he admits as he takes his seat.

John Hughes founded the independent record label Hefty in 1995, under which his own electronic music appears. He has helped local and distant bands get started under his musical guidance, he has written movie soundtracks and he has organized collaborative releases between artists. He is also a self-proclaimed “studio-hermit,” which is quite a phrase to be coming from the mouth of someone who in the first five minutes of being seated seems to be a class-A mingler, a sweet-talking latte negotiator .

Since his 1998 debut album, “Confidence in Duber,” Hughes' music has appeared under the alias Slicker. When he first started Hefty, Hughes was producing the music of his band, Bill Ding. Slicker's style diverges from Bill Ding, borrowing the throaty vocals characteristic of his early work, and fusing them with gritty electronic beats. Hughes has put out two full-length albums as Slicker, as well as an album of remixes and a few collaborative releases; his third full-length album has just finished production.

When both of our coffees are set on the table facing each other, my coffee and his coffee, it's time to begin. I pull the tape recorder from my pocket and place it one the table between the two of them, our friends, the coffee, hoping it will blend in up there with the sugar packets and the salt. But recoding devices generally don't blend in with condiments, and today is no exception. The conversation dies. I may as well have as nonchalantly placed an alien baby up there and expected it to promote casual dialogue.

We took at the tape recorder. We look at each other.

“Aw, now I'm going to freeze up,” he says.

“Really?” I ask, moved that I'm not the only one with a sensitivity to having my words played back to me at a later date.

“No, I'm used to it.” He smiles.

He smiles a cat's smile, the type of cat that has no qualms about knocking over your beverage after beguiling you into thinking you two really had some kind of cosmic cat-human connection.

“I am speaking with John Hughes III,” I say into the tape recorder.

I quickly center the recorder between us, as if this statement might be a point of contention.

Which it's not.

I ask him how Hefty got started.

“As an artist, I've always wanted to be involved in the way a record is marketed,” he says of Hefty's conception, “I didn't want to be embarrassed by anyone else's decisions. I guess it has something to do with wanting control over every little aspect. When you're working on a record in the studio, so much attention goes into detail that it's weird to turn it over when you're done. I like being involved in every step, and I think that artists appreciate a label that's run by an artist.”

Hefty Records began, more or less, after Hughes less-than-profitable college experience, as a way to get his own music out. He spent a year as a telecommunications major at the University of Ohio in Athens, OH, before coming back to Chicago to launch Hefty Records. Since 1995, Hefty has picked up enough speed for Hughes to take other artists onto his label, although it initially was an outlet for him to take an active role in his own music's production. These days, Hughes is enthusiastic about collaborating with artists Joshua Eustis and Charles Cooper of Telefon Tel Aviv, whose forthcoming record has recently finished production. Originally from New Orleans, Telefon Tel Aviv sent their demo to Hughes and have since relocated to Chicago as Hefty has taken them onto the label.

Hughes explains what he looks for when screening the quantity of music Hefty is sent. “When I listen to demos I try to scrape away everything and see what's left once you take away all the programming and effects and trickery. [Telefon] originally caught my attention because they Fed-Exed it to me. No one had ever Fed-Exed me a demo, which I thought was funny. It got me to rip it open right away. I listened to it and was completely blown away. I just look for good songwriters.”

(go to page 2)

You can tell that Hughes is indeed used to being interviewed. He can pontificate; he knows how to maintain eye contact for long stretches of speech. It must come with the territory of being the frontman for a record company. What, then, justifies Hughes' claim to studio-hermitism?

“I like being at home,” he says. “I like feeding off of being in the studio, working one-on-one with people.”

Hughes works in his home, a home with a yard to maintain and a lot more space than he's used to having available. His forthcoming Slicker album, the product of much time spent in his studio/home, will be released in March.

“I wanted to sit down and do a record that was a little more live,” he says “less about glitchy programming and sound design, and more about seeing what I could actually write, and trying to worry more about doing records that are going to hold up in a few years.”

Hughes' music notoriously couples a dirty electronic style with organic vocals and instrumentation, and his new record is no exception. The record is extremely vocal-heavy and influenced, according to Hughes, by a lot of the jazz and soul albums he's been digging up lately. “I tend to get into something and then I'll buy every record and totally indulge myself,” he says. “Then I'll get on to something else but go back to it in little pieces.”

A vacuum starts up behind the bar and stirs panic in the air. There is a pause in the dialogue. His eyes widen inquiringly. Our brains fill with the sound; sucked bar carpet noises replace the lobe of my brain in charge of maintaining a guise of witty dialouge. I raise the tape recorder unflinchingly towards his mouth like an airplane spoon delayed, mid-air, about to drop with all its passengers in it.

“You've worked on some soundtracks,” I somehow come up with. “What is that process like? Does the way you work differ knowing your result will supplement a film, rather than stand alone as the main event?”

“It's a lot easier,” he says, “It's just filling in the blanks … it's the difference between working at home and being your own boss and going into work and doing a project for your boss. One's about pleasing someone and making it work for the film and the other's about pleasing yourself which can be so much more complicated.”

Hughes' process as a musician is one that thrives off introspection as much as it does off collaboration. When asked when the music “happens” for him - as he's writing it, recording, releasing, or performing - Hughes is quick to assign his home as the site of the music's “making.”

“I don't feel like a performer as much as I feel like a songwriter. When I make a record I feel like my part is done. I've written it. I've recorded it. What I could take live as a performance wouldn't do as much for me. With electronic music I feel guilty, I feel like I'm almost cheating the audience. I don't want to go up somewhere and open a laptop and just hit the space bar. It's boring to me.”

Having been present at a few too many shows in which the performers flaunt the minimal action of their index fingers as the main attraction, where the performers themselves look bored in a stoic, self-important kind of way while audience members take turns shouting a snickering “Hey, turn up the art!”, I find this sort of self-awareness as a performer remarkable in Hughes. He doesn't want to bore anyone.

“Boring, huh?” I ask.

We forget about the recording device. We are, at the moment, having a candid conversation without overt self-concious tendencies. We are not boring.

“Actually the few times I did play live, I had a lot of fun,” he says. He's quick to dispel my assertion that he doesn't see music as a performative art. “It's just not my priority. I think it'd be interesting, especially on the new record to see what it looked like live. If I could get the people together that worked on the record.”

Hughes' forthcoming Slicker record has been such a product of collaboration that live performance may lie somewhere in the future this time around. All the jazz albums he's been digging up have increased his interest in performance lately. The new album has been heavily influenced by jazz and many of the musicians that have played on the records are, according to Hughes, great performers: Dan Boadi of Ghanatta, as well as Wendell Harrison and Phil Ranelin of Tribe, to name a few.

“These guys played live music their whole life. They would crush me.” He pauses. “As an observer I'd like to see all those people together, see what it would be like.”

“And, what? You just happen to be on stage too?” I ask.

“Yeah,” he laughs, “I'll just be in the middle, conducting.”

title: please skill me

pages.html:
but I definitely have some fatal flaw that I can't dissolve. And it's keeping me from eating at restaurants, from buying those leather pants I walk past every day, even from paying my rent. It's keeping me from getting employed.

People say it's the market. People blame it on the weather. They blame it on how you dress when you drop off your résumé, they say it's got to do with the swinging economy and your use of to-be verbs. The excuses are florid and abundant, and can typically alleviate — for a few hours — the guilt of being a louse. But the dissatisfaction from short-term fixes and the discomfort from unpaid DSL bills had eventually driven me to the streets. I needed answers.

I've seen people walking around in the day with us unemployeds. They wear their little suits and charge lunch on their business credit cards. I've seen them smiling their salaried smiles, overflowing with health benefits and just so happy feeling valid. Examples:

Congressional representative: Judy Biggert.

President of the country: George Bush.

Host of the television series “The Today Show”: Katie Couric.

All of these high-profile jobs obviously exist, and are clearly taken. And I'm not bitter that my work ethic has not landed me one of these positions. But surely there are thousands of jobs that are less evident. I'd been idly dangling like a spider over the hell of job search engines for too long. It was time to push myself into some obscure vacancy with whatever force I could muster.


Victor.

My first stop was SushiSamba. Located in the Loop, it's a classy restaurant with a well-chiseled staff – in both the good-looking and well-chosen senses. The wide rooms are splashed with color, from orange light box tables to flickering reflections off pools of water. In order to accommodate its menu selection, featuring Japanese and Latin American cuisines, the restaurant has two kitchens. Since patrons can order a combination of plates, it is probable that their requests will come from both locations. It is the duty of the food expeditor to organize the preparation and delivery of all dishes served in the restaurant.

I have no restaurant experience. I cannot balance trays, I've been told I should be embarrassed by my customer service capabilities and I can't boast agility with sharp kitchen utensils. But I remember well squatting in the bushes playing G.I. Joe with my brother; I am an expert with a walkie-talkie.

I settled into a couch near the bar to wait for Victor, the lead food expeditor at SushiSamba. He didn't bring his walkie-talkie to the interview, but he promised me that he uses one. His post is tucked in the center of the restaurant, at the end of the sushi bar. A small cove speckled with post-it notes, it blends into the hubbub of the restaurant. I admired the fact that his position keeps him out of reach of disgruntled customers, but he assured me that the servers and hosts do a superb job of instilling in them a good mood.

Maybe it's some extra rum in the mojitos, or maybe the patrons truly believe there are sharks swimming in the pools of water under their tables. Victor came to Chicago three years ago from Mexico, and said the restaurant is always purring in both languages. Japanese is usually spoken among the Sushi chefs. I asked Victor if he ever thinks they are speaking about him, and before I could even finish releasing the question he blurted out a most certain “yes.” But since he has experience as both a server and a line cook, he knows the demands of each side, and can slip easily into a spot between them. He confessed he can't really make a mistake.

He assured me he loves his job.

The problem with restaurants is the same problem with dating: people always want you to already have experience, but they don't want to be patient enough to give you a chance. While I like the idea of skirting away from needy customers and hiding behind a jungle of sticky yellow papers with a two-way radio, I don't think I could handle upsetting a person swathed in white, carrying a blade the size of my leg — and the knowledge of how to use it.

(go to page 2)

Merle.

My skills at the Dewey Decimal system are definitely lacking. I have suffered so many library late fees that I probably have paid Merle's salary for the past two years, and my clumsiness always betrays me in the rudest of ways in the middle of the quiet rooms. But I have been a discerning reader for all of my literate life.

I needed to sign my name in the ledger in front of a security guard in order to get onto the elevator. There was another woman screening anyone who spilled onto the 9th floor lobby of the Harold Washington Library. She let me in to see Merle with a keycard. I didn't need to ask Merle any questions: she discussed her job with utmost pleasure for all of the 45 minutes we spent together. She hasn't read every book in the Chicago Public Library, but in order to decide which books land on the shelves, Merle puts on her best poker face and analyzes every book review she (and her clerks) can get her hands on. She critiques every publisher's catalogue, she combs through each publicity blurb.

When she finds under-publicized gems from obscure presses, Merle smiles with understated exhilaration. How she uncovers these hidden jewels in the midst of hundreds of thousands of books published each year, I know not. Diamonds in the rough tend to surface only in my wake; needles in haystacks prick me like I'm a pressurized blister. I sat across from her, imagining what would happen to a stack of papers that high if it were my desk. I had to sit on my hands just to keep myself from succumbing to the desire to fold gum in each corner.

Even though Merle decides which books are ordered for all branches of the library, those are only a portion of the books on the shelves. Because Merle makes sure all of the Clancy-Steele-Grishams are stocked, as well as the Britannica-Websters-McNallys, branch librarians are free to adjust the collection to the specific demographic of the surrounding neighborhood.

Merle confessed that she has an amazing record for book choosing.

She also told me that her job was “the best in the world.”

I remember the first book I read. It was small, purple, square, and I think it had to do with a sheep. But the first book I read that I actually enjoyed was about a girl with a ribbon around her neck. One day her man untied the ribbon, and her head fell off. I can't keep up with bestsellers lists, let alone predict them. And I don't think Chicago wants me picking out books with people's heads falling off.


Phyllis.

I've tried all the tricks: newspaper, coffee filters, etc., but whenever I attempt to clean a mirror I just make more smudges. I can't even enter a hotel bathroom without taking every mini-bar of soap and shoe shine kit, even though I don't shine my shoes. But, thanks to my military-influenced upbringing, I can fold a hospital corner like no one else.

Besides what I saw in Mission: Impossible, I had no idea what to expect of the Drake Hotel. We sat at a window overlooking Lake Michigan and discussed her responsibilities: Phyllis now reports to the lobby. She used to clean rooms after people left, but she explained that “the lobby is [her] hobby.” She's too social to work away from guests. Phyllis moves with ease, acknowledging each cluster of patrons with a friendly comment, slipping furtive punch lines to passing co-workers. I didn't even have to ask her opinion of her job, as her contentment is evident. She keeps the Drake's lobby like she keeps her own living room. A woman came up to her once, showing a skirt that had ripped all the way up the side. Phyllis took her into a private room and kindly stitched it up for her herself. I thought of the times I might enjoy mingling with guests, but then I thought of the times when I would want to take a seat myself in one of those big plushy chairs and let someone else clean the mirrors.

The Drake is the seat of international traffic. From highly recognized state officials to dateless prom attendants, the hotel welcomes all guests through lobby reporters like Phyllis. In the evenings, when the candles are lit in the lobby bar and a harpist is plucking Chopin, Phyllis slides into the Powder Room. A dim lounge lined with mirrors, it seemed to beg you to stay and chat. With hundreds of employees, the Drake constantly hosts events that continue to feed its reputation. If I worked there, I would give their reputation two months tops before it would take a plunge steeper than the side of the Sears Tower. Don't underestimate the power of one domino. (Or check this site, but don't say we didn't warn you. NSFW.)

 

John.

My stomach flips inside out when I think of what gravity would do to me from that high up. I can't even walk by the second story railing at the mall without getting nauseous. I know I said I could multi-task on my resume. I was exaggerating. But I do like working by myself.

I tried to play it cool by the edge. I held the camera and told him what to do in quick bursts, so that he couldn't detect the shaking in my voice. John and I met after he finished a day of working; he took me up to one of the highest balconies so that I could enjoy the view. John is a “journeyman window cleaner” for Service One, Inc. He climbs on rigs and swings from skyscrapers like Spiderman, except he also happens to be cleaning glass — and a lot of it. At night, even though he may close his eyes to go to sleep, he still sees windows. When he first accepted the job, “[he] had no clue on what [he] was in for.” As a kid, John remembers climbing his cousin's pine tree, sitting at the top and swaying in the breeze. Now, when he drives into the city (despite his family's teasing eyerolls), he proudly points out which spires he's dusted along the city's skyline.

Service One places its employees all around the city. Only extremely competent workers are allowed to work alone; John's boss told me that he's one of the best in the industry. Even though they are trained excessively, John confessed that tragedies do occur. The ropes can hold hundreds of pounds, but if they catch something sharp, they snap in a wink. Somehow I know that just as I would start to trust the rig, the thing would send me spiraling into the Kennedy. If I were to pursue this occupation there would be a new sign on the roadside: Keep your window wipers wiping.

Before this little escapade, I didn't even know these jobs existed. Now I know of even more jobs that are already taken. I can't fly from skyscrapers fearlessly polishing enormous panes of glass, I can't offer warm salutations to venerable global citizens, I can't select which published words will become available to the Chicago public, I can't coordinate the delivery of cold plates of sushi with hot plates of Peruvian beef. Fine. Victor, Merle, Phyllis, and John have their jobs.

I haven't even logged onto monster.com in three weeks.

Who needs a paycheck when there's unemployment?

seriously, what is that smell??




Yea, so I'm driving back from Joliet with a lady friend and we're about halfway home when this wall of smell hits my nose! It seriously smells like a two week old cadaver bathing in vinegar and immediately I always assume it's the other dude (person), so my head started to wonder. This girl just let one rip in front of me! I bet she tried to let one out silently and had no idea she was letting Satan out of her ass! Oh my god, I have to open the window! Should I ask her? No, I can't. How do you ask someone, “Did you just let go of your dignity? And if so, can you please open the window?” Shit, I can't ask her because I don't know her that well. That couldn't be the case because she told me she never farts in front of anyone. Holy shit! I bet you I farted without thinking about it! No, I would remember exhuming something that smelled this bad! It's got to be from the outside. But if it's from outside, does she think I farted? I don't get it. She looks like she doesn't smell a thing. There is an invisible fire entering this girl's nose and she isn't fazed one bit!? This girl is either super embarrassed or super human ! I am at the brink of tears and vomit and she looks like she's enjoying roses?? Maybe she can't smell? Some people are color blind or can't hear out of one ear, so maybe she can't smell. Wait…no, I remember her saying she doesn't like the smell of smoke! What the fuck is wrong with her? She had to have noticed why I opened the window. Holy shit this is awkward!! Jeez, it's been like three minutes and it's still not gone! Fuck it, “What the hell is that smell?” To which she replied, “I don't smell anything.” WHAT?? How the fuck do you not smell that?? It's starting to melt the epidermis layer of my skin and she doesn't notice it?? Wait…there is no way, I bet you ... ah, she DID fart! She is playing dumb! But her intonation wasn't awkward or reluctant? Maybe she isn't lying? Is it possible that she didn't smell anything and it stayed on my side? Aw, fuck it ... I don't really care.

pages.html:
technology:
camouflauge and coats















“He's mad,” said Kemp; “inhuman. He is pure selfishness. He thinks of nothing but his own advantage, his own safety. I have listened to such a story this morning of brutal self-seeking! He has wounded men. He will kill them unless we can prevent him. He will create a panic. Nothing can stop him.”
                                            - H.G. Wells, The Invisible Man

Invisibility has secured its place on the scientific vice list. The quest to attain invisibility, the entire discipline of alchemy and the Fountain of Youth: these are topics most often found in science fiction movies and novels. But these pursuits are not just for Trekkies anymore. While popular culture has categorized these ideas neatly into the History and the Sci-Fi Channels, they maintain their universal appeal by hinting at our own questions of humanity and immortality. What would happen in a world where any metal could be turned to gold? Do we really want to live forever? What aspects of ourselves would be revealed if we could go unseen?

Various attempts at providing the illusion of invisibility have popped up in nearly all aspects of culture. From the ninja adage to "Be one with your surroundings," to the development of optical cameras and reflectors, the science of invisibility seems to permeate our lives. The two techniques that we'll look at illustrate both the common sense and complex attempts at invisibility. You may or may not believe that they work, but you will not understand either of them.

Or at least, we don't.


Low Tech: Camouflage.

The most basic type of camouflage is worn on the battlefield, where concealment is good for obvious reasons. Conventional camouflage has two basic elements: color and pattern. The trick to this type of concealment is to color the material with dull hues that match the predominant colors of the surrounding environment. The pattern of the material is also critical. The point of the seemingly random pattern we see in camouflage clothing is to hide the contour of the body. The visually disruptive pattern actually helps your brain to connect the lines of the colored blotches with the lines of trees, ground, leaves and shadows.

As science defines the mental processes of perception when viewing camouflage, taken from this paper:

A number of psychologists studying visual perception investigated the accuracy of edge localization under conditions of varying blur and varying contrast. Research by Watt & Morgan, Mather and Morgan, Morgan et al. and Georgeson & Freeman clearly show that for blurred 1-dimensional edges there is a shift in perceived edge location away from the zero crossing. The magnitude of the shift increases with the increase in magnitude of both the edge blur and edge contrast. Their proposed model of the shift is based on non-linearity of perceived brightness, with the saturation function (1) where c is a constant.

We didn't understand it either.

Continuity is key in visually deciphering something. Imagine a stack of ten Legos. If all of the Legos are colored red, you perceive the pile as one unit. However, if the bottom five Legos are red, and the top five Legos are blue, you may perceive the pile as two separate units. We tend to recognize some things as a separate object if it has one continuous color, so a person who is wearing one single color is much more likely to stand out than a person wearing a jumble of colors. In the jungle (or any other environment), you perceive the jumble of colors in camouflage material as many small components of the surrounding foliage.

It is this strange habit of the brain that allows a person in camouflage to go undetected even though they are in plain sight. Once you have spotted a camouflaged person, they stand out, and it may seem odd that you didn't notice them earlier. This is because your brain is now processing the visual scene differently: it is looking for a single person. Makes you wonder ... why do you ninjas wear all black?


High Tech: The Personal Cloaking Device.

If you took a camera and put it on your back, and then hooked it up to a monitor that you held in front of you, people would be able to, in a sense, see right through you, right? Yes, but of course no one would actually say that you were invisible. It's more of a stupid trick that this author tried at parties as a desperate attempt to impress girls. Not only does it not work on women, but it doesn't make you anywhere near invisible. The next step is to find clothes that take the place of the camera and the monitor. What if your jacket, instead of just large amounts of alcohol, allowed people to see right through you?

This has been the goal of Susumu Tachi's team and their cloaking system. Unfortunately, however, Tachi's cloak (which is more like a shiny raincoat) is more gimmick than practical prototype. Nonetheless, from the right angle and under controlled conditions, the cloak seems to make the wearer some sort of ghost. A camera behind the wearer feeds the background images through a computer to a projector, which then paints them on the jacket as though it were a movie screen. The wearer appears translucent, so long as they are being viewed at the right angle and as long as it's not too bright outside.

Tachi, a professor of computer science and physics at Tokyo University and also the founder of the Virtual Reality Society of Japan, designed the coat using microscopic reflectors which act as the movie screen. They can even reflect images if the material is wrinkled. Tachi is uncertain of the technology's practical uses, but he likes to think that one day we will have glass bottom airplanes and surgeons who would be able to see through their hands while they are performing surgery. Or, and this is a real stretch, it just might be used to help those on the battlefield kill even more people. Everything has a military application.

Conclusion: The Next Step.

The invisible man, were he alive today, would have used his abilities for far more nefarious purposes.

“He's mad,” said Kemp; “inhuman. He is pure hornyness. He thinks of nothing but his own libido, his own urges. I have listened to such a story this morning of brutal male adolescents! He is an aroused man. He will photograph them unless we can prevent him. He will create a panic. Nothing can stop him.”
                                               R.U. Horny, “The Invisible Man Goes to the Locker Room”

Why do we really want to be invisible? Without trying to break this down into some kind of Freudian psycho-babble, I present this case study, the ultimate expression of invisibility.

title: intersection section

pages.html:
click to enlarge photo

any moron can review music or movies. it takes a special kind of genius to review an intersection.

Wandering about, or, perfecting the art of inconspicuous staring.

I spent two hours wandering around the intersection of Michigan Avenue and ... well, nothing, really. Just Michigan and the Chicago River. It's not even an intersection per se, but more a main thoroughfare on the south end of the Magnificent Mile. Just a street that passes over a river.

The underbelly, however, is what makes the intersection interesting. It's a maze of girders and metal and a few cross streets, most notably East Water Street, at which the world-famous Billy Goat Tavern resides. It's another world from the upper level of upscale shops and the seat of Chicago journalism, one where water drips from metal above and traffic drives through on a simple journey from point A to B, instead of the sightseeing tour buses and cars filled with people more interested in the shops and pedestrians, it seems, rather than driving.


What you need to know: Crossing the street.
Michigan Avenue at that particular intersection is a divided street, so you don't necessarily have to look both ways before crossing, just in one. But make sure you get that right. The area's notorious for taxis, as there's a popular U-turn/taxi waiting area right next to the river. While it's not as bad as New York, where a cabbie will hit you, back up, do it again and give you the finger the whole time, don't cross ‘em. They don't like that.

Since there's no cross streets on the above intersection, you're fine there. On the below one, however, there's a mess of cross- and feeder-streets, with girders galore. Columns to hold up the street above and all that. But almost no worries: there's very little traffic down there. But what there is does count, as much of it consists of deliveries for the Tribune.

Public service announcement: Don't get hit by a truck. The staff of 606 cares about you.


The Plaza of the Americas, or, a good space to sit.
Chicago is patriotic. It loves a good flag, especially its own. The four-star emblem is everywhere downtown, from a top a pole to the left sleeve of a police officer. And, of course, the flag and the city need to have their own mindless dedication to something no one looks at anymore: a three-times life-size sculpture of Benito Juarez, a former president of Mexico. What he's doing there, I don't know. The plaque only reads that it's “dedicated to the city of Chicago,” and that Juarez lived from 1806-1872. But it's also got a nice garden area. Sit and smell the roses for a minute. Then go across the street and go buy an electric bread slicer or something equally technological and worthless at Hammacher Schlemmer.


The Billy Goat “Cheeseborger” Tavern.
Trust me: You've heard of it. The Tavern has become an ubiquitous pop culture reference. Ever heard someone say “cheeseborger, cheeseborger” with a faux-Greek accent? How about “No Coke. Pepsi”? It's one of those things parents say to their kids without the kids knowing where it really came from. That was Saturday Night Live's takeoff on the Billy Goat Tavern.

Oh Bill Murray, you influenced millions before they even knew it.

The Tavern itself is so unassuming as to be near-invisible. I'd venture that most tourists passing by the Tribune building on the upper Michigan Avenue level don't know it exists. It was described to me by a writer at the Trib as “a journalist's hangout: out-of-the way enough, and loud enough so your conversations aren't overheard.”

The food's just that. Food. Nothing amazingly special. I was hoping the worker behind the counter would launch into a rendition of the classic SNL skit. But apparently they have a business to run, and I had to nod my head yes to the “Cheeseborger?” inquiry, then pick up my pre-filled Pepsi waiting by the register. It was a good burger, though.


The mainstay: Starbucks.
What fun modern thoroughfare would be complete without a Starbucks? You can choose from more than 30 varieties of coffees and from more than 20 types of teas! They'll even make your mocha with skim milk if you're a health nut! They also have cafe-type foodstuffs, like carrot cake and scones!

Get over it. It's just a Starbucks.

But there are some great newspaper machines next to it, where you can pick up the latest apartment finder index or the copy of the Pink Pages, if that's your thing. That's pretty much the best part about the Starbucks.






The Tribune Tower, and the stones in it.
Of course everyone knows about the embedded rocks in the side of the Trib building. The Great Wall of China, the Berlin Wall, Notre Dame Cathedral. Lots of stuff. There's a glut of classical and modern references made physical, as you can reach out and touch a piece of the Colosseum or the White House.

One caveat: Staring makes you look like an out-of-towner. What I wasn't expecting was the number of strange oblique looks I got while being a shameless tourist. It was as if I were tagging my gang turf instead of looking at a wall and writing on a clipboard. I guess the spirit of capitalism is so pervasive that stopping to appreciate is no longer in vogue, having fallen to the wayside for the ostensible purpose of Michigan Avenue: shopping. But knock yourself out.

No one appreciates culture anymore.

Architecturally, the Tribune Building is an imposing structure, jutting its Art Deco facade out of the riverfront. It represents the quintessential American goal of constant achievement, as only the first nine or so floors of the building hold the offices of the venerable Chicago Tribune, and the rest is residential. The goal, naturally, is to make enough in a paycheck to do all shopping, working and living in the same block of the Magnificent Mile. Personal living space. Sure would be nice to live there. You know, amazing building, great location, walking through the lobby of a major world-class newspaper to get home. Not too bad.

A broadcast booth for WGN radio is located on the corner. Make faces at talk radio personalities while they're on air; that alone is worth the trip.


Walgreens: The Pharmacy America Trusts When It's Convenient.
Right across the street from the Tribune Tower is, naturally, a Walgreens. I've never felt so high-class buying Q-Tips and Chef Boyardee. Granted, it was the most expensive can of ravioli I've ever purchased, but the location alone was worth it.

Bonus: the two guys fighting turf wars over who's allowed to sell StreetWise, Chicago's weekly newspaper to benefit the homeless, outside the doors. The one with the beard won. The other was relegated to selling outside the Starbucks a few doors down.


The lower loading dock.
The guys working here are more on par with the Beefeaters guarding British royalty than the average guard; they don't like jokes or surprises. I had legitimate business here once and, unwisely, tried to make small talk with the guard in the booth:

Me: “Hey, how's it going?”
Guard: ( deadpan ) “Yeah.”
Me: “Umm … I'm supposed to pick up a package here.”
Guard: ( deadpan ) “So is everybody else.”
Me: “Umm … so … here's my name.”
Guard: ( deadpan ) “Who's it from?”
Me: ( stumbling, thinking he wanted to know where I got my name ) “Umm … I was just told to pick it up.”

You get the picture. And this all happened pre-9/11, so this wasn't from Homeland Security. It was just the School of Surly Loading Dock Security Workers. Think of all the fun things you could do with them, though. Impersonating Tribune editors, umm, and doing some other stuff. It could be a great time.

Remember: the 606 staff has never encouraged law-breaking. In fact, if you do anything illegal or stupid, it's not our fault.

pages.html:
"THE KINDNESS OF STRANGERS"
OR
"THE LITTLE ATOM WHO COULD NOT"
 


Maps really aren’t that helpful. There’s just a bunch of geometric shapes, numbers, and names that randomly highlight sites with dots like stars in the sky. My editor had given me a task, and I needed to find my way to the site of Enrico Fermi's lab, where the first nuclear chain reactions were successfully achieved. Science has always held my fascination, and the lab’s achievement was a milestone for science and for history. The only maps I could locate, however, included an online Chicago Transit Authority system map and the one in the phone book. But these maps, as well as my sense of direction, were lacking, so I decided that if I wanted to get to the site of the first nuclear chain reaction I had to take it to the streets.

There are one million and one ways to travel from point A to point B. Every person in this city relates to their physical location differently from the next. My hope is to get as many maps of this city as I possibly can, and so I armed myself with a variety of pens and paper so people could locate their moods with their writing (mapping!) utensil. I was entirely reliant on everybody to get me to my destination. Would I get there?

Chicago often boasts of the grid system that manages its streets. The zero mark is at the intersection of State and Madison, and the site I wanted to go to today was 56 blocks south and an undetermined distance east from there. I needed a map, bringing me face-to-face with my original problem.

“Excuse me, do you know how to get to 56th and Ellis?” I inquired of the boy who joined me at the bus stop. Since we were standing at the same stop, I made the assumption that he was traveling to the same destination that I was and, therefore, knowledgeable about the area and the events occurring at the University of Chicago 50 years ago. Naturally.

“I don’t really know where that is, I’m not from around here,” was his simple response. I was not to be deterred by this evasion. He couldn’t get off that easily and I implored further into the tenuous associations of his mind. I badgered him to get my coveted directions. Instead, he went on a tangent on how to get to the Newberry library. “Yeah, I’d take the Red Line up there, and it’s only a few blocks from the station. South of Division, and it’s next to a park, umm, besides that, it might also be just north of State. You can’t really miss it,” he said.

Thanks a lot, I thought.

The bus arrived, dumping fumes that plumed onto the street. My friend with the backpack and I sat in opposite seats, signaling the end of our conversation. I was map-less. The boy wasn’t interested in devoting any more time to my quest, and it was evident that my time was up with him.

Six minutes passed till I arrived at my stop, when I shamefully displayed my ignorance of Chicago city buses, trying to get off by pushing on the doors too soon, which set off the alarm. I looked back towards the boy. I received an affirmative nod that I was on the right path. Or maybe it was a good-luck-I-don’t-really-know-where-I’m-sending-you kind of look. No turning back now.
The usual response when stopping people on the street and requesting a drawn map is a quarter-turn at the torso, maybe accompanied by a foot kick in the right direction if you’re lucky. Instead of my desired drawing, I get vague particulars: an ivy wall, next to a park, it’s across from the gas station, it’s south, north from here or there. How many fucking parks are in the city of Chicago? How ubiquitous is ivy on a wall? It grows all over the city. Ivy grows on the wall of my apartment building. They must know where I live.
 


Before my trip, I had only been down in Hyde Park once as a child when I went to the Museum of Science and Industry. Places as exotic as the museum can seem as far away as Sumatra when you’re little. I had no idea how I arrived there and you know, it really didn’t matter. My favorite part of the museum was the giant heart that you could walk through and see all the parts inside moving, pumping. The inner walls were a translucent, glowing membrane and I felt my arm could puncture the artery with one accidental gesture. It’s fascinating to me how this “mapping” of the heart made sense to me, and unbelievable now, knowing how blood and organs work together to coerce my nausea.

I interrupted more and more people traveling on foot in search for a comprehensible map. In choosing to forgo the safety of their cars, these pedestrians were just begging to be asked for directions. People that leave their arms unfolded from their chests or have an invitation within their smile, pace or stride: I can pin-point you a mile away. I can smell you coming with your profuse knowledge of urban planning. I will hunt you down.


(go to page 2)

The directions I collected got me to the University of Chicago campus. I found almost everyone that I accosted who attended the university knew of the site for the first nuclear chain reaction. It must be included as part of their orientation packet, along with, of course, all the accomplishments and successes accrued by fellow alumni.

The scientists at Fermi’s lab worked on The Manhattan Project beneath the football stadium on secret experiments as they raced to split the microscopic - to create chain reactions, to create the first nuclear bomb. Direction wasn’t outlined in concrete gridded blocks for them. The tension that mounted, the beating hearts inside chests as scientists scurried underground, working against the ticking of a clock counting down two inevitable conclusions - that they would discover the secret to nuclear power, or someone else would first. There were no precedents for their task at hand, no reference points, no landmarks, no maps. Some trust was there in gambling away the safety of the city for oblivion.

Sometimes moments hand us our options in closed fists, and by the very nature of curiosity, the thrill of the knots in our stomachs we listen to that quiet voice inside our head. The scientists got their necessary direction. Now I needed to find mine.

Over and over again I tried to ask for a drawn map to my location. What if I needed to get there again? Memory misshapes spoken directions, reducing the odds of ever finding my way there again. Conversations were regulated by a prescribed number of seconds, and then I’d be swatted away like a pesky fly. No one wanted to draw. They wanted theater, gesture and eloquence, but they didn’t want to draw a damn picture for me.

On my way home, I descended into the Red Line subway tunnel from the street. A quiet voice called from the middle step of a paralyzed escalator, “I’m having a heart attack.”

It echoed from his chest to a barely audible whisper. “I’m having a heart attack.” Another middle-aged man, well-built and with silver hair, changed direction to climb the stairs and descend down the escalator. He lifted the man up to bring him to street level. He offered assistance, his shoulder. That’s the key: He offered. Or, at least I assumed he did so as I stole my sideways glance. Turning, I continued with a clench and an ache. Something acidic singed my tongue …was that an ambulance I heard? Is it coming? The train collected us and before the doors shut, the man with the silvery hair slid in.

I watched the man with the silver hair ride the red line with me. More people filled the space between us, and eventually I didn’t see him anymore. That someone helped. I didn’t.

I found Fermi’s lab. But who cares? Find it yourself, without a map. I dare you.

 

The site? It’s situated around 56 blocks south from the loop and some number east. There’s pink construction paint on the sidewalk. There’s a Henry Moore sculpture that blocks a circular portion of the sun. A fuzzy snowball is lying by the curbside.

title: hopscotch

pages.html:
HOPSCOTCH

hop  your  way  through  seemingly
unrelated    tidbits   of    knowledge
(throwing     stones     unecessary)
 

enter

• Invisible ink is normally associated with childhood pranks and recess tricks. But when did it become a matter for the CIA? In an effort to become unclassified, documents from World War I written with invisible ink outlining various treatises – such as the formula for invisible ink and invisible photography – are now the subject of litigation. Well, classify this:

    Write your own invisible message using lemon juice heated with a little water. After writing on a piece of paper spread a little iodine over the writing. Think you're clever? Well, drop us a line.
  • “In the early days of the process of identification, the identity of a person was established through his signature . The invention of photography was a turning point in the history of this process. It is no less significant for criminology than the invention of the printing press is for literature. Photography made it possible for the first time to preserve permanent and unmistakable traces of a human being.”
                                                                        – Walter Benjamin, The Paris of the Second Empire in Baudelaire, 1938

  • Next time you're thinking about streaking in the Loop or expressing your gregarious and righteous self, be aware that you have a voyeur: Big Brother is watching. The public eye is sharper than ever before with the installation of several more security cameras in the Loop area of downtown Chicago. There are a good number of cameras functioning, divided into the usage categories of government, private, traffic and public domain. At least 10 exist solely for the purpose of monitoring traffic intersections. New York artist Dennis Beaubois employs theatrics to address the growing concern of surveillance on the streets of his home city. His art interacts with the cameras through the use of posters directed towards the cameras to communicate his concerns of identity and privacy.


  • Scientists in Britain are lobbying to build the world's most powerful matterscope. Unlike its archaic microscope counterpart, a matterscope bounces around neutrons that make the waves needed to create an image of individual atoms. The neutrons hurdle down a concrete tunnel one kilometer in length to gain the necessary speed. At $1.7 billion per scope, they better see something.


  • The next time the power goes out in the middle of the night and nature calls, rest assured that all public rooms such as bathrooms are marked with Braille, as required by law for public buildings. Braille illiterate, are ya? Just don't have an accident.

  • The Talking Book Center provides the free loan of recorded and Braille books and magazines, music scores in Braille and as well as recorded materials for residents of Chicago who are unable or have difficulty reading standard print materials because of visual or physical impairment.

  • Looking to increase security or have a little spying to do? Check out Chicago Spies and find products ranging from pepper spray to hidden cameras. It's your all-in-one spy shop depot.


  • Ever wish you could look through people's clothes walking down the street? X-rays have a higher frequency wave than visible light, which is why we don't see it during our daily lives. They can penetrate through skin and tissue – but not denser objects like bones and metal – making what lies beneath visible without peeling off our skin. Conventional photographic film is used because it causes the same chemical process as visible light. Doctors only use the negatives from the film to view our bones and organs.


  • You're leaving the house and you're through the door when a little nagging voice calls out, “Did you turn the coffee pot off?” Shit! No! Umm … maybe! Rushing upstairs, you prove that you turned it off. Oh, no! Now where are your keys?

    In only a few years, the Boston-based company Micro Optical will place their newly developed memory glasses on the market. The glasses contain a miniature television that transmits prerecorded messages that flash at you throughout the day. The images zoom at your eyes at 180 th of a second, a speed not consciously detectable. But the company claims that the glasses will improve memory by 50 percent. So, where are your keys now?

  • Citizens of Alaska, don't expect to see sunshine for the next few weeks. The sun officially went down November 18th and won't appear again ‘til January 23rd.


  • Dust mites, whose microscopic size allows them to feed on dead skin while remaining undetectable to the human eye, thrive in pillows and sheets. If you need an incentive to do laundry this week, visualize this microscopic meal while falling asleep as a mental exercise.


  • The left and right retinas of babies are not sufficiently developed enough to work together until about four months of age. Until that time, babies, like dogs, need high contrast images to make visual sense of their surroundings. Black and white patterns are said to work best.


  • The Chicago Harbor Lighthouse, the first lighthouse built on Lake Michigan, dates back to 1832 and is still functioning, but not open to the public.


  • In 1972, Harmony Wonder created a cartoon television series on a low budget. The Inviso-Team was composed of five superheroes that were never seen on screen, so they never had to been drawn. Later in the series, the Team developed the power to walk through solid matter, allowing the animation of doors opening and closing to be eliminated. But we're not sure the series even existed. E-mail the guy at the above link and ask him. Who knows? It may just be his attempt to justify his existence.


  • A German restaurant chain in Berlin and Cologne, Unsicht-Bar (achtung: this page is in German), serves meals that are concealed from patrons' view. All customers are blindfolded and forced to focus on their other senses while eating. The concept was created by the Organization of the Blind and People with Poor Eyesight. More than two-thirds of the staff is visually impaired.


  • Astigmatism is defined as an uneven curvature of the eyeball's front surface, or cornea. Eyeballs are often assumed to be round like baseballs, but many eyes are actually more akin to footballs in shape. It is this oblong shape that can cause distorted vision in astigmatic eyeballs.


  • In 1933, Ralph Wiley, a college student working as an equipment washer in the Dow Chemical Laboratory, wasn't able to scrub off debris on a piece of glassware. What he actually discovered in the debris was a Saran film. The product of a chemical reaction, Saran films were found to seal out moisture and air and eventually were used to create Saran Wrap.

comments.text: Hotscotch was first developed by ancient Romans in the area that is now Great Britain.  Originally the "board" was as large as a football field - or larger.  The board was filled with obsticals in which training soldiers had to practice running through.  The purpose of this was to help the Roman fighters form balance so that they could kill with more accuracy and strength when on foot.  Local children quickly created their own modified version of the military excersize - which is similar to how it is still played today.  The oldest American form of the game has 10 sections with the final goal to enter into Heaven. Today hopscotch still aids in helping people improve thier physical balance.

pages.html:
BATTERY

Here's the scoop.
Pick an issue. Any issue. There are at least two sides to whatever you just mentioned - potty training your cat, that ugly car your neighbor just bought, whatever - and each can be argued. Our writers pick an interesting and pertinent topic, perform some exhaustive research, and give you their final product: the plus and minus polarity on the most charged elements of that issue.

This month, Chicago's Millennium Park.


Chicagoans can finally take a refreshing breath of air as Millennium Park nears its completion.

Near completion? If it would only be done.
How long have we been waiting for this park? How many years?

Hey, the park will be well worth the wait. It will introduce trees, gardens, acres of parkland, fountains, and sculpture.

Please, this project is $300 million in the hole,
four years past due, and it's still far from completion.
How much more wasted time and money can we sacrifice?

Are you kidding? The money is very well spent. So there are a few loopholes in construction and it's not done. The bottom line is that Millennium Park will be something for everyone to enjoy. It's so conveniently located and accessible, and all amenities that the park offers are free!

Yeah, it's located next to the financial district and the
million-dollar mile. I'll tell you what the bottom line is. It's
$4.8 million taken from the TIF fund that was promised
to the community, since at its expiration it releases any
unused money. It's only three more years ‘til the Central Loop
TIF will expire, and the money would have been redistributed
to public schools and community spaces. The depletion of
funds by Millennium Park's deficit deprives future
recipients of the original intent of the TIF: to give back
to the community.

The park should easily be able to replenish the money with the increase of tourist revenues! The money will never stop rolling in because people will be able to enjoy it year-round. With the refuge of parks and fountains in the summer, and the ice rink and heated bicycle parking facility in the winter, the activity will never cease.

Well, I've never known any Chicagoan to ever have
hidden out in the winter. That's what makes us
Chicagoans. My question is, what's with that egg?

You mean, the critically acclaimed Anish Kapoor sculpture? It's a fantastic addition to the city's already celebrated collection of public art.

That egg's gonna have better heat than
most Chicago housing. The chosen materials
require an elaborate heating system so it
doesn't crack in harsh Chicago winters.

But the cultural ramifications of having the Kapoor will be a far greater benefit. The artist has never created a public artwork in the United States before! Chicago will be the first for this internationally renowned artist!

Do we want artists that are environmentally
irresponsible? He wouldn't budge on the cold hard
fact that his materials will not weather Chicago's climate.
He's already shown he did not take any consideration
of the site that he was working with. Now, we have
to heat the damn egg so it doesn't snap? It seems to
me that it will blind more people in its reflection than perform
its ideal function: to reflect the skyline.

Well, he already troubleshot that issue. The curvature of the surface will deflect light away from drivers and park visitors.

In theory, sure, but it hasn't been tested. And don't even get me
started on the Frank Gehry amphitheater . Good lord, how many
garages are they going to have to bomb and rebuild, again?
More artists' and architects' egos that get in the way of
engineering these “dreams” in the real world. Poor or non-existent
communication between Gehry and the contractor let the
weight of the materials slip by in consideration on the first
garage that was built, which would have collapsed.
Shouldn't he, as an architect, have figured out these details?
Oh, I'm sorry, these practicalities must get in the way of the vision?
Come on, now.

My god, how many times do I have to explain to you the cultural assessment of this? By bringing Gehry in on a high-profile project, Chicago will be able to maintain its distinction as a center of architecture. Please correct me if I'm wrong, but one of the things Chicago is most proud of is its grand architecture. Not only is the Gehry amphitheater keeping us in the contemporary age, but it will lure architects and artists back to this city.

Were they ever gone?

comments.name: beanboy
comments.subject: Not that I'm complaining
comments.text: Clever piece.  I worked on the bean, and not to be picky but 1) there is no heating system in the sculpture, 2) stainless steel will have no problem with Chicago winters and 3) you don't really need to test whether a polished convex surface will send out burning light...it been established for about 4000 years (physics).  But that sounds snotty...there are some very good criticisms of the bean...but just not the ones you made.  Still, clever article.

pages.html:
here's how it works: we pick a day here in chicago and make note of the weather. our reporters scour the globe looking for cities with a similar forecast, and then pull an interesting random fact from that place. It's not a forecast, it's a backcast of useless information.
  
Fruita, Colorado
Temperature: 43 degrees
  Check your chicken. According to local custom, the citizens of Fruita, Colo. celebrate a headless chicken day every year. Mike the Headless Chicken made his mark in history when on September 10, 1945, his head was cut off. Decapitation, however, didn't stop this life; he lived on for another four years without his head.

Aloha, Oregon
Temperature: 43 degrees
  Another Story of the Never-ending Giant Animals that Pop Up in Podunk Towns: Starting from 182nd Avenue, turn onto OR-8, or Tulatin Valley Highway. Continue approximately 1.5 miles to arrive at 21250 SW 3, Tualatin Valley Highway, and see a giant anthropomorphic rabbit head atop a human body outside of Harvey Marine.

Lansing, Michigan
Temperature: 40 degrees
  Midwesterners find yet another use for corn. The Lonier's Shady Lodge Farm devised a way to incorporate crop circles and good old-fashioned fun: a corn maze (maize, get it?). Participants encounter a 10-acre field of corn supposedly in the shape of the renowned Scarecrow from The Wizard of Oz. World record for escaping from the maze: five minutes. Average: 4.8 hours, if you're from the boondocks.

Anywhere, Pennsylvania
Temperature: 40 degrees
  Be careful driving in Pennsylvania. According to state law, "Any motorist who sights a team of horses coming toward him must pull well off the road, cover his car with a blanket or canvas that blends with the countryside, and let the horses pass. If the horses appear skittish, the motorist must take his car apart, piece by piece, and hide it under the nearest bushes."

Madrid, Spain
Temperature: 48 degrees
  Death to Death! Warnings on packages of cigarettes are supposed to be a beneficial service, right? Marketers are now providing the perfect tool for ignorance: cigarette wrappers. New packaging enclosing these harsh health messages come in several different styles, including hearts, ducks and cannabis leaves. Some even mimic the packagaing of American brands Marlboro and Camel with witty "health" warnings imprinted on them.

pages.html:
sixosix recipes 
 
We raided the refrigerators of the apartment building of two of our staff members to see not only what you can learn about people from the food they keep around, but what they could possibly be making with the food they had. What did we learn?
1. These people must eat the sickest creations ever. Viva America!
2. Everyone loves Country Crock.
Here are the recipes that we created based on the food we found in our neighbors' refrigerators:
apartment 4C
"Mason-Dixon Cupcakes"
fridge contents:
6 containers hot sauce (assorted variety)
2 jars blackberry jam

comments: Seriously, this is way too easy to make fun of. I'm not even going to bother.

recipe difficulty rating (of 5): 2.5

recipe:
Empty the six containers of hot sauce into a small mixing bowl. Add the two jars of blackberry jam. Mix well. Pour mix into cupcake tin. Bake at 350 degrees for 20 minutes. Remove cupcakes. Get in your car and drive to Macon, Georgia. Hold a bake sale and prepare for the choir of "'sho is good".

apartment 4A
"Angry Roommate and Veggie Butter Sauce Casserole"
fridge contents:
1 tub margarine
1 container garden veggie cream cheese
1 jar tomato pasta sauce

title: astigmatic history

pages.html:
I carry my keys on a keychain of a bloody ear.

I bought the keychain in the torture chamber gift shop of a castle outside of London. After tourists file through the dim hallways full of terrible machines, past “the rack” and the tiny hole in the ground reserved for solitary confinement, they reach a room packed with things to buy: notecards of torture devices, posters matching crime to punishment, keychains mimicking dismembered body parts.

Popular culture has its way of translating tragedy into commodity. Hollywood blockbusters reach millions of viewers, yet the films inevitably embellish dialogue, adjust character roles and distort events. The films might expose new perspectives on historical catastrophes. S chindler's List focuses on the involvement of a businessman with the Holocaust. Saving Private Ryan concentrates on the search for a soldier in World War II. Titanic follows a young couple and their relationship on board and during the sinking of the ship. All of these high-revenue movies are based on “facts,” and all three of them feature an individual's story in order to make these overwhelming tragedies more personal. But this ploy, this toying with the viewer's emotions, persuades the viewer to sympathize with the character, to believe in them and in the “facts” that they might represent.

While these movies can promote a greater awareness of the past, they also instill movie-goers with a skewed and sensationalized perspective. The possibility of getting the story right is moot, especially since there is no “correct” telling. By narrowing the scope of an incomprehensible event, a more personalized presentation can whittle a large scale horror into a smaller, bite-size chunk — something accessible, and often (unfortunately), something more consumable. The reproduction of an event can slink away from accuracy in order to capitalize on the effect of the horror. This effect is made consumable, and the gift shop profits: T-shirts, wall posters, movie soundtracks, plastic figurines. We pull out our wallets, as I did for the bloody keychain.

Theodor Adorno argued that there could be no poetry after the Holocaust, that because of the supreme horror and inconceivable loss it was impossible to represent the cold truth of real events. Tim O'Brien has argued that the only way to possibly grasp the wretchedness of real catastrophe is to fictionalize it. These two opinions open a dialogue on the treatment of historical tragedy in fiction; but in this society, it's only a matter of time before that fiction is turned into an empty commodity.

The Western Electric Company had scheduled its employee picnic for Saturday, July 24, 1915. Five ships, one of which was the Eastland , were to transport employees and their families across Lake Michigan to Indiana. People were expecting a day of festivities. Instead, the Eastland rolled over while at dock at the Clark Street Bridge in the Chicago River. Two thousand five hundred people had already boarded, 844 of whom died in the capsizing. More passengers died in the Eastland disaster than in the sinking of the Titanic.

While previous generations seem to know of the Eastland disaster, at present, public awareness remains relatively minimal. Maybe we should televise a reenactment of the event, and let Fox TV cast their best sitcom actors as the main protagonists. Maybe we should contact the post office to highlight some of the key rescuers in their next stamp release, after they have finished running the Elvis line . We could organize a halftime show during a huge football game, and read off the names of the victims while cheerleaders solemnly bow their heads on the sidelines. Perhaps McDonald's wouldn't mind including a plastic replica of the Eastland in their Happy Meals , with detachable lifeboats so that kids can learn one way that the tragedy could have been avoided.

After the sinking of the Titanic , all ships were required to have more lifeboats in case of emergency. But the extra weight of the boats only added to the ship's instability. In a matter of seconds, the celebration on the Eastland's decks turned into disaster. The ship fell over and crashed into the Chicago River, throwing hundreds of passengers into the water. People hung from the railings, dangling like spiders. Passengers who couldn't swim dragged others down with them, desperate at any attempt of survival. As one survivor said, infants were floating like corks . (go to page 2)

(the north branch of the chicago river between lasalle and clark streets)


History books have more than one edition; facts are malleable. Facts are presumed to be secure, but in actuality they shirk being anchored, bobbing up and down, sinking quietly out of sight. How fiction is represented affects how we render fact in our consciousness. Tellers of stories have an agenda, which will in turn affect their telling. Their agenda might be educational. It might be founded in a desire to promote awareness, to prevent future generations from suffering similar pain — but it might also be to sell more hamburgers. History has traditionally been told by the victors, by the power-hungry, by the people who could afford to tell it. But the opinions of the victorious and the moneyed are not infallible. Objectivity is impossible, as all information must travel through a subject. High-commanding German officials would probably have portrayed World War II quite differently than Hollywood has. It has even been denied by some groups that the Holocaust ever happened. History is not linear.

The ship's upturned hull became a site of struggle, rescue, and grief. If you had been on the upper deck, you had a better chance of survival. But if you were on the lower decks, you wouldn't have made it. If they didn't drown, passengers below suffocated. Groups of people were found trapped in piles, with fingernail marks on the doorframes from their scratching to get out. Others were discovered speared by broken mirrors, toppled by mounds of luggage or pressed helpless beneath the piano.

The movie Titanic cost $200 million to make. In order to make the movie look real, a replica of the ship was built that stretched 775 feet in length. To simulate the sinking, the ship replica was dunked in a 17 million gallon tank of unheated water. James Dawson had been on board the real Titanic; in the movie his name is Jack. When Jack and Rose first kiss, it is in front of a real, not simulated, sunset. In postproduction of the movie, computer animators added fake breath to the victims. While the movie was being filmed off of the coast of Mexico, they had to make it look as if it was incredibly cold.

I went to see the Titanic (the movie). It was during the holidays, and I was one of the only people in the audience. I sat in the middle of the theater and had my own private showing. The special effects impressed me. The drama fed my imagination. I left feeling heavier than when I arrived, in disbelief of the magnitude of the tragedy, of the intensity of the suffering, and of the high price of matinee showings.

It's not necessarily a problem that I didn't walk away from the movie with a wealth of “facts” about the Titanic . Maybe that's not the point of a blockbuster production. Maybe it's entertainment. However this perspective sets up a false dichotomy that fiction is entertainment, and that history is truth. This doesn't leave room for the possibility that history itself contains elements of “fiction,” and that fiction contains elements of history. Entertainment includes elements of both fact and fiction, a position that can make millions for Hollywood and that can significantly influence the interpretation of past events. Under the guise of entertainment, popular culture can bastardize tragedy, melt it down and remold it into keychains.

Temporary morgues were set up to house the bodies until family members could identify the deceased. Rescuers fought to save as many victims as possible, but many times their attempts remained futile. Twenty-two entire families were wiped out in the event. Even if you knew how to swim, you might have been dragged down by someone who didn't. Parents clutched each other impatiently on shore as infants' bodies, blue and stiff, were carted away from the scene. Since there was no system of organization, the identification process of the dead spanned multiple days. Chicago fell into mourning, the raw stench of decaying carnage a constant reminder of the tragedy that could have been avoided. It was already known the Eastland listed in water. The additional lifeboats that added to its top-heavy state were never even used, because there was simply no time. But the mistakes that bred the catastrophe were never accounted for. Victim's families never received any compensation. The Eastland was turned back over, and shortly thereafter went back to sea.

I could argue that I have recounted this event truthfully, that I have researched facts and quoted real survivors. I could emphasize a desire to raise consciousness of this tragedy, a horror that has remained obscure to many of the general public. The Eastland did exist, and it did roll over in the Chicago River: this is a serious historical event that deserves comparable representation. I could also argue that I have exaggerated this story for effect, that I have fabricated details, and that I could have fictionalized character's names in order to harness readers and demand their emotional investment.

Keep your eyes peeled. Watch the marquees around the city: the Eastland disaster might be the next big blockbuster. This tragedy is ripe for further exploitation. (back to page one)
