title: don't talk to...

pages.html:
The nice thing about living in the city is that I get to take the el to and from work every day.

The el, if you really think about it, is an amazing and interesting environment. The oddest thing is that much of the time you are riding with the same group of people but you never say a word to them.

Most people who ride the train get into a routine when it comes to their commute, standing in the exact same spot on the platform everyday, at the same time, getting on just about the same car, and sometimes entering in the same door each and every time. The rider usually has a preference as to where the best seats or standing spots are as well.

Because I am guilty of this pattern, there are a handful of people who I see a few times throughout the week, both to and from work. We make eye contact – a little acknowledgement of one another – and we are on the way. But there is a huge catch: I never, ever speak to these people because they are, in fact, strangers.

The messed up part is that we already have some elements of our lives in common. Generally, we reside in the same neighborhood, commuting to and from work in the same fashion each day, and we probably work within a few blocks of one another. Yet we are total strangers with the exception of the eye-contact-hello.

Sometimes, one of the regulars doesn't appear for a while. Maybe they moved to a new apartment, got a shift change or even found a new job. Normally, this missing person goes unnoticed, until one day a few weeks later, they hop on at their regular stop at the regular time like nothing happened; it is then that you realize, “Hey … I haven't seen her or him in a while,”. There's the eye contact, and then an almost a sigh of relief. I think about asking them where they've been, but I can't. I don't know this person.

This entire phenomenon is like riding in a carpool, but never speaking with any of the other passengers. That's unheard of, and yet the same practice is totally acceptable on the el.

The worst is when an attractive somebody of the opposite sex jumps into the routine. I see this person more times in a week than I see some of my friends, and yet I don't know their name, what they'd order at a bar or anything else. Hell, I spend more time with this stranger than my parents. And I can't talk to them, because a) I don't know them and b) there is definitely no hitting on people on the el.

I have been in awkward situations three times because of all this.

First, there was the time I was walking down a very busy Michigan Avenue during the holiday shopping season. There were about a million people there, all hurrying from one store to another while I, cursing the suburbanites for invading my Michigan Avenue, yet thanking them in the same breath for helping stimulate the Chicago economy, was just trying not to hit anyone with my bags. I saw a break in the pedestrian traffic and skittered to the left side of the sidewalk.

I looked up and there she was: one of my el friends. Only I was so preoccupied with where I was going next that I thought she was someone I was supposed to know. I slowed down and stared at her, probably looking like a creep from her perspective, but then she stared right back at me. I don't think who I was registered with her either. Five steps later we were past one another, and I was asking myself, “Who the hell was that,”? I thought maybe I should be polite and go back to say hello and then it clicked: she rides home from work with me a few times a week. It would've been nice to say hello to my el friend, but we can't talk on the el, so why would we talk in any other public setting?

There was the time when some friends and I were out at a tavern having a few beers. The place was packed, and the wait to get served by the bartender seemed like an eternity. It was my turn to buy a round, so I made my way up to the bar and stood there. I have enough trouble getting women to notice me, and now I have to do this with a bartender? Life is not fair. As I waited, I was glancing around the bar to see if I knew anyone in the joint. Nope. I looked straight ahead and saw this girl, standing directly across from me on the other side of the bar, staring in my direction, dumbfounded. Another co-rider. I peered back and we gave the eye-contact-acknowledgement that substitutes a hello on the el. I found myself confused. Can I go talk to her? Is that against the rules? What if she has no idea what I'm talking about? Yes, she will definitely think I am crazy. No way am I going to talk to her. She doesn't even recognize me.

I walked back over to my friends and forgot about what had just happened. It was probably better that I didn't talk to her; it would have taken away the mystery that is our “relationship” on the el, if you can even call it that. And like I've already said, you can't talk to people you know from the el.

The last incident was the granddaddy of them all. I went to a party at my friend's girlfriend's house, and guess who her roommate was? Yes, the theme here is recurring. She was one of the riders on my el. Holy shit. When we were introduced, she recognized me too, and she was the one who asked if we ride the el together and if I recognized her. We jabbered back and forth for a bit about funny things that have happened during our commutes – yes, that is kind of a lame topic of conversation – and the whole time I was trying to play it cool because I knew I'd probably see her again on the el and I don't want that to be weird. We wrapped up the discussion and went our separate ways to mingle with others at the party. That was painless, right?

Well, the next day my friend who had invited me to the party gave me the impression that the girl thought I was a weirdo. She's probably right, but I swear I didn't say anything too crazy. I was trying to play it cool, man … but come to think of it, I did have about nine cocktails before we were introduced. Oops.

The next time I saw her on the train, we were across the car from one another and there was the eye contact and the recognition. Then came a weird look from her before she glanced down and never looked back for the remainder of the ride. It felt kind of awkward.

This was the defining moment when I finally understood why the rule is that strangers who ride the el together, even every day, just don't talk. While it would be fun and interesting and friends would be made and the commute would be livelier, there is an odd sense of camaraderie and uncertainty that comes along with those other familiar riders. The strangers are silently recognized as friends and acquaintances, yet the fact that they, as people, are totally unknown makes the prospect of a verbal friendship almost undesirable, as the mystery of who this person actually is would disappear. You are friends because you ride together so often and yet there are the unknowns that should never and will never be explained.

It's the el, and there's no talking allowed.

title: technology

pages.html:
That night was the celebration of my friends' and my very own birthday, and we decided to spend it on the rocky shores of Lake Michigan .

I was drunk. I admit it. We all were. Being the people that we are, we had the insight, the vision – no, the genius, to record the whole evening on videotape. You know, in case we came across the meaning of life , or some “truth” equally as useful, and we wanted to share it with world.

Encoded on those tapes were faces, friends, places, stories and, due to our lack of thumb agility and the confusing placement of certain red buttons, these tapes all include the time and events in between. And by “in between,” I mean events that happened not during the parts of the night that I actually remember. The following morning, despite the nagging and ever-growing pain in my head, I crawled over to the camera to discover it had recorded multiple hours of debauchery. How was this possible? Even if we had recorded every inane situation from the night before, which we had, we weren't at it for a very long time, right? Time code doesn't lie .

You've heard it before. When you are sitting with someone you like, time seems to pass very quickly. The converse of this is also true: If you are with someone you don't particularly enjoy, time will seem to stand still. Perhaps it was the company, or perhaps it was the large amounts of alcohol, but either way, what I did manage to remember from the evening seemed to pass by in the blink of an eye.

The videotape told me otherwise. Why the hell is time out to get us? Why does it insist on affecting us in such different ways, allowing us to measure it differently in a certain context? It's a simple question with a complicated answer, so let's just start with this: How in the hell do we measure this worldwide convention, this mistress of memory, time?

Low Tech: Rotation of the Earth

It seems simple, right? There are 24 hours in a day because that is how many hours it takes for the earth to rotate on its axis.

This statement is wrong . A flat-out lie. Instead of correcting it, we have just invented cover-ups, hence leap years . Being that we just had a leap day and that I, myself, was born on a leap day, let me explain.

In all of this discussion, remember the sun is time's inadvertent corrupter. Not since Superman 4 has the sun been a source of this much misfortune. When the earth spins on its axis, we calculate a full rotation by watching the sun; this is estimated to be 24 hours. The problem with this estimation is that while the earth was rotating on its axis, it was also following its orbital path around the sun. Simply, we were at point A when we started the rotation and we are at point B when finished. That difference in position is about 1 degree of our orbital path, equal to about 4 minutes. Confused?

Look up at the stars. Pick one . If you were to locate it in the sky, start a stopwatch and didn't stop until that same star was in the very same location the following night, your stopwatch would read 24 hours and 4 minutes. That's because we are not orbiting around the rest of the stars, just one and we call it the sun. If you're still confused , too bad. We're moving on.

So on to the next myth to debunk: that it takes 365 days to orbit the earth. If you watch the stars instead of the sun, you'll see that it takes 365.242199 days to orbit the sun. If looking at the sun is making our time calculation wrong, why do we do it?

Unless you're one of the idiots who went out and bought a star so they would name it after you, what have the stars ever done for you? Now, what has the sun ever done for you? In fact, the sun has done a lot. You regulate your life by it. Assuming you're not a vampire, you more or less rise with the sun to start your day and settle down as it sets. Again, more or less, people. I know all about drinking and how it destroys this sentence.

Because of humanity's link to the sun, we use it to tell what is called civil time. But what about those extra 4 minutes every day? Quick calculations: A year is really 365.242199 days. If we add an extra day every four years, then it gives civil time an average of 365.25 days to orbit the sun. Pretty damn close, even for government work. It gets better, and it takes a man born on leap year to expose this one.

Look back in your calendars to the year 1900 . You'll see there was no leap day that year. But why? It is a year divisible by four, right? Well, even if your math skills do not disappoint, there is another rule that helps civil time keep pace with reality. There is only a leap year at the beginning of centuries if that year is divisible by 400. Yes, 2000 had it but not 1900, or 1800 for that matter. What this does is bring the year average for civil time to an astounding close 365.2425 days a year.

So we've exposed humanity's affinity to the sun and shown our clever little tricks of making time fit into our need to bask in the rays of our closest star. But we've also shown how it is still imprecise. Among other imperfections, the earth's rotation is slowing down. But that's a whole other story. So how are you ever expected to be on time? What about all those devices that need accurate-to-the-millisecond time stamps, like astronauts or even the damn phone companies? How do they keep time?

High Tech: Atomic Clocks

You've seen them in the The Sharper Image catalog, the precision clocks that tell the most accurate time. And at the low low price of only $49.95. Don't be misguided; this isn't an atomic clock. Read the fine print. These clocks actually just tune into the U.S. Atomic Clock's WWVB radio signal in Colorado . To explain, let's start with what the hell an atomic clock is in the first place.

Like many discoveries in the world, the invention of the atomic clock is a little arcane. For our purposes, we are not going to question the boring lives of some people and their pursuit of strange, but useful, technologies.

With that said, this is how it works: Scientists take a tube and fill it with cesium atoms. They heat up those atoms and then, using a magnet, run a frequency through them. At a specific frequency, cesium atoms change their electric state at an impressive rate of one pulse per second. An analogy: If I took a whole bunch of fat kids and gave them all enough food – just the right amount of food, mind you – that they all began throwing up at the rate of one upchuck per second, then I'd be a sick asshole. But you get the picture.

There are a number of different elements that have this wonderful phenomenon, but the cesium atom has the most long-time accuracy, millions of times more accurate than staring at the sun. So we have clocks now that won't become slow or go too fast, but what about that whole rotation-of-the-earth situation? Glad you asked.

Because the atomic time is exact and precise, we can figure out the difference exactly between atomic time and solar time: It's about 0.07 seconds a year. But remember that other story I told you about how the earth's rotation is slowing down. It's true. It is slowing down at a rate of 0.02 seconds a year. Add it up, kiddies . This means the atomic clock is off from our idea of the sun-based time by 0.09 seconds every single year. Enter the leap second.

Every year, since the atomic clock became the standard means of time measurement in the United States , we have to add 1 millisecond to the atomic clock to keep it in line with solar time. The reason for this is obvious: it's a hell of a lot easier to adjust a clock that we build than to fix the rotation of the earth. But in the end, even our most accurate of time telling devices is still subjugated to our need to enjoy the sun and its cancerous UV rays.

Don't forget those “atomic clocks” from The Sharper Image. The U.S. government broadcasts from Colorado on radio waves the exact time that the U.S. Naval atomic clock is displaying. The Sharper Image clock is always listening for that radio signal and adjusting itself accordingly.

Conclusion:

All we've done here is present the case that, despite our best technological efforts, time really is subjective. Or as some famous guy once said, relative . I think his name was Al.

I guess it brings me back to that night that we recorded every drunken moment, worthy and unworthy alike. Time, which I've always thought of as an objective convention, was really subjective that night, at least to me. But when you really look at it, time is and always has been subjective. Your time is really what you make of it.

title: BYOB

pages.html:
Let's face it. The allure of a motorcycle show is like a black hole:
too dense to escape.

On Feb. 9, 2004, I attended the annual World International Motorcycle Show with the same high expectations one might carry into a NASCAR event, WWF wrestling, or a monster-truck bash. I knew what I wanted to see, and I knew who I wanted to be surrounded by. I dreamt of crowds of bearded men in black leather chaps, older women with confederate flag tank-tops and fake-breasted women displaying their thongs and the newest hot rods in one fell swoop.

It appears that I was not the only one with these aspirations showing up at the motorcycle show. A slew of decidedly non-trashy onlookers took up quite a lot of space at the event, and I blended right into the crowd. In fact, it seemed we nearly outnumbered the people that we had come to see. I had failed to take into consideration that a convention, even a motorcycle convention, is still a convention: An event that families flock to in order to spend quality time together, even if the main attraction is the other spectators. next >>

title: white noise

pages.html:
Isaac Newton measured it. Albert Einstein questioned it. Kurt Vonnegut forecast fluctuations in it. Yet, we still have no answers as to its nature and origin.

White traditionally symbolizes purity and cleanliness. 606 guest photographer Christine Taylor took the concept of "white" and stood it on its head, sometimes literally. Using the force of gravity as a jumping-off point, Taylor shows the interplay between the human body and common household objects.

title: asphalt

pages.html:
Cows get mad cow disease by eating the flesh of their own kind.

I remember the day I stopped eating meat. I was 15 and I was eating a late lunch at Burger King. I had ordered a Whopper not because I needed a sandwich that large but because I despised the term Whopper Junior. It was a Saturday, the end of October. I had on red pants. Maybe it was the color of my clothing or maybe it was the poor cooking job, but after one gaping crescent bite in the side of the burger, my stomach cried mutiny and my tongue ejected the unwanted mouthful. The fleshy strings of the meat patty looked remarkably like what I knew the inside of my leg looked like, and I couldn't do it anymore. I made a firm decision that from that day on, I could not ingest anything that had previously owned a set of eyeballs.

Hardly a day goes by without someone asking me why I'm vegetarian. Almost immediately, the person will begin their best to persuade me to eat animal flesh again, as if I am the one who has gone mad. To convince me, they kindly remind me how much I'm missing. Oh, the chicken Marsala! Oh, the Thanksgiving turkey! Oh, how it falls off the bone! Most of these people can't see the futility of their efforts to save my soul from the meatless anguish it must be suffering—which is too bad since the reasoning behind my food choices is not necessarily vegetarian-specific.

Anyone can become more aware of the food they consume. Perhaps you decide you will win a place in heaven by choosing to eat only the decomposing fruit that has naturally fallen from trees. Or maybe you will only find satisfaction choosing to eat onion rings fried in the lard of pigs raised west of the Mississippi River. The point isn't exactly what you eat; it's why you eat it .

Themed parties seem to saturate the social scene these days: you've got your James Bond parties, your ‘80s metal parties, your Dante's Inferno parties. However, I recently heard of a party being sponsored by an organization called THONG —Topless Humans Organized for Natural Genetics. The theme, cape and thong, seemed somewhat up to interpretation, but still representative of an organization with a purpose. Electronic rumors of locally grown food, body painting, and organic beer had been dribbling into my inbox throughout the week, leaking into my curiosity.

I walked into the party with a skepticism that sits on my shoulder like a parrot, and squawks in my ear whenever I see the word “free” in advertising or listen to a Bush speech. Skepticism took a liking to me in college, when students were scraping for causes to cling to , and it's followed me ever since. I can't seem to get rid of it. Sometimes I clamp its beak shut with a rubber band and join the progressive bandwagon; other times I let it call those voices out. I could feel its claws pinching me lightly through my makeshift cape.

Clusters of people wearing combinations of capes, thongs, neither and both lined the perimeter of the room. A sample table promoting self-sustainability featured foods grown around the neighborhood. A Chicago resident had fermented her own wine, and garlic and egg sauce over rhubarb impressed the lot. Despite the uncooperative Chicago climate and limited amount of space, she had found a way to provide for herself. Another station set organic food next to modified food, asking tasters to compare the differences. The atmosphere, a kind of sensory circus, seemed saturated with the group's message. Thonged moderators swirled paint onto partygoer's exposed skin and brushed red Xs over their mouths. The gallery's wood floor pulsed as people jumped to music played by a group of interactive musicians dressed as fruits and vegetables. Chants against hamburgers, Kraft macaroni and cheese and Ronald Reagan bounced between the walls.

go to page 2 >>

I wobbled across the room to find space to make sense of the chaos, trying to steer clear of stray body parts and dancing produce. The informative tables, the inclusive band, the protests against modified food — I may have stopped eating meat, but maybe that wasn't enough. I swiveled my head and straightened my back, a call for attention to my day to day habits. What had I been doing, going to Jewel and filling my basket with Preferred Card specials, allowing corporate pricing to dictate my food purchasing decisions? Buying organic was a way for me to take charge of my life, to influence the ebb and flow of the food market and international trade. Why should I support the injection of toxic chemicals into food that I put into my body? Why should I buy products that are clearly hazardous to my health and to the environment? I took a cleansing breath and decided to turn a new leaf in my life, a meaningful, green, organically grown leaf. I only needed a glass of organic beer to toast in my new lifestyle and solidify my stance.

With my new found hope for the future, I pulled out a dollar for a beer and thrust it proudly across the drink table.

They passed me a cold can of Pabst Blue Ribbon.

Organic farms have higher standards than non-organic farms . Non-natural pesticides and fertilizers are not used on organic food, making organic food free from toxins that might be found on non-organic food. By choosing all organic food I can improve my health, but I can also make a serious impact on the future of the environment, as organic codes are more ecologically friendly. While organic foods used to be sold only by specific grocers, they are much more accessible now. Walking down the aisle at most supermarkets, I can find organic products cuddling up right next to their non-organic counterparts. My decision rests within a six-inch span: save the environment and my health or support hazardous chemicals.

I had tried making organic choices before. I switched from plain pasta noodles to organic whole wheat pasta noodles, from baby spinach to organic baby spinach. My cabinets became their own ad campaign, scowling disdainfully at my roommate's environmentally destructive choices. Organic broccoli, organic bread, organic sugar came into my apartment in reusable canvas grocery bags. I brushed my teeth with all natural paste, and rolled my underarms with all natural deodorant. As part of a macroscopic plan, my microscopic decisions seemed to make ripples. I began to feel connected, active, responsible.

Sipping on an organic soy latte, I scooted into my desk and clicked onto Internet-based international news. The warm latte coated my throat, a perfect blend of subtle vanilla and creamy espresso. Out of curiosity, I began to trace our country's imports and exports, noting enviously that my food travels more than I do. Bananas from the Dominican Republic. Coffee from Kenya. Soy from Brazil.

I sunk beneath a wave of guilt, not unlike that leftover from Catholic grade school.

Soy from Brazil.

Brazil : in response to the growing demand for soy around the world, the Amazon rainforest suffers from a massive increase in deforestation as Brazil clears land for soybean farms

I looked at my Organic Vanilla Soy Latte, for which another section of Brazilian rainforest had perished. The problem with having forward set eyes, as all humans do, is that I can't see in more than one direction at once. While I was focusing on milk choice in the line at the coffee shop, my decision fed into a much larger problem that I had no idea existed.

Maybe the spinach I bought came from a farm that overworked its migrant workers, or maybe it used farm equipment that had not been checked for safety in 30 years. Maybe the toothpaste I used had been transported by the distributor in a vehicle that had been filled at a Shell station, who is responsible for enormous oil spills in Nigeria. Maybe the package from the whole-wheat pasta I have will be ignored by the recycling plant and buried into the nearest landfill where it will create toxic fumes.

Sipping on my decidedly non-organic PBR, I circled the gallery like a shark, slowly and deliberately, asking partygoers their reasons for costuming.

“THONG—I can't remember exactly what it stands for, but it's an organization that's been around for awhile trying to spread the word and educate people about what's out there for you organically. I'm just here supporting the cause and supporting the education.”

“Some people would just call this a silly expression of rebellion. I think that what's happening visually is actually a very poignant expression of a different point of view, and a different vision, where people are individuals, and people have freedom to make decisions, people are also free to know, and to be informed, to make decisions about what type of media, what type of food they want to consume.”

“I hope that this party will make people realize that it's ok to dress up funny, or dress up sexy, or interact with people on various levels.”

All attention moved to the corner of the room, where a performance was unfolding. A group of people wearing strips of white fabric passed a microphone among themselves, and a quickly paced call and response session flew from the speakers to the crowd. I stood amidst the screaming spectators, tiptoeing as if it were my height that was keeping me from understanding what was happening. A beige canvas tent with a single slit down the front began to shake, and suddenly a man began to tumble out of its mouth. Covered in an oozing white film, he rolled onto the floor, playing the part of an overgrown newborn. Several of the crowd took what appeared to be sugar and tossed it onto his placenta covered skin.

I turned inquisitively to the person standing next to me.

A middle aged man, proudly sporting a plain black cape and thong, sunglasses, and a hat, hunched forward to sip on his Busch Light. We were standing near the edge of the birth scene, which happened to be the loudest and smokiest part of the party. He seemed to be into the performance, and definitely into the theme.

“We are all kind of products of the food we eat—these are our bodies, this is what it looks like, and we can certainly be comfortable with that….it's just about body awareness,…an acceptance of what you are,” he said.

I sat back on my heels. While his interpretation seemed to have a certain amount of attractive idealism, there must be a point where this argument falls short. Two people might eat identical meals, but to assume that their bodies would process the food in exactly the same way is a gross oversimplification. We turned back to the performance. “Rooooon-ald. Reaaaaaaaagan.”

The movement of the hand from one's plate to one's mouth does not require steadfast concentration. This motion has been part of our daily routine for nearly all of our lives. Stopping our hands mid-arc, for reasons other than a loose hair or an intruding bug in our food, might be too ambitious a task for the empty-stomached. But the information behind the food we put into our bodies might give us ammunition against our consciences next time we choose broccoli that is twice as expensive as the next bunch.

I scanned the room, taking a last glance at the remnants of a good cause. It was two o'clock in the morning, and a giant carrot was swaying between a person in street clothes and a person in a thong. The food had run out hours ago, the cheap beer cans lay collected along the floorboards like the crushed, empty shells of dead insects. I pulled my cape tightly around my shoulders, the warmth of the room escaping with each drifting thonger.

Some people choose to eat all organic products to save the environment. Some people choose to eat vegetarian to save the animals. Perhaps they are well informed of the international food market, perhaps not. Personally, I do what makes sense in my head. The phrase “you are what you eat” might better be expanded to include that “you are what you choose to care about what you know about what you eat.”

pages.html:
When I want popcorn , I want to press one button that's labeled “popcorn”. There are just some foods you should labor over, but popcorn is not one of them. There is enough inconvenience in everyday existence to justify the convenience of the one-button rule for popcorn.

If I'm feeling ambitious, I will put a tomato in the microwave for 45 minutes. I can be making my own sun-dried tomatoes while I'm watching my favorite re-runs of M*A*S*H. If I'm in the mood for a spectacle, I'll stay in the kitchen with my face pressed up against the microwave's glass door, watching the expansion of a marshmallow as it puffs in and out like a little lung.

The microwave knows no limits, and renders all other kitchen appliances obsolete. If you want to waste your time hovering over a conventional oven like a 19th century housewife suffering from hysteria or diphtheria, fine. I don't have the time.

When I was a kid, reheating food in my parents' kitchen, I would ask, “ How long should I reheat this food ?” And they would shout over their shoulders, “Nuke it for 20!”

Nuke it for 20. Nuke, as in nuclear. Nuclear bomb, nuclear family, nuclear catastrophe.

It's in the name. Microwaves use micro-waves of radiation to cook food. Maybe the Soviet Union was on to something when they banned microwaves in 1976. But we were too preoccupied with the nuclear arms race to notice that we were eating radioactive potatoes and electrically charged Lean Cuisine. Ninety percent of American homes have a microwave as a part of its nuclear unit.

Since nursing babies has fallen out of fashion, along with crimped hair and stretch pants, babies' bottles are warmed in the microwave. Researchers (not just commie pinko researchers) have claimed that microwaved milk is a serious heath hazard. But keypad-cooking habits are still very much in vogue. When we all get cancer in a few decades, and we need radiation treatment, maybe we'll wish we all didn't OD on it earlier in life.

RADIATION = SPREADING ENERGY WITH ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES
 
Radiation, as defined by physics terminology, is "the electromagnetic waves emitted by the atoms and molecules of a radioactive substance as a result of nuclear decay." Radiation causes ionization, which is what occurs when a neutral atom gains or loses electrons. In simpler terms, a microwave oven decays and changes the molecular structure of the food by the process of radiation. Had the manufacturers accurately called them "radiation ovens", it's doubtful they would have ever sold one, but that's exactly what a microwave oven is.

pages.html:
Medium Cool - 1969

Long before reality TV captivated American audiences with its stunning plots and cultural insight, Medium Cool placed its viewers, as well as its actors, in the middle of a riot. Cinematographer Haskell Wexler wrote a script in which the movie's main characters were searching for each other outside the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago . On the day of the convention, the film crew began shooting and the crowd began to riot. What was left was a love story literally framed by the events of the time. Go rent this film.

Fact: The title of the film is a reference to the way different medias were being understood by the masses. Hot media did not require much of the user, but cold media did.

 

The Rules of Attraction - 2002

Did you hate this film? Did it make you feel really uncomfortable? Good. This film tries in so many ways to make the viewer as uncomfortable as the characters in it. From having entire scenes play out in reverse, to graphic depictions of sex and drug use, this film never had a chance with American audiences. Too bad, really. Our favorite Dawson's Creek hopeless romantic is hysterical to watch as a sexed-up drug dealer. If you're a student of film conventions, then this film is for you. It attacks every one of them. Oh yea, Shannyn Sassamon!! FAP FAP

Fact: Sean Bateman, the character played by James Van Der Beek, is the younger brother of the infamous Patrick Bateman, the main character of American Psycho , a film also based on the novel by Bret Easton Ellis. (imdb.com)

 

Time Code - 2000

In the theater, it was dreadful, painful and downright rude. Most of my distaste came from the fact that this film is a gimmick: four stories, all on screen at the same time, all filmed in one take. The idea is fine and the execution was pretty good, but the stories just sucked. But alas, hope returns on the DVD. In the theatric release, your attention is brought to a certain story on screen by raising the audio of that storyline and lowering the others. On the DVD you get to choose on-the-fly the volume for all the stories. Let me tell you, watching Selma Hayek sit in silence in a car for 22 minutes is amazing.

Fact: The film was shot 15 times over two weeks, using one continuous take each time. (imdb.com)

 

Intacto - 2001

You ever been to one of those parties where people gamble with and absorb the luck they can steal from others? Yeah, neither have I. The plot of this film is still one of the strangest but amazing displays of originality in filmmaking. Sam, played by Max Von Sydow, went into the Nazi gas chambers as a boy and came out alive. He now owns a casino in the desert and is considered the luckiest man alive. People from around the world compete in these strange luck tournaments to try and make their way to the big game. A one-bullet showdown with our man Sam. Again, Amazing!

Fact: This is a Spanish-language film, except for Von Sydow, who for some reason speaks perfect English and German, but not a lick of Spanish.

 

Lady in the Lake -1947

The verdict is still out on whether or not this film is genius or utter crap . MGM billed it as “YOU and ROBERT MONTGOMERY solve a murder mystery together!” The entire film, every damn shot, is filmed in the first person. For those confused, the camera is the main character, and you only see what the main character sees. I'm still not sure if this was a good idea for a film, or for a mystery dinner somewhere in the northern suburbs.

Fact: An actress named Ellay Mort is credited in the role of Chrystal Kingsby. This person does not exist. The credit is a joke, as the name is phonetic for the French phrase “she's dead.” (imdb.com)

 

Secretary - 2002

Maybe I'm just stupid, but the whole time I watched this film, I kept saying, “ That's Steff , from Pretty in Pink. I knew he was weird,”. I speak, of course, of our man James Spader and his role as a sexually dominating lawyer. He hires a, let's just say, a spanking secretary, and well, you have yourself a plot. What I really love about this film is how it has gotten everyone,including housewives, on the Internet asking questions about S&M. A sample, reproduced verbatim:

“For all of you whom are involved in BDSM and have seen “Secretary”, do you think its portrayal of the lifestyle is accurate or not? I am a newbie to the lifestyle and found it to be a rather positive portrayal, but was it accurate?”

Fact: The filmography for the leading lady who enjoys being spanked in Secretary, Maggie Gyllenhaal, includes such films as Strip Search, Criminal, Riding in Cars with Boys, Pornographer: A Love Story and A Dangerous Woman . Can anyone say typecast?

 

Run Lola Run - 1998

“ Jeden Tag, jede Sekunde triffst Du eine Entscheidung, die Dein Leben verändern kann.” Now that's a fucking tagline! No idea what it means. It's like watching Groundhog Day with Bill Murray, except the main character is hot. You can't understand a single word, the soundtrack kicks all forms of ass and the same day is only played out three times. Other then that it's the exact same film. Except the plots have nothing to do with one another and … oh hell, it's not the same at all. Run Lola Run is better. If you haven't seen it, give yourself 10 lashings now , Secretary style!

Fact: During filming, Franka Potente, who plays Lola, could not wash her hair for seven weeks. Her red hair color was very sensitive to water, and would have gotten lighter with every washing. (imdb.com)

 

Baraka - 1992

Watch this film for the first time when you have the time to sit and see the whole thing. I can't tell you what is going on, but I can tell you what is not going on. There are no actors, no script, no dialogue, no sets and no reason this isn't one of the best films ever . Ever. Filmed in 70mm stock and set in more than 24 countries, Baraka is sometimes one of my favorite films and sometimes my least favorite. Besides, monkeys are funny. Watch it, you'll know what I mean.

Fact: Baraka is an ancient Sufi word, which can be translated as “a blessing, or as the breath or essence of life from which the evolutionary process unfolds.”

 

Grand Hotel - 1932

I'll tell you this right now: people are going to tell you this is a slow-paced, outdated melodrama about rich people in rich places that isn't worth watching. And on some overly-cynical mornings , I would agree with this. But ladies and gentlemen, not today. Back in the days when the different film studios actually made films, someone got the bright idea to get each of their biggest talents and pool them together in one super-ensembled film. And they did. Greta Garbo, Joan Crawford and John Barrymore all star in this amazing cast that set the precedent for all ensemble cast films .

Fact: Crawford was irked by Garbo's insistence on top billing and decided to take her revenge. Knowing that Garbo loathed tardiness and Marlene Dietrich in equal measures, Crawford played Dietrich records between shots, and made sure to arrive late on set. (imdb.com)

 

The Parallax View - 1974

It's a little bit Clockwork Orange and a little bit All the Presidents Men with a touch of Conspiracy Theory mixed with a cup of Dick Tracy rolled up in Easy Rider, served warm with … ah, hell. This film is amazing on its own. Warren Beatty stars as a reporter trying to uncover an assassin ring that – surprise, surprise – has ties to the White House. This film does it right, with the paranoia, the drama and the action all done in a way that makes my head spin. Look up the meaning of parallax before watching this film and let me know what you think. And yes, this is my own guilty pleasure.

Fact: The scene in Zoolander when Derek is being brainwashed to kill the prime minister is a direct spoof of the brainwashing scene in The Parallax View .

pages.html:
As an employee of the foodservice industry , I know - or at least I think I do - a thing or two about the practices of 20- to 40-somethings looking for a good time at a bar. The most widely-used method is also the most amusing: getting sloshed. You know the experience. The one where you consume beer, liquor and anywhere from six to 15 shots in a span of only three hours, and then tell yourself the next day that you're a horse's ass and that you'll never do this to yourself again, only to repeat the process in a couple of weeks. However, there are many people that reserve these moments of self-reprobation for only special occasions, such as a national holiday. There's New Year's Eve, the day before Thanksgiving and of course, St. Patrick's Day.

St. Patrick's Day in Chicago brings out the primal being in both the experienced and novice drinker. I find that the line that normally separates the two groups of people on any other day, somehow becomes blurred on St. Pat's. It's like there's a tacit understanding that it's not only OK to act like you're on Spring Break, boozing it up and acting like a complete idiot for the resident sloths that are MTV viewers, but it's actually expected. Yes, Chicagoans on March 17 understand that it is their patriotic duty to convene at several drinking establishments and keep the tradition of unabashed debauchery alive. I understand this ambition. Everyone, myself included, has embraced the role of obnoxious drunk . And in my experienced and professional opinion, it's this type of bacchanalian behavior that makes every St. Pat's reveler an amateur drinker. So I've taken it upon myself to give some unsolicited guidance on how to make the most of St. Pat's, the sacred drinker's holiday, to those that will ultimately be wearing beer goggles.

Tips for the Greenhorn

When to Go : Well now that depends on your tolerance level. If you don't know your tolerance level by now, you should just stay inside and watch the History of Irish in America on the History Channel. If you consume alcohol at least three times a week, you're probably at the intermediate to advanced level of drinking, so you and your buddies can probably start drinking as soon as the bar doors open, which is normally between 10 and 11 a.m. If you truly are a rookie at this sport, I'd recommend leaving your house no earlier than three in the afternoon. Please know that once you leave your residence, there's no turning back. You won't be in bed – either yours or someone else's – until long after last call. So the later you start drinking, the less idiotic behavior you can reprimand yourself for later.

What to Bring : As it is a national holiday, I presume you'll be somewhat in the festive spirit. After all, March 17 does come only once a year. So bring and/or wear anything green or gold or glittery or a combination of the three in the hopes of standing out from all the other idiots that are trying to do the same thing. Stupid gallon hats, boas, midgets posing as leprechauns are fun too , and they're great for conversation starters.

Maps : If you need a map, I'm assuming you're either retarded or an out-of-towner. If you fall into neither one of these groups, I recommend you just stay in and watch the History of Irish in America on the History Channel.

Photography and Video : A personal choice. If you bring a camera, try to bring a digital one, so you could erase all the photos you deem unfit for anyone's eyes, including your own. However, be wary of misplacing your $450 toy, in which case you'll really hate yourself in the morning. So if you insist on recording your shenanigans for future generations to see and laugh about, your best bet would be to bring a disposable camera. Hopefully, it'll end up lost anyways.

Dangers and Annoyances : Pretty much you and your friends, you lush.

Emergencies : In case you find yourself in a situation in which you are afraid for your immediate personal safety , you can either scream for help like the deranged lunatic you are, run like hell, fight like hell or call 911 on your cell phone. If you didn't know this, then you don't even deserve to watch the History of Irish in America on the History Channel. You should just stay home and watch MTV.

go to page 2 >>

Getting To the Bar or Pub and Home Again

CTA : The el isn't always reliable to get you on time for where you want to go, nor is it free of homeless solicitors also partaking in the spirit of the holiday, but it's still there if you need it.

Cars and Motorcycles : Not a highly recommended use of transportation in or around the city unless you plan on staying overnight at a friend's house, so then you'll be behind the wheel only when you're half-drunk the next day. It's your call.

Taxi : The preferred method for people that hate public transportation and know to leave the car at home. Finding one shouldn't be a problem . Please try to puke either before you've entered the cab, or once you've exited it. You don't even want to deal with your bile, much less some undeserving stranger who's chauffeuring you around.

Bicycle : Weird and unorthodox for getting to and from bars on any day, let alone St. Patrick's.

Walking : It's good exercise, so I hear, and obviously inexpensive. Try to do this during daylight hours if you're by yourself, or with groups at night. Safety first. If you're still bipedal by the time last call rolls around, why not take a stroll to either yours or some random hookup's place. And if you're not with someone, walk home at night as a last resort, that is, if you have no money and you don't know who you are, much less what a cab is.

Hitchhiking : Daring. You have my blessing.

Places To Eat

Let's face it. You're probably not going to eat much if at all this day. If you do, it'll be off some random strange guy's chips and salsa plate at the bar, or maybe some stale chips you might find at home, at your buddy's place where you're crashing or at the same random's whose chips and salsa you mooched off earlier. In any case, food is not a priority. Count on consuming your carbs the liquid way.

 

Places to Stay

Hotel/Motel : If you want to stay at a place where you don't have to clean up your mess the next morning, try the HoJo or Holiday Inn or YMCA, any place where you and friends and strangers alike can gather after last call and drink some more.

An Apartment Other Than Yours : Staying at your own apartment wouldn't be a party. Thus a good refuge after a hard day's drinking can be either: 1. Your friend's pad, or 2. A random hook-up's place. Both are free, and neither requires emotional commitment. The second choice, however, is far more embarrassing for you and the party involved than the first choice, unless of course, the random stays with you at your friend's place, in which case it's awkward for pretty much everybody. But if such fleeting moments of awkwardness refrained people from ever boozing and hooking up, what would happen to St. Patrick's Day and all its drinking glory? Shudder to think.

An Open Field or Alley : A very plausible situation. The whole stretch of Lake Shore Drive has lots of room in the form of grass, stone, concrete and sand for those that just can't get enough fresh air. For those obliterated individuals who aren't nature lovers, but still like a brisk breeze, there's an abundance of alleys ready to accommodate you. Just choose a nook near a Dumpster and plop yourself down! Be careful as not to infringe on anyone else's permanent living quarters, as you don't want to create a scene. Hopefully, you will have already saved that for while you were conscious.

 

Finally. . .

Above all, please remember to make the tradition of a complete drunken, public spectacle of yourself alive and well. It would be quasi-sacrilegious if you didn't. And it certainly wouldn't be St. Patrick's Day. Have fun.

title: about face

pages.html:
Everyone knows that all terrorists look the same. They all have that terrorist look to them: a prominent brow line, or shifty eyes and a scowl. Viewed in a lineup beside normal faces, it is easy to point one out. Bricklayer … blacksmith … terrorist … attorney … line chef … terrorist. Luckily, unlike vampires, whose images evade film, terrorists can be photographed, so we can soon start catching them in our airports.

From Plate LXXIV, Lavater, Essays on Physiognomy (trans. Thomas Holcraft) London, 4th Edition c. 1844 Text additions from pp. 456, 457

Exercise 1: Do you resemble a terrorist? Go to your bathroom mirror and measure the distance between the centers of your eyes in millimeters. If the number exceeds 60mm, there is potential that you are one. If you additionally have felt what could be interpreted as aggressive behavior, you may want to pursue Exercise 2.

In the late 18th century, it became clear that just by looking at someone's face, it could be determined he was a criminal. One hundred years later, photography's accessibility as a tool of documentation popularized a method of cataloguing faces into groups of physical attributes that could be linked to psychological disorders. Physiognomy, as a respected science of the day, traced patterns of delinquency to the physical layout of a face. Illustrated research diagrammed faces, categorizing certain physical features as typical of criminal behavior. “If you see a forehead or a nose like this photograph on the street,” articles emphasized, “you're looking at a criminal. Watch your purse!”

Slight gestures and gait were also analyzed as telling factors of a subject's personality. It was socially acceptable at the time to make the assumption that looking a person in the eye was a view into the soul, so the physical placement of the eyes was crucial to determining whether a person could be trusted. High brow-lines were always found on the faces of the wealthy, the upright citizens, while heavy, hooded lids and deep-set eyes were typical of the uneducated and the morally depraved. Clearly, eyebrow shape is crucial in deciphering a person's morals. It is from this type of unbiased analysis that the current terms highbrow and lowbrow make the equally logical distinction between high art and pop culture.

In contemporary thinking on the topic, since there are no such distinctions as class and morality, we naturally no longer judge each other by physical appearance. Attractive people have to wait in line at the bank, right along with all the unattractive people. Blue-collar worker's wives have access to the same plastic surgeons as CEO's wives do. All races gather around the same bottled water unit in the morning at the workplace. Thanks to our country's deep commitment toward political correctness , there is no reason to talk out loud about physical differences, so it's easy and convenient to ignore skin color and class and treat each other like amorphous and sexless amoebas that we strive to emulate.

go to page 2 >>

Exercise 2: What do your cheekbones say about you? If an imaginary line were drawn from the base of your nose to the protrusion of your cheekbone, it will form an angle with your profile functioning as the missing vector. Is the angle acute? Let's hope not. While obtuse angles (especially 105 degrees or more!) suggest emotional stability, acute angles are most often associated with vagrancy and intuitive knowledge of how to build explosives .

Grandville (Jean Isadore Gerard, 1803-46), "Man Descending Toward the Brute" 1843, from:Heads of Men and Animals Compared, 1844  

At the height of physiognomy's popularity, sketches were made by travelers and brought to the West to show all the people back home diagrammed pictures of the faces that were found: This is an Asian. This is an African. Illustrations of animals often accompanied these pictures to see how certain racial groups shared physical traits of animals and could therefore be expected to behave like animals: This is a Boar. This is a Rat. Physiognomy proved very useful in this country when the practice of slavery was called into question, as it made the convenient comparison between African-Americans and animals. This science was also a favorite of the Nazis who, while rounding up Jews to murder, made careful notes of the quintessential Jewish face, which were later used for propaganda posters to raise social awareness of the race's destructive behavior.


Physiognomy has lost relevance in contemporary politics as differences between races have been unanimously agreed upon as unimportant. Soon, when we all will have genetically altered our faces, we can share one ideal set of features so it will be a lot easier to remember not to make any racial slurs , or not to call anyone “ugly.” When we all have the same pair of eyes to gaze into, they will obviously be the windows to our same souls too, so our collective morality will be top-notch. It will cease to matter that this country provides for freedom of religion, as we will have entered a state of moral utopia where there is no room or reason for dissent.

Beginning January 2004, foreign travelers to the United States have been required by law to undergo screening in all international airports and seaports before entering the country. Photographs and fingerprints are collected and stored in a database that catalogs information on all foreigners in the country at any given time. As passengers' photographs appear on screen, their image is compared to stored images of alleged terrorists and potential U.S. threats. Should a photograph resemble one of those alleged threats, the passenger is detained and pulled aside to be interrogated before entering the country. Most passengers claim that the inconvenience lasts only 15 extra minutes. The photographs are extremely high quality, taken with $368 million digital equipment, while the stored pictures of alleged threats are grainy, sometimes outdated, passport or ID photos. Only 1 in every 750 passengers scanned produces a false positive reading. The face of every traveler is compared to stored eye sockets, nasal bridges and foreheads that have been predetermined as dangerous and threatening physical arrangements. Guests from 27 countries, mostly European, whose races would not produce a face of any stored dangerous features, are exempt from submitting to the new U.S. admissions process. Visitors from France or Italy and vacationers from the United Kingdom just don't have that look of trouble to them; visitors from Brazil apparently do.

To combat the profiling of visitors to the United States, Brazilian security officials have implemented a widely publicized program of photographing and fingerprinting only American visitors to the country. Americans are outraged, as it seems clear enough to us that not a single one of our melting pot full of physical attributes could create a threatening profile. The whole world knows that Americans are a fair and morally upright group of people, who would never act in their own self-interest. Douglas Skolnick, the New Jersey man who was recently subject to $17,000 of fines for sticking up his middle finger for his fingerprinting screening in a Sao Paulo airport, showed the world that Americans have a great sense of humor too!

After the event, he defended himself as an American, in case his action left any confusion over his ethnicity, when he said, “I'm an American citizen. I'm not a monkey.” Apparently monkeys, like Brazilians, Iranians, Puerto Ricans and Russians, have a natural predilection toward giving samples of their fingerprints to government officials. Monkeys must be terrorists too. American zoos might benefit from a screening process before new animals are allowed into preexisting cages.

<< back to page 1 go to page 3 >>

Exercise 3: Measure the number of inches between your brow line and the peak of you hairline in inches. Place this number as a fraction, with the number or teeth visible when you smile functioning as the denominator. Is the product divisible by two? It should be unless you consider yourself maladaptive or edgy.

Physiognomists believed that the most essential way to graft the essence of a person was to study his features without knowledge of the subject's identity getting in the way, and before allowing the subject to speak. German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer, in his1851 essays Parerga and Paralipomena, wrote on objectivity during analysis:

"The first condition of success is to maintain a purely objective point of view, which is no easy matter … There are some people whose faces bear the stamp of such artless vulgarity and baseness of character, such an animal limitation of intelligence, that one wonders how they can appear in public with such a countenance, instead of wearing a mask,".

It is clear that the science of physiognomy requires the analyst to empty his brain of all preconceived notions of beauty. It is good that plastic surgery is available to everyone today, so that in cases in which the analyst cannot divorce himself from natural human preference and cultural identity, face lifts and nose jobs can rise to the occasion.

The technology used to match faces of airport travelers to those of potential terrorists is filtered through a security official who watches each image appear on screen and makes the final assessment whether an individual needs to be detained. According to Simson Garfinkel of Discover magazine, the technology that informs the security official's decision is made possible by one of two programs, each of which rely on a system of facial measurements or comparisons. One program renders a digital photograph of every person, then classifies that photograph as one of 128 possible default facial combinations. A template is created based on the person's features and classification, which is then compared to all saved templates of the FBI's U.S. terrorist threats. If the template of the face in question bears a resemblance to any saved templates of terrorists, the person is pulled aside to undergo further questioning. The second program, instead, takes measurements of up to 80 facial features based upon a digital photograph, then compares each distance to the values between facial features of those dangerous alignments of stored in a database.

Exercise 4: Place your nose between two fingers and rock them from side to side. Now take a string or a piece of dental floss from your medicine cabinet and trace your nose's potential arc of motion. The diameter of this imaginary circle determines your degree of sociability. Large diameters suggest ability to work well with others, while noses with short diameters or immobile noses are typical of those with antisocial tendencies, a red-flag attribute when dealing with martyrs and psycho killers.

While the layout of a face takes precedent over gesture, physical movement was also analyzed in the late 18th century, both in terms of a subject's gait and slight movements when speaking. Involuntary facial gesturing is also apparently grounds for reading terrorist behavior. The FBI and CIA are currently working closely with researchers who can read faces, detecting true emotion in a face, even in cases when that emotion differs from what a subject voluntarily shares verbally. In his article published by The NewYorker , Max Gladwell explains how psychologist Paul Ekman created a catalogue of all possible combinations of facial muscles. By studying the anatomy of the face, and forcing his own facial muscles into every possible gesture, electrically shocking each muscle to locate the minor ones, Ekman has divided the face into 43 possible action units, each of which can be combined to create thousands of series of gestures. There are some action units that are nearly impossible to imitate in the absence of the accompanying emotion. Eckman can, for example, detect the difference between a forced smile and a sincere one, based on the lift of muscles surrounding subject's eyes while smiling. If a smile is not sincere, a subject cannot voluntarily raise that muscle. Such analysis in very useful to U.S. security branches in order to detect if a subject is lying. Classes are being constructed in a counter-terrorism effort, in which FBI agents learn to read involuntarily gesture.

If you download a copy of Digital Physiognomy for $17.00 , there is a sample of the program's process to curb skeptics. When clicking through the program's library of free samples, the first to pop up is of Osama bin Laden. His features apparently suggest “predilection to shyness” and “patience,” with a “confidence factor of 60 percent.” “Don't worry,” says the intro to the analysis, “ Digital Physiognomy not so much allows you to determine psychological characteristics, as it allows you to understand how others see this personality.”

This means that everyone will be safe, not only from terrorists, but also from people who look like terrorists, who are just as dangerous. The next time you are in line at the video rental place, take a few minutes to evaluate the faces of your fellow consumers. Are their noses suggestive of selecting movies with anti-American sub-plots? The next time you hold afternoon tea in your home, practice trafficking at the front door. Wear a pistol on your hip and politely ask guests to stand in profile while you make quick thumbnail photographs of them with your digital phone. It's the responsibility of every American to take these practices to the public sphere. Whoever said “don't judge a book by its cover,” was obviously un-American, and probably a terrorist, too. We should be judging books exclusively by their covers, layouts, and binding. We should be selecting our leaders based on the shape of their teeth and skulls. Never open a book again unless its cover has red, white and blue in its color scheme. Never listen to a public speaker who lacks the proportionate smile of blissful middle America . Never trust a set of eyes that squints at this country's logic.

title: traveling chicago

pages.html:
One of us was going to break down – it was either my keyboard or myself. I pounded and pounded on the keys, but the computer beeped instead, laughing in defiance. I had reached my breaking point.

It was one of those weeks. The ones when you have more to do than time allows. I had too much on my plate, and I was about to give my keyboard a crack over my knee when a pop-up ad caught my attention.

“Cheap Tickets,” it flashed.

I decided to give it a click with the mouse, which doesn't let me down like the keyboard does. Instantly, I was asked where I was leaving from and going to, when I was departing and would return, and how I would travel: Round-trip? One way? I clicked away: San Francisco , Seattle , London . The idea of an escape excited me.

Until I saw the price.

“Cheap Tickets” was not as cheap as I had hoped. I was about to click out of the pop-up ad when suddenly I spied my mistake.

The last entry was wrong. It was backward. Instead of requesting a plane ticket from Chicago to London , I requested the opposite. From London to Chicago .

The error didn't seem like that big a deal, but it got me thinking: People from London and all over the world travel to Chicago , so why can't I? Yes, I know: How can you travel to a place when you already live there?

I have done it once before. I could do it again.

During college, I studied abroad in Rome for a semester. My goal was to travel somewhere new every weekend. However, one weekend my plans for a trip to Sicily fell through. I was devastated. I felt I had missed an opportunity and wasted a weekend. Luckily, my travel companion knocked some sense into me, suggesting we explore Rome instead. How silly of me, I thought. One of the most beautiful cities in the world was right out my door, and I had not even seen it. I gave it a shot, and it was one of the best weekends of my semester.


Reflecting upon that Roman moment motivated me to explore Chicago . I have lived here most of my adult life and there are still many things I have yet to uncover. I wanted to stay away from the tourist route, the buildings, the fountains, and the museums. Rather, I wanted to escape keyboard and explore like a traveler. Where would I begin?

I would do what I did in Rome : Go to a hostel.

Hostels are different from hotels and motels . Hostels have the cheap, open rooms with a bunk beds and lockers and a community kitchen. Some of my more memorable travel experiences were had at hostels.

Like the time in Austria, when two portly Germans stuffing their faces with biscuits and liverwurst would not leave me alone once they found out I was from Chicago. Their favorite show was, as they put it, “The Al Bundy Show.” They could not stop spitting while laughing while retelling episode after episode as if I remembered or cared.

Then there was the time in Ireland , when I had the pleasure of bunking next to two travelers engaging in, how do you say, “hostel love.” The squeaking of the bed and the fuss about a broken condom kept me up all night.

Hostels are different from the norm, and so are its people. But they're also places to find hardcore travelers; not tourists, but explorers, who wanted to escape their burdensome lives.

My first stop was at Hostelling International-Chicago on Wabash and Congress, the second largest hostel in the nation. I pushed through the revolving door, passed the security desk and took the elevator up to the second floor. There I met Thomas Applegate, executive director for the hostel, and he showed me around the five-floor, 500 bed mega-hostel.


go to page 2 >>

It was nothing like any of the hostels I had ever seen before. I could not escape here. Everything was super-sized and super clean. The community kitchen was the size of my apartment. There was a pool table, a ping-pong table , a library and a conference room. My idea of “roughing-it-hostel-style” was now in question.

The place reminded me of my college dorm. I found out later it is a college dorm. Columbia College across the street rents the top three floors during the school year – the hostel's off-season – and then turns the rooms back over to the hostel for the summer.

I could not believe it. This was not a hostel according to my romanticized European version. Applegate tried to convince me that the modern traveler prefers hostels to hotels because hotels do not advocate any sense of community.

“Hostels encourage relationships, meeting people and learning from them,” Applegate said. “Hotels, on the other hand, destroy the idea of a community and separate travelers into closed rooms.”

I couldn't agree more. Travelers board at hostels to meet people, to share ideas and to give suggestions on where to travel next. Tourists conversely book hotels to swim in the pool or watch cable TV.

But my question to Applegate simple: where do the travelers go? In the three hours that I had spent with him, I saw one hosteller walk by, and he might have been going to his dorm room.

I was convinced this mega-hostel was not a hostel at all. It was a hotel, or at least felt like one. I need to find the hostel that I was looking for in order to find the traveler that I was seeking, the one that would tell me how to travel Chicago, the one that would help me explore the city, the one that would give me an escape from reality.

I jumped the el for the far north side. Tucked into a window seat, I questioned my reasons behind traveling. Sure, I wanted to escape, but there had to be something else that drove me on this quest.


I just couldn't figure it out yet.

I remember an article Pico Iyer wrote for Salon.com discussing the reasons why we travel. He suggested, “We travel, initially, to lose ourselves; and we travel, next, to find ourselves,”.

In a way, I agreed. I wanted to lose myself, leave my paltry existence for a new unexplored life. But I'm curious about the second part, the part about finding ourselves.

I believe on some level, we all feel alone, that too many times others do not understand us or care to know who we are. We trick ourselves into thinking that the Internet and cell phones have brought us closer together, when they have really pulled us apart. We do not walk around parks or to storefronts, talking to each other anymore; we would rather stay in a chat room. We do not turn to our neighbor on the el to ask for the time because she is yapping on her flip phone. The isolation is sometimes chilly .

All we have is our stories of who we are and what we want to be. Maybe that's it. Maybe that is what drives me to travel more than just escaping. Maybe I want to take my stories, and connect them with those with similar stories.

A friend of mine traveled with his father this past summer to many old Civil War sites. Why? He confessed to his desire to connect with the past, to history. I believe, more broadly, that is why we are so compelled to visit landmarks, memorials and ruins. Pompeii. The Parthenon. Ground Zero. We travel to them to connect, be a part of history, to not feel alone.

It is in that connection of story to story that we feel meaning and significance, because it is then our story becomes a part of the greater human story of struggle and survival. For some of us, historical landmarks are simply not enough. We need people. We need our story to connect with other people's stories.

My stop was quickly approaching. I closed my notebook, where I was scratching down thoughts throughout the ride, and packed my bag. I was ready to meet people, talk with them and hopefully connect with them.

Near Loyola University 's Lake Shore campus is the Chicago International Hostel . The place was small and cozy, and was everything the mega-hostel was not. There were a handful of chairs and tables spread around the lobby. A sign above a basket of bagels read “Please, take one before you go.”

In the corner of the room were two couches in an L-shape facing a modest-sized TV set. Three travelers from Korea , two men and a woman, were eating a breakfast of Subway sandwiches on the couches. I approached them.

English was not their first language, so we tried our best to communicate. I tried to ask them, as hardcore travelers of Chicago, what kinds of things they had seen and what types of places they will see next. Yi Kyonng Tae, who was 26, said so far that they had viewed the city from the Sears Tower observation desk, watched the baby sharks at the Shedd and taken pictures in front Buckingham Fountain.

I frowned. I was not connecting. They were tourists. I wanted travelers.

I inquired further if there was something that he and his group planned to do that was off the tourist's conventional path.

Tae nodded and said, “Our real reason for coming to Chicago …”


<< Back to page 1

go to page 3 >>

My eyes widened. This was it, the reason for traveling Chicago, what I was looking for. I wanted to know so that I could follow suit.

“… was to find out about Mark Twain .”

What? Twain? Was he kidding? Twain hated Chicago .

Apparently, the trio had read about the Mississippi River and Twain in their English classes back in Korea and wanted to learn more about them. I dropped my head and moved on.

My hopes had fallen but were not completely dashed. Just because I didn't want to travel the ole Mississipp' did not mean I would simply give up. I wanted to stick with the city, so I would try again.

I spotted a bubbly group of women from southeast England packing their bags and picking through the bagel table. I figured I could ask them a few questions about where they were going.

They weren't sure yet. They had just arrived from San Francisco the night before and would be leaving for New York in a few days. This was the last leg of a five-month around-the-world trip.

They couldn't offer me much. They didn't know anything about Chicago except for that it was cold and they needed, as they put it, warmer jumpers and overcoats. I directed them to H&M on Michigan Avenue .

I was about to move on when one of the women, Coralie Wright, 22, stopped me. She said she understood my story – at least the part about the cost of travel – and how Cheap Tickets wasn't so cheap, and how that tends to keep us from traveling.

“Traveling costs so much, but it's worth every penny,” she said. “You could buy a wide-screen TV with that money, but why do it when you could go there?”

I felt a semi-connection but needed more. At this point, sadly, the idea of banjos and steamboats didn't sound that bad. I was getting desperate. I looked to the couches to see if the Koreans had left. They had. I turned back and watched the English women slip out the door.

Disappointed, unconnected and alone, I looked for my coat and decided to go home. Walking back over to the couch to pick up my jacket, I noticed to my surprise a little man slouched down on the armrest quietly eating cereal of some kind and watching CNN.

Allen Lu, 22, was a foreign exchange student from Taiwan who was studying in Toronto . What was he doing in Chicago ?

“I had to see Alicia Keys.”

The night before, R&B singer/songwriter Alicia Keys rocked out at the United Center to a sold-out audience. This concert was a must for Lu. As a self-described music junkie who owns over 100 CDs, he admitted music drives him to travel.

That was different. That was unconventional. Unlike the Koreans, he hiked off the tourist path. Unlike the English, he knew the city.

Lu planned to chill at jazz clubs, specifically the Green Mill, and dine at steakhouses for his remaining two days. He had done the tall buildings and museums already and now wanted to get, as he called it, a sense of Chicago .

That was it. We connected. I wanted to get a sense of Chicago. I wanted to escape away from my keyboard and meet new people. I wanted new places to explore in the city, places the unconventional traveler would seek out. He had given it to me.

I asked him if he ever felt disconnected and alone, yearning to meet others.

He smiled and opened up a tiny notepad.


It read:

A little boy
Alone, all alone
Brave, so brave
A little boy going to a big city
An unknown venture creating a colorful page
Beautiful, yet dangerous
Like a sheep wanders on endless grass
No destination, no beginning
Only determination, and believing
In himself and his faith
Getting everywhere but the south (side)
When the little boy returns home
He will never be alone

I smiled and he closed the tiny notepad.

Then he left, most likely for jazz and steaks.

I didn't need to travel to San Francisco or Seattle or London or even Chicago after all. Yes, I needed to escape my overworked life, but more importantly, I needed to understand why. I needed to meet with people, talk with people and connect with people, something the Internet and cell phones can't do for me any more.

So I'm off for the Green Mill to get a sense of Chicago and a sense of myself. See you there.
