title: pursue happiness

pages.html:
When I was a kid living in the Chicago suburbs, the city changed my area code from 708 to 630 due to the flux of people moving out into the suburbs. Now, 708, that made sense to me. I wasn't living in the city proper, so I wasn't expecting 312, but I had, for a time, a nice, docile suburban area code. I wrote out my new phone number and remember it looked wrong with the zero hanging off the end, like a gaping mouth with food falling out of it. Conversely, if I ever saw a 312 or a 773 area code, I assumed it belonged to some older girl with a haircut like Patti Smith and a penchant for knives. Or maybe it belonged to a bar, full of drug addicts and no bathroom. The numbers of the city area codes looked experienced and mean, and I wouldn't pick up the phone and dial one if it was the last number left in the world. Who knew who would pick up?

Maybe I was a little neurotic, but I wasn't far off from what all the soccer moms around me were thinking. Everyone in my neighborhood knew that the city was a death trap, only good for museums and field trips, or maybe a play, but it was to be dealt with in small doses and in big groups, with chaperones. All our grandparents had lived in Chicago. They settled into the neighborhoods that spoke their language and worked in factories or stockyards or bars to pay rent, and on the weekends they went swing dancing at the Aragon Ballroom. Our parents had worked hard to get the hell out. They saw how our grandparents lived, kids half-stuffed in a single flat of a house, with suspicious quarter-inch holes in the windows and no yard to speak of. They wanted their kids to have more than just a yard; they wanted their kids to have neighborhood swimming pools. Eventually they bribed the grandparents to follow them out of the old Chicago neighborhood too, so that us kids wouldn't have to dodge bullets when coming to visit. Now all us kids, the product of the suburbs, are moving back to the city, working at an office in the Loop or in a neighborhood bar, going to see bands play on the weekends at the Aragon Ballroom.

America is a country of immigrants. It's in our collective blood to keep shifting our homes – and so then, our identities – every now and then. Happiness becomes a matter of being at the right place at the right time, and this migratory trend shifts with each generation. When the first generation of immigrants came to the industrial America of the new twentieth century, the West had long since been won, there were no new territories to map, no wilderness to be conquered. The American city, with all of its dangers, risks and potential rewards, had replaced the wilderness of earlier generations. The city had become the place to stake a claim, to seek social acceptance and economic freedom.

Their children found new ways to civilize un-staked claims on the cities' periphery: the suburbs. With suburbia, manifest destiny found its perfection, in that even nature could be controlled and managed in the form of identically plotted green lawns. This generation bargained with the city and took what it could, then escaped with the goods to the suburbs to live divorced from the congestion and danger of the city. Urban landscapes became synonymous with decay, and the move out of the decay marked a fresh start.

This idea of a fresh start infiltrates national consciousness. In his book “Restless Nation: Starting Over in America,” James Jasper notes the American obsession with the move doesn't always necessitate a physical relocation as much as it concerns itself with the idea of movement. The West still looms before us as a fantasy of open road and unincorporated land, and though the land has already been tamed and the freeways have already served as a stage for millions of soul searches and road novels, the American West is upheld as a bastion of self-realization and fulfillment of every escapist fantasy imaginable. According to Jasper, “America was a symbol in world culture long before it was a destination, and its image as the land of liberty was first crafted elsewhere, out of the psychological needs of foreigners.” We graft attributes upon a location, a location where the attributes will aid in the excavation of our “ideal” selves. We correlate that locale with attaining happiness.

go to page 2

We work in cycles. Like the immigrants who idealized the American city as a wilderness of economic opportunity and self-realization, a new generation, born during the exodus into the suburbs and reared on the family values that gave rise to the suburban sprawl, again confronts the city as a contemporary frontier. This untamed area is ripe with sensory bombardment that mimics our national fetish with opportunistic bohemianism, as we are a nation that views relocation as progress. The same decaying city that drove our parents out into the suburbs is, to our generation, completely unfamiliar, and thus suitable for exploration.

Every once in a while, I'll go home and run into a kid I went to grade school with that still lives in my old neighborhood. These kids sometimes hang out in the bars and bowling alleys where we grew up. They go to the same dentist. They have a dentist. We, the newfound city kids, haven't had our teeth cleaned since high school. We're too busy drinking cheap independent-organic-fair-trade coffee and looking for parking spots on our one-way streets. We are waiters and receptionists and painters, and sometimes we never sleep. The point is we are not our parents. The point is we are pursuing the next generational American dream. But we won't label it as “American,” because we are, in truth, saving up our money at the restaurant or office or coffee shop to move to some small eastern European city with better coffee, where we will eventually die like Kafka. But some of us still get money from Mom, or we spout theory about politics based upon the liberal arts education Dad paid for. But we are happy to pay the 8.75 percent sales tax, happy to eat lots of beans and rice, happy to take public transportation everywhere. Some of us think the “ghetto factor” of public transportation is “charming.” We're living in the city anyway, and that's a start.

With this in mind, the Pursuit of Happiness becomes very distinctly about domesticating new territory. When that phrase was plopped, last-minute, into the Declaration of Independence to fill the space where “property” used to be, the pursuit of happiness was a phrase that had more to do with a community sensibility than it had to do with self-interest. In 1776, “pursuit” implied action for the “common good.” Now the phrase has become synonymous with personal satisfaction and a well-rounded social or professional life. But with the way we chase happiness in and out of the city, the phrase might have read, “the pursuit of finding the right place to live,” or maybe “property” would have worked all right after all.

In his 1969 interview series, “Division Street: America,” Studs Terkel speaks with immigrants from other parts of America and across national borders about the city and their place in it. In one interview, Native American Benny Bearskin describes “getting urbanized” as tantamount to learning to live in the wild: “You have to learn the ropes … just like a person moving out from a prairie country and into the woods. There are certain dangers in such a transition and it's the same way in a city.”

Learning to negotiate the urban or the suburban is a contemporary attempt to discover uncharted space in a country that has been thoroughly mapped out for over a century. My roommate works on Division Street. Two mornings a week she opens a café, and walks down Division at 5 a.m. to get the scones ready. She keeps her stride fast and her head tucked toward the sidewalk; her keys are laced between her fingers. She once was attacked by a wild animal (a dog on a leash) that took a bite out of her down jacket. She tells me she never feels so much a part of a city then when she's forging her way down Division Street to make ends meet. The city street then becomes an urban frontier in which opportunity can be measured in relative danger and sacrifice. Our acclamation to unfamiliar conditions measures our adaptability, success, and by proxy, our degree of contentment. It is, of course, another idealized survival fantasy, but it works.

title: intersection section

pages.html:
The Pullman Historic District is like your grandmother's house: interesting and full of unappreciated miscellany, but you never go there. This intrepid reviewer, however, is here to bring it to all ye uninitiated. As always, there's a 10-point scale. Ten is good. One is bad.

01. Locating yourself in history, or, dystopian funlands. Rating: 8.2
Not having a car, I'm not that mobile in this city. I function fine without one – while I do pay more than I would like to cabbies, that's just par for the course – and make the Chicago Transit Authority my main means of transport. But the Pullman district is barely in the city. This isn't “South Side.” This isn't “far South Side.” This is “take-the-highway-to-get-there South Side,” sitting between 111th and 115th Streets.

My only previous contact with the area is most likely shared by so many in my position or, really, by anyone who uses I-90/I-94 to get to the city : the Pullman Bank building. I would use it as my personal highway marker, marking it as Chicago 's boundary point. Naturally, I had a firm grasp on what went on there, since I knew there was this guy named Pullman . And he started a bank. ‘Nuff said.

I had also heard of these things called Pullman train cars . But I thought of them as quaint and charming, like all rail travel in the United States, following the phenomenon of saying “boy, that sure would be great to take a train trip,” without meaning it in the slightest. It's the same as doing your taxes or running a marathon. While it would be great to complete the race or get your refund or ride the iron locomotive, if the opportunity presented itself I'd most likely be found impulsively checking my e-mail for the eighth time in an hour.

To give some real facts, the Pullman district was built between 1880 and 1892 as a living area for the employees of George M. Pullman, creating one of America 's first planned communities. That was 1880, and that trend hasn't become any less nefarious: Let's see – row after row of the same house, clones walking to and from a job in the same building for the same boss, never having to leave the safety and comfort that is their enclosed hamlet. Sounds like Microsoft employees. Or Naperville residents . Whichever.

02. Ugly historical societies resembling giant post-modern toasters. Rating: 9.4
The entire area is kept in good condition, well-maintained and groomed. I'm making a wild guess at this, really, since I visited at the end of winter, when things have a tendency not to grow. But from the remnants of foliage, it was apparent rose bushes and other such pleasantries bloom in the warmer months. There's maroon row houses, multicolored park benches, a restored hotel and … jutting out of the middle, an ugly grey concrete monolith more resembling a toaster than a building. That's jarring enough, but upon closer inspection, you discover it's the home of the Pullman Historical Society. I hope the amount of history contained herein isn't proportional to the architectural budget of the structure.

I'm contemplating this metaphysical impossibility of a horribly unfortunate granite slab structure in the middle of a plaza on the Chicago Landmarks list when the door opens.

“We're open,” the head poking out the door says. “You can come in.” The voice belonged to my angel, the woman who would show me the Gospel of Pullman, the Way of Landmarks.

She was direct from a place called Heaven That Was Bad Fashion: 1978, wearing a sweater that could only be described as “colorful.” Remember the kaleidoscope of color given off by those iridescent green Oakley windbreakers – the ones with “Thermonuclear Protection” written on them for some odd reason – when viewed under strong sunlight? There ya go. Her footwear was so old it was back in style, since she had on some variation of those hideously ugly Ugg boots. But, appealing to the passive media whore in me, she showed a video in lieu of giving a museum-style tour.

Like an Aesop fairy tale , the end of any story is ripe for the passing on of wise aphorisms, like “Slow and steady wins the race” or, for the lightweights among us, “an ounce of liquor is worth an hour of idiocy,” but in the case of the Pullman Historic video, we're presented with a question. “Who saves a landmark?” the voice-over asks. It was too much to hope for the query to be rhetorical, for that horribly third-rate video technique deserves neither response nor ridicule, but the cringe-inducing answer was on the way: “We all do.”

Who saves a landmark? We all do. Great. Let's just pretend this isn't a shameless pitch for property owners or developers in the area, and go with the civic duty angle of the call to action. Score for the Historical Society.

go to page 2

03. Green churches dedicated in 1882: symbol of life or conduit to Satan? Rating: 3.7
I've reviewed church-intersections before , but very few spiritual edifices can match the grandeur of stonework displayed by the Greenstone United Methodist Church . With a congregation led by Bille J. Westmoreland and walls of – as the name demonstrates – green stone, who could be led astray by the temptations of the Wicked One? Let's review our symbolism via quick Google searches : green can be a neutral representation of plant life around us. It can also be a sign of vitality and pleasure in heraldry. And, let's not forget that in the Middle Ages, green was a direct association with the devil, as the Prince of Lies hunted souls in a green frock. Like any good historian, we can be as revisionist as we please , so let's say – for argument's sake – that the Greenstone Church is the permanence (here's the symbolism of stone) of life's ever-present cycle of rebirth, or the continuance of sin in the realm of mortals or even the vigor of the human spirit all made manifest in a house of worship.

Or you could call it all schlock, and say the stone came from a quarry in Pennsylvania and looks cool. I'm espousing this one, but to each his own, as the saying goes.

In a fine ‘80s film, Dan Aykroyd tells a group of prisoners, “the architect must have been a certified genius or a certified wacko.” Bonus points go to anyone who can name the movie, but I don't think I've ever found a more perfect use for the quote. The wood around the stained-glass windows is yellow. Dragons are carved in relief all over the place. The place is, like a girl who wants to make you sandwiches all afternoon , interesting and unique. Were I a Methodist living in close proximity to the church – of which neither is true – I would most certainly spend my worshipping hours in the green confines of Greenstone.

04. Attached-row homes spanning entire blocks: being different is bad. Rating: 4.5
Our intrepid guide to the Pullman area, my angel Ms. Moore, gave me a pamphlet that told me the ever-useful information that “intricate brickwork and gingerbread can be found throughout the Pullman Historic Landmark District.” Naturally. “Gingerbread,” once I looked it up, of course, refers to intricate saw cuts in a building's decorative latticework. And all this time I thought it was a baked holiday delight . But since the row homes are one of the district's distinct selling points, they were worth a look.

The thing about row homes is their cookie-cutter similarity. They are, quite literally, all the same. None of this ugly suburban sprawl, where the nasty blue siding house is jutted up against the regal brownstone or the dilapidated shack shares an alley with the red-brick white-picket-fence job. No, these are row after row of sameness. Makes me think of A Wrinkle In Time , where all the kids were jumping rope on the same beat and all the mothers poked their heads out the front door simultaneously. Except I don't recall seeing very many kids, so I guess the metaphor only works so far.

I have to celebrate the one house on St. Lawrence Avenue , however, that proudly displayed its individuality by shamlessly tacky-ifying its front yard with the addition of quite a few plastic pink flamingos . Now these are residents with some flair, with some panache. But such a decorating scheme has its downfalls, since the residents are most likely the reasons for town hall meetings where someone stands up, screaming, “You can't handle the truth!” or something similar, inciting mobs to riot, ensuring the imminent destruction of the pink flamingos, the source of all the ire in the first place. It's the great wheel of karma.

Pullman is like an island in the sea of Chicago's south-side. It's edges are somewhat desolate dry shores and the center is one part brooklyn to one part elgin. Kids are there (probably bored to death) at least i saw some. People are mixed colors and cultures -thankfully.Nearbye Beverly get a bit homogenated.  

The black owned car wash in a historical horse stable was ironic and the hispanic corner store with 20 cent doughnuts a 1950's holdover. Arches abound in windows and overhangs in the vernacluar of Chicago School era buildings there. 

The community was a failure at the end of it's historical heyday and holds a charged air of pride and stigma in it's streets today. Imagine a Norman Rockwell picture of a low rider blazing ground effects for a modern rendition of Pullman.

People were cool to me when I walked around there that day. It is entirely possible that the only real tourists who go visit are from outside this country. Ogling this working class proto-suburbia is in itself rewarding. I remember thinking that if you stood a row of row houses on end you would have the first skyscraper, which also was constructed around the same era downtown.

comments.text:
“...someone stands up, screaming, “You can't handle the truth!” or something similar, inciting mobs to riot, ensuring the imminent destruction of the pink flamingos, the source of all the ire in the first place. It's the great wheel of karma.”

Green churches dedicated in 1882 are the stuff of much scare.  The walls of my room are green, and I could feel the presence of a succubus prying her way through my chamber walls.  I sought salvation in your link to the yard with “a few plastic pink flamingos,” but was met with those inciting mobs that threatened pink-flamingan destruction; they took the guise of the dreaded 404 Error.  A few semi-Jungian observations:

404: Not Found, 
606: Not Allowed to Leave.

Green Flamingos and Pink Flamingos are at opposite points of the color wheel. How many green flamingos has anyone ever seen?  My maternal grandparents knew the power of flamingo pink and set genuine plaster flamingos in their front yard.  I believe they also had one of those silver spheres on a pedestal to reflect flamingos of pink.  Not to worry should the demons of green pierce their walls: the switch plates in their bedrooms were equipped with holy water receptacles. 

Throw green+flamingos at Google and see how few hits you receive.  Certainly, John Waters, anointed by William Burroughs as the Pope of Trash, recognizes the “source of all the ire in the first place.”  I leave the gentle reader to green symbolism in Waters' works.

title: 30 under 30

pages.html:
“30 Under 30: The New Chicago” is a look at people from all backgrounds and professions. From entrepreneurs to artists, performers to priests and athletes to scientists, the list displays the remarkable and eclectic talents of the rising stars in Chicago. Peruse at will.

Although all of our featured 30 maintain varied careers and objectives, they all shared similar advice and motivations: passion.

We were going to include the staff of sixosix as a whole, of course, but thought that would be shameless self-promotion.

While it certainly took some time to collect all 30 of these amazing stories, it made it even clearer that it truly is the people that make this city worth living in. Keep an eye on these 30 talents, and check out their additional information. Make the right connections and you may find yourself on our next list.

 

 

Let's be honest: perusing a review of four-star restaurant Trio is like reading a foreign novel. Casual references to “demitasse of hot lamb consommé” and “puddle of curry emulsion” jump off the page as a culinary departure from more standard fare like tuna melts and cheeseburgers. But for chef Grant Ashatz, a 29-year-old graduate of New York 's prestigious Culinary Institute of America, French-infused fare is standard. According to an interview in the Tribune , he believes “there's a food revolution under way around the world” and he wants to be part of it. The Evanston restaurant, which owner Henry Adaniya redesigned from its Asian-inspired décor to better fit Ashatz's French background, now serves four- and eight-course dinners rather than a la carte items. But there is a cardinal rule of dining that can't be broken: “Whether the techniques used to produce it are new or old,” Achatz says, “there's one fundamental rule: If a dish does not taste good, it does not go into the dining room.”

More info: http://www.trio-restaurant.com/staff/chef/

 

 

While debates on homosexuality take place around the world, the smaller issues of the gay community are often overlooked. An actor with About Face Youth Theatre, a nationally-recognized troupe that examines the gay, lesbian and bisexual communities, Tony Alvarado-Rivera, 23, has built a reputation as an outspoken activist for gay issues related specifically to Latino communities. Alvarado-Rivera's recurring feature on outlineschicago.com, a publication of the Windy City Media Group, typically mixes Spanish with English while serving as an online diary of sorts where he discusses topics as far-ranging as growing into an adult relationship with his father to his first drag experience. In addition, he supports the Oak Park Area Lesbian and Gay Association, which has one of the highest community-based gay memberships in Illinois . The secret, he says, is to build bridges through knowledge and education: “ If we can build an intergenerational setting, there is so much change we can all make for the next generations to come.”

More info: http://www.outlineschicago.com/gay/lesbian/news/ARTICLE.php?AID=242

 

 

Since becoming a household name in 1995 after an accident with a Metra train that cut off half her leg, Rachel Barton has not missed a beat. She began violin studies at the age of three, making her professional debut four years later with the Chicago String Ensemble. By age ten she was appearing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. One might expect that a woman this devoted to classical might might not be any fun, but this couldn't be further from the truth. She has performed at Bulls halftime shows, and has even performed violin-arranged Metallica covers. Barton has received many awards, including Chicagoan of the Year from Chicago Magazine in 1996. She has also given back to the city that has supported her throughout the years, teaching young musicians at a number of different institutions around the city. Barton's latest album, violin concertos composed by Brahms and Joachim, was released last year on Cedille Records.

More info: http://www.rachelbarton.com/index.htm

 

 

While American soccer doesn't have the fan support the sport enjoys in Europe or elsewhere, there isn't a shortage of premier players. DaMarcus Beasley, a midfielder for the Major League Soccer squad Chicago Fire, has proven himself a world-class athlete. While the Fire suffered a loss to the San Jose Earthquakes in last year's MLS Cup, it didn't hurt Beasley's season, going on to score eight goals in both regular-season and tournament play. He focuses on his game with dogged determination, but at the same time understands how to keep perspective. When asked how he stays calm in the face of major national matches, Beasley responded, “It's all about business, just another game. I just played.” To further add to his already impressive list of achievements, Beasley scored the only goal in the United States' 1-0 win over Poland in an exhibition match March 31, 2004.

More info: http://www.chicago-fire.com/roster/player.asp?pCode=DBEA

 

 

Real estate isn't the easiest business. And while real-estate celebrity isn't easy to come by – here you should think of Chaz Walters' “Hot Property” campaign – it's hard work that propels you to the top in the market. Twenty-four-year-old Peter Brandel has obviously paid his industry dues, completing 16 residential transactions last year, a figure that becomes all the more intriguing given the recent economic downturn. Brandel uses the situation to his benefit, however. “While the economic climate is less than perfect, low interest rates and high rents make a person secure with their job seriously consider buying,” he says. “I find buyers through referrals.” His age brings a certain level of prestige to the job, as Brandel was even tapped as a source for a New York Times article on media trends in men his age. But when asked if there are any hidden perks to the job, Brandel is quick to reply. “I know the city well enough to correct cab drivers,” he says.

More info: http://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/29/technology/29guy.html?8dpc

Jeffrey Brown believes graphic novels are “probably the least tapped medium in the arts today,” he says. “People are beginning to realize that comics are a powerful language.”  Brown explores and intensifies that power through his trio of graphic novels, “Clumsy,” “Unlikely,” and his latest publication, “AEIOU,” all of which explore the complexities of heartache and loss through stark, sparse pen-and-ink panels and soul-baring storylines.  Brown finds that the sharing of the personal self helps the artist to connect with his audience, and his works push past what he refers to as “thinly veiled metaphor and fictionalization,” which is completely true, as one character voices the simple line “I don't like being alone after sex,” for example. How true-to-life are they?  Each issue of AEIOU, the final chapter in the trilogy, comes with a piece of a note or letter from the girl.  That's right, the girl.

More info: http://www.margomitchell.com/thc/jb.htm

 

 

Carolyn Brundage has her hands full. She started ten years ago as a nationally-ranked member of DECA, Inc., an association of marketing students, and has steadily become one of the nation's leading fashion advisers. Her ideas and advice are commonly sought out in the press; she has appeared in Chicago Scene, TCW and UR Magazine, to name just a few. She brought her fashion sensibilities to the Web and founded Chicago Design Group, an organization dedicated to Web design, hosting, maintenance and promotion. CDG's clients run the gamut from the Chicago Fashion Foundation, YM Chicago, and Salon Mor. In addition to this already-loaded plate, Brundage runs Chicagobeauty.com, a product of the Chicago Design Group, a Web site that rates and locates salons in the Chicagoland area. As if all this weren't enough, Brundage offers advice to the fashion conscious and hopeless alike in a weekly column that appears in the Chicago Sun-Times' RedStreak edition. Brundage lives in Chicago with her husband, Brian, and her two-year-old son.

More info: http://www.chicagobeauty.com/carolyn_brundage.htm

 

 

How great would it be to work for Saturday Night Live? After years on the comedy circuits, Second City alum Liz Cackowski is about to find out. As of Feb. 24, 2004 , she's headed to NBC's flagship sketch comedy show as a staff writer. Cackowski was a player in the ComedySportz theatre beginning in February 2001 and made the move to the Second City in September 2003. She obviously didn't get to spend much time with the theatre that launched the careers of such notables as Dan Aykroyd and Bill Murray, but a Saturday Night Live invitation isn't something to be taken lightly. But she's no stranger to putting in the time to get the job done. “Between rehearsing and performing, I'm looking at some 60-hour weeks,” Cackowski said of her stint at Second City . In addition to her Chicago experience, she also worked on the Chicago-style sketch comedy troupe Boom Chicago in Amsterdam .

More info: http://www.improvisation.ws/mb/showthread.php?t=22676

 

 

The mark of a critical and valuable columnist is in the details. And the details. Besides working on political organization drives, writing Legion: For They Are Many, a book on the Cook County Democratic Party, and endlessly researching Chicago cityscape and history, Ramsin Canon writes as a political columnist for Gapersblock.com. At 22, the language found in his columns is decisive and his understanding of political events in Chicago is researched, informed, and comprehensive. What's critical to Ramsin is “finding truth about how each local political organization works … and how democracy has faded in favor of a feudal organizational system in Chicago.” While he has covered events such as the hired truck scandal of earlier this year, where the city paid drivers for doing little or no work, and issues like “The Gentrification Myth,” a series of essays, Ramsin says that his most demanding writing is on the current Illinois Senate race. In the tradition of Chicago reporters, Ramsin Canon's observations, much like Chicago politics itself, strikes the reader as hard, a bit gritty, sometimes hilarious, and unyielding – commentary not to be taken with a grain of salt.

More stuff: http://chicagolife.blogspot.com/2004_01_25_chicagolife_archive.html

 

 

For most of us, the 8-bit video game revolution ended sometime around 1995. But, keeping pace with the current trend of making yesterday's consumables the new Hip Thing, Mark DeNardo and a small cachet of musicians are retrofitting the Game Boy as a music machine, creating beeps and loops for a generation weaned on cartridge music. In an interview with Wired , the 29-year-old DeNardo discussed the relative merits of his unlikely music source. “The digital medium may have more accuracy, but it doesn't have as good a vibe,” he said. “But when you can hear the sequence and feel it, it's like listening to a live band rather than someone singing along with a digital karaoke machine.” His lyrics tend more toward the superficially fun: “We're going to a bad party / drink beer and meet ladies,” he chants over a loop that wouldn't be out of place as the music to a boss in Super Mario Bros. For the video game generation, it's the perfect mix of kitsch and modern.

More info: www.markdenardo.com

After receiving a master's degree in fine arts from the University of Illinois in Champaign-Urbana, Julie Farstad relocated to Chicago and, in short order, was featured in New American Paintings, Book XLI , a bible of sorts for up-and-coming artists. True, she is a provocative visual artist, painting scenes of crawling infants and eerie babies. Her work exudes a minimalism, where the infants are often presented on plain colored backgrounds, lending a starkness to the pieces. But most astounding is her technique: she uses glazing, which applies additional layers to the paint. Her work has been displayed at the Zolla/Lieberman Gallery. She is also a part-time faculty member at Northeastern Illinois University, and gives lectures around the city. In addition to creating visual art, Julie is the co-publisher and editor – as well as a writer – of Mouth to Mouth magazine, which aims to open up the Chicago art scene to more people, and to invigorate discourse surrounding art and culture by publishing only interviews without images.

More info: http://www.zollaliebermangallery.com/artists_pics/juliefarstad.html

 

 

Anyone working in Chicago arts education understands both the lack of funding and the inversely proportionate need for art in classrooms. To tackle both issues is a demanding endeavor, but one 24-year-old Taryn Fisher feels is crucial, even obligatory, to professionals working in the arts. For the past three years, Fisher has worked as studio coordinator and teacher at Chicago 's Lookingglass Theater Company, where she manages off-sight classes and works with 37 different schools in arts-integration, including schools with students with autism. A self-stated “professional camp counselor,” she has also worked as a tutor in a maximum-security youth prison. Arts education, she says, “teaches kids self-confidence and growth,” both of which are critical components of theater and education. Fisher's attention to both is vital to her character and deeply apparent as she discusses her career. With poignant gestures and a subtle, qualifying vocal tone, you are convinced of one thing – this woman cares about what she does. As a Chicago educator, she is as indispensable as the art she teaches.

 

 

Asking for money from total strangers is like trying to dress yourself with one arm. You think it's not going to be that hard, but by the time you're done, it seems like there is little energy left for anything else. This is the life of a fundraiser. Kelly Glenn, the finance director for Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich, spends most of her time raising money for his campaigns. “I have to convince CEOs that I am just as important as they are to get them to listen,” Glenn says. Kelly started her career in fundraising for then-Congressman Blagojevich and, after his election, she traveled to Washington , D.C. , to continue her political career. When Blagojevich decided to run for the governor's seat, she came back to Chicago to run the campaign fundraising. “I would always be the youngest person in the room by ten or 15 years,” she says. “My age was definitely something to overcome.” Glenn has indeed overcome her age as she continues to raise money for the governor's campaign and also assists in the fundraising for the community and other Democratic nominees at both the state and federal level.

More info: http://www.illinois.gov/default.cfm
 

 

In sixth grade, about the same time The Cure released Disintegration and De La Soul released Three Feet High and Rising, Michael Guarrine decided that excitable and sometimes-danceable rock and roll was for him. Music has been part of his entire life: his mother played piano and his father was a church singer. One of his first memories, he says, is singing the National Anthem at the age of three for his parents' friends, a different cry from his sixth-grade influences and current three-year role as lead singer of the Chicago-based band Watchers. “The band,” 27 year-old Guarrine states, “wants to present challenging to play and entertaining music.” The audience seems pretty damn entertained at Watchers shows as Guarrine works them into an unbound frenzy by leaping into walls, people and the stage, inviting their often unused and compelling energy into the open. Simply, Watchers make people move, an appreciated alternative to the sometimes stand-offish, stand-still indie-rock Chicago scene.

More info: http://www.pitchforkmedia.com/record-reviews/w/watchers/to-the-rooftops.shtml

 

 

If you had started your own successful company by yourself by the age of 25, do you think you'd stop what you were doing and do it all over again? Dawn Hancock is a self-taught print and Web designer who had been working in Chicago since 1999, when she started SomeOddPilot, a small design firm. “My father passed away and it made me re-evaluate some of my priorities,” Hancock says. Standing up for various causes has been both a part of her personal life and her work. Hancock has focused her new design company, firebelly designs, toward “working with socially responsible companies and organizations.” Hancock began volunteering in 1999 with the Lesbian Community Cancer Project and designed the site www.lccp.org. In the fall of 2000, she stepped up to be the organization's creative director and worked on the BitchToQuit anti-tobacco campaign. “[That] was the moment I realized firebelly could really affect people,” she says. “It has been the most rewarding project.” Working with firebelly, Hancock is in a different place than she was five years ago with SomeOddPilot, and she attributes it to passion. “You have to be passionate about what you do, whatever it is,” she says.

More info: www.firebellydesign.com

What's the hardest part about being a young professor at a major university?  “Efficiently managing your time,” says Mark Hersam, an assistant professor in Northwestern University 's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. He also directs the Hersam Group – a research collective focused on nanotechnology – in a field that studies miniaturization and the possibility of performing calculations at the molecular level, with applications ranging from computer chips to refined DNA sequencing. As a young professor in a challenging field, Hersam has met the challenges of academic life head-on.  After completing a master's degree in a single year, and a Ph.D. in only three more, Hersam knows what it takes to be a successful teacher and researcher. His advice to students thinking about a career in academia?  “The best thing an aspiring academic can do as a student is learn to be as efficient as possible in all aspects of student life, including classes, extracurricular activities, community service, research projects and leadership positions,” Hersam says. Research, he adds, is the most important of these elements, because that is where students “learn the challenges and excitement of generating new knowledge. A deep understanding of the research enterprise is invaluable once you begin a career in academia.”

More info: http://www.hersam-group.northwestern.edu/

 

 

For new, emerging artists, finding that first gallery show can often be half the battle. Enter the Tangerine Arts Group. Founded in March 2002, the TAG is a Chicago-based media collective for the presentation of new art. Managing Director Jessica Hoff describes its conception as “the brain child” of five friends living in Kalamazoo , Michigan , who, once graduated and collectively moved to Chicago , very quickly decided they were not interested in the type of sucking up and social climbing necessary to get their art seen and funded. The TAG was created out of this frustration, and currently funds not only the projects of the core group, but also takes as its goal community outreach to connect collaborating artists of all media. The organization is 100 percent volunteer-based. The collective brings artistic events into the community that are affordable and open to the public and that encourage interaction between the artist and the community.

More info: http://www.tangerinearts.org

 

 

In high school, Jessica's Hopper's camera was stolen. So, instead of becoming a professional photographer at the age of 18, she started the music-based Hopper PR, which aims to “represent our clients' vision with integrity, accuracy and take great pains not to muss our hair while doing so.” At 27, Jessica says she is still invested and interested in getting to know her clients and how “art is impacted by capitalism.” Or, in the case of the music business, how they can clash. Music is “a young people's industry” full of the energy and determinism of youth. “It's difficult to be past 30 and not bitter in the music industry,” Jessica states. “It's intrinsic in the business.” Though as a confident, creative leader in the music business and three years shy of a “bitterness” that may never come to her, Jessica stands out as a professional and personal supporter of significant music in Chicago .

More info: www.hopperpr.com

 

 

It's interesting, speaking with an artist whose primary focus at the moment is to focus on his own pieces, to make sure he's where he needs to be with his craft, as opposed to working directly for the sole purpose of another gallery show. “Since graduation, I've been in a few group shows,” 27-year-old visual artist Shane Huffman says, referring to his 2002 master's degree in fine arts from the University of Illinois-Chicago. “I've become a bit reclusive, trying to create a large body of work – something that I can feel strongly about.” Most of his pieces are a juxtaposition of different styles, including photography and sculpture, but he's not particular about the medium. “I'll tend to work on more than one piece at a time, to find connections in the work,” he says. But through these connections, his pieces still have a deeply personal bend. “I want to understand my place in the universe and the way that I work with my family, my personal life, my job, my emotions, and presenting them in ways that are personal and idiosyncratic,” he concludes. Sounds like the reclusive period is working.

More info: http://www.uic.edu/aa/college/gallery400/01-exhibit_pages/01_ate02_huffman-text.htm
 

 

Halena Kays is a hypocrite. More specifically, she is part of the The Hypocrites ensemble cast, a theatre group that performs regularly at Gallery 37's Storefront Theatre. The group has put on a variety of shows, most notably an adaptation of Edward Gorey's “Dispirited Diverson For Christmas.” She is also the artistic director for Chicago-based Barrel of Monkeys, a five-year-old comedic organization that performs stories and plays written by children in the Chicago Public School system, and conducts writing workshops with the children. BOM cast members will later perform the work in their schools . Kays is the director of BOM's critically acclaimed “That's Weird, Grandma,” which is currently playing at the Neo-Futurarium. In the same vein as “Too Much Light Makes the Baby Go Blind,” the mainstay performance for the Neo-Futurists, “That's Weird, Grandma” is an hour-long show that changes weekly based on audience votes. Kays is also a regular correspondent for “Artbeat Chicago,” a Channel 11 production. Apparently hypocrisy has its merits.

More info: http://wttw.com/artbeat/hosts.html#halena

Artists typically undergo years of instruction and training, imitating the styles of established masters before emerging into their own unique style, if they make the transformation at all. Kevin Oswald decided not to wait: He picked up a brush for the first time at age nine and now, by age 14, has created more than 100 works. His paintings have been displayed at gallery shows in Chicago and Blue Island , and some have sold for upwards of $650. “I paint pictures I see in magazines or on line, not something going through my head,” Oswald said of his inspiration. “I let it come to me because some days you don't feel like picking up a brush and other days you can't stop painting.” Oswald said he turns over a portion of all his sales to two charities: Joliet 's Guardian Angel Home for abused women and children, and the Nazareth Home, a Northwest Indiana-based agency that takes in orphaned babies. “Where you hear some parents tell their kids to go practice the piano for an hour, I don't think I've once ever had to tell Kevin to go do art,” Oswald's mother, Patty, said. “If anything, I worry about him spending too much time in the studio and forgetting about his other school subjects.”

More info: http://www.kevinoswaldgallery.com/

 

 

While many of us may vaguely claim that the children are our future, Eboo Patel has a more specific view: “Kids have the opportunity to create or destroy,” he commented in an interview with Conscious Choice, a healthy-living journal. “If you don't give them the opportunity to create, they will destroy.” In the hopes of helping children of all faiths to create profound social change, the 26-year-old founded - and is now the executive director of - Chicago 's Interfaith Youth Core, which brings together children of different faiths for the sake of social projects. Patel was cited as one of 30 social visionaries under 30 changing the world by Utne Reader in 2002, and his essays have appeared in Spiritual Perspectives on America's Role as a Superpower, God Within , Global Uprising, Initiative and Interreligious Insight. Patel received his doctorate from Oxford , where he studied as a Rhodes Scholar. He also speaks on interfaith issues worldwide.

More info: http://www.youthactivism.org/EbooPatel.html

 

 

Newspapers are in an interesting position: on one hand, they have to objectively report the news, but on the other, it's just human nature to put together some sort of commentary on any number of topics. Hence the role of the columnist. Interviewing can be tricky, however, since “so much of it is about whether you have your clients' confidence and whether they're willing to listen to you and accept you as an expert,” she says. Pickett came to Chicago five years ago, and is currently something of a journalistic celebrity for her “Sunday lunch” pieces where she mixes questions with self-referential commentary a standard news reporter couldn't pull off. For example, when discussing John Elway's endorsement contract with Prilosec, she wonders whether or not to make a drinking game out of the phrase “road to relief.” She's now in-demand enough to begin penning book-jacket reviews, like she did for the recent “The Family CFO,” where her personable writing style remains intact. “One of the things that's been really emphasized to me is how important it is to get out,” she says, “to be in the city and be in the world, and be writing about things that are happening, things that are out there.” She's doing a good job of that.

More info: http://www.suntimes.com/special_sections/sept11/voices/cst-nws-911pickett08.html

 

 

Ten years ago, Amy Schroeder created the first issue of Venus Zine in her dorm room, done entirely in one night using a word processor, a glue stick, a few photos and a copy machine. Once she discovered her niche market of “ample coverage of lady rockers,” as she calls it, it was all uphill from there. Today, Venus has established itself as a major magazine, covering the role of women in the arts and entertainment fields, boasting an international circulation of over 60,000 while remaining an entirely independent entity.  She credits the city of Chicago with the magazine's growth, not having to deal with the sheer numbers of publications in the Bay Area or the high cost of production in New York . The key to her success?  “We haven't compromised our vision or our content as we continue to grow,” claims Schroeder.  “Each new issue of Venus gets better and better and all of the editors and contributors see it as an ongoing project.”

More info: http://www.venuszine.com/
 

 

At 21, most of us were stressing over college finals and research papers. At 21, Alpana Singh was passing the advanced test of the Court of Master Sommeliers, the international examining body for wine and beverage service, becoming the youngest to do so. At 27, she manages the wine selection at Everest, the four-star restaurant atop the Chicago Stock Exchange. “My job is not to pick the wine for them, but to help them pick a wine for themselves,” she says. As an additional honor, Singh was one of Restaurant and Hospitality's Rising Stars in 2001 and has been named as the new host of WTTW's restaurant-review show “Check, Please!” She is currently preparing to earn her master sommelier diploma, a test which has only a three percent pass rate. As it stands, the youngest person to pass the test was 27. Only 11 of the few who have graduated are women. Talk about the wine glass being half-full.

More info: http://foodandwine.netscape.com/invoke.cfm?objectID=C8B3370C-7803-4D90-9E457FFC8C5BA3E0

When he answered the phone, he was in Arizona , and had just won another race. Corey Steinbrecher is a cyclist. It's what he does. He's raced just about every state in America as well as all over Europe . After graduating early from high school, he moved to Arizona when he was 17, and, by the time he was 18, he was racing professionally. Steinbrecher explained that it all started back in Glen Ellyn , where, as a ten-year-old, he would hang out at the bike shop. Soon local cyclists invited him on group rides, and encouraged him to develop his skills. Being so much younger than other cyclists – he's currently a member of the U.S. National Under-23 squad – has its share of both advantages and disadvantages. Unfortunately, his college credits are rolling in slowly and his social life is frequently put on hold. But, at 21, Steinbrecher has nurtured a passion for cycling and an addiction to hard work that will be a strong foundation as he approaches his peak cycling years, estimated to be 29-32 for most racers.

More info: http://www.jellybellycycling.com/Team_Members/steinbrecher04.htm

 

 

In a day when knock-off Louis Vuitton bags run rampant on the arms and shoulders of both women and men, Chicago has given us our very own DIY approach to bags, courtesy of thirty-year-old Jennifer Velarde. When discussing her previous career, Velarde spoke of time when she was “searching for other things, but nothing was connecting.” That same search lead her and her associates from the hobby of making handcrafted bags in Velarde's studio apartment to a full-time entrepreneurial business. Started just four years ago, Velarde has opened stores in Chicago and Boston to provide people with “a really good time while they shop.” Customers come into her stores and choose from a large selection of fabrics and designs to build their own bags, assisted by employees with PDAs that place the orders wirelessly. Velarde credits this technology with helping them expand and deliver the products quickly. “Being young helped me. It gave me the freedom to take bigger risks,” she says. “Everyone out there needs to keep searching. Do not be afraid to invest time for your passions.”

More info: http://www.1154lill.com/home/
 

 

Steve Versaw, the 28 year-old drummer for the emerging Chicago band The M's, attributes much of his music career to community and environment. At the age of 15, though, Versaw was helped by building a music club with his friends. To him, rock and roll comes in built stages. “You sacrifice a lot, but the fun, the beauty is the road,” he says. “The Chicago environment is very supportive and shared.” But it can also be humbling, since “every time you think you've made it, you realize you're at the bottom of the ladder again.” Stages and stages. Versaw started playing music at the age of 12 and has been playing with The M's for the past two years. The M's consists of “four people, good friends, who work well together … a small community,” Versaw said. “We're making it up as we go.” In this way, Steve echoes much of the relevance of Chicago rock and roll, an intensely intertwined rhizome community, packed between amber cornstalks, mid-cities and persistent American voices.

More info: http://www.brilliante.tv/ms.htm

 

 

Name a restaurant where can you smoke apple-flavored tobacco, watch
belly-dancing goddesses shake their hips dangerously close to your couscous and
eat some of Chicago's best Middle Eastern food. Souk, located on Milwaukee, is
a good guess. Just a few years ago, the restaurant was only open a few nights a
week. But things have changed, and much of this can be attributed to chef
Daniel Wright. The 28-year-old has not only been reviewed in almost every major
Chicago publication for his amazing dishes, but also has cooking in his blood,
which goes back as far as he can remember. "My parents got divorced when I was
young," Wright explains. "My brother threatened to kick my ass if I didn't cook
for the family." Not only does his cooking set him apart, but he also makes a
habit of having his hands in everything. When he's not working, you can catch
him sitting in a back booth, chatting with Nasser Rastom, Souk's owner, and
coming up with fresh ideas for the restaurant: Marketing concepts, ways to keep
the crowd from getting rowdy or even a new preparation method for the lame
mashy are all fair game when discussing business. And business is good these
days.

More info: http://www.chicagourmet.com/event031604.html

 

 

Life's moving along at a pace that could only be described as breakneck for Sho Yano. He enrolled as a pre-med student at Loyola University Chicago when he was nine. By 12, he had graduated with an undergraduate degree and now, at 13 years old, is a Ph.D. and M.D. student at the University of Chicago 's Pritzker School of Medicine. His media exposure has reached a critical mass, with a front-page story in the Tribune , an interview with Anderson Cooper on CNN and a spot on 60 Minutes II . His numbers far outstrip the average student: a 1,500 SAT score. An IQ of approximately 200. A collegiate GPA of 3.9. But through all his experiences, he's remained amazingly calm. “People think I am made different or affected because of media exposure, but not at all,” Yano says. But there is, of course, the question of how he'll feel with multiple advanced degrees around his 20th birthday. “People have been joking with me, telling me to grow a beard and a mustache to look older,” he says.

More info: http://www.cnn.com/2003/EDUCATION/08/25/sprj.sch.wonder.kid.ap/

title: editor's note

pages.html:
According to exhaustive Internet research, themed parties work much better than non-themed events. Reference toga parties or masquerade balls, where the ignominy of dressing in strange, fantastic garb somehow brings people together. Alcohol helps, too. So when the theatre troupe Collaboraction presented their Carnaval party – sponsored by sixosix, of course – I found the body-painting and carnival masks made for an interesting evening.

Let me clarify: Part of an entire room was dedicated to painting either fully- or semi-naked bodies. Very attractive bodies. Modesty was a foreign concept. Let's do a quick recap.

The whole thing made me wish I had grown up in Brazil and knew how to rhumba and samba and such.

Fashion shows where a logo that I helped to create sit atop the heads of attractive people is a rare occurrence, one where I can feel two emotions that I don't normally belong together: drunk and proud.


Collecting e-mail addresses from people who don't want to give out their e-mail addresses is best left to the professionals. By “professionals,” I mean “attractive girls who know how to work a front desk.”

People from all walks of life show up to these sort of events: slick businessmen and men with Morrissey tattoos, women with dreadlocks and women who walk around topless because “my boyfriend said it was a good idea.”

I spent the majority of the evening being turned down by men when I asked them for their e-mail addresses, and just plain being turned down by women.

But I did learn two important things: One, key-lime-pie Martinis are always a bad idea, and two, how much respect should be given to bartenders and others in industries that routinely deal with drunks. Ever tried to coordinate a few hundred people who have been drinking for hours into a huge game of Twister?

When progress is the aim, a collective goal is usually the best path for obtaining it. When the collective goal is art and supporting or promoting art, you have a hell of a better time getting it done. Booze doesn't hurt either.

title: awkward architecture

pages.html:
Ahh …Chicago, the first “Modern City” of architecture. We are the big leagues. We start architectural movements here, and people from all around the globe come just to ogle at the glass and cement colossusus and the prairie-style structures that dot our urban landscape. If you want to learn about the famous architecture of Chicago, take one of the many fine tours or pick up one of the countless books on the subject. But what about those overlooked buildings? What about the buildings that you walk by and rather than inspiring awe, they make you uneasy or confused? What about the buildings that the tours won't take you to? Don't worry, because we at sixosix are happy to take it upon ourselves to fill you in on the buildings that make us go “huh”?



  see previous photos

St. Mary of Nazareth Hospital
2233 West Division Street

This building is part of the Resurrection Health Care system, which may seem inconsequential, but is extremely important: This is the health care system that reconstructed this photographer's cheekbone after it got smashed to pieces. But what does this have to do with the building's architecture? It's simple: the future. My cheekbone was pieced back together from something like 20-plus different pieces. That's the stuff of the future if I've ever heard it. Now look at this building and think about it.

Whether or not you believe that this building is a portal into the future of science or not, kudos to architects who designed buildings that will be nothing but a reference to Kubrick films for much of the population.



  see previous photos

“The Mafia House”
The corner of Montana and Greenview

I may not know much at the tender young age of 24, but I do know that nothing good can be happening inside a building with only two entrances: the steel-gated door entry and the steel-reinforced garage door entrance. I'm not one to judge, or speculate, but I think that the pedophiliac coke dealers or Yakuza underbosses that live in this place might be attracting a little more attention to themselves living in a place like this. It's just begging to be tapped by the FBI.

If I were a good investigative reporter, I would have been brave enough to go knock on the door of this place, but the reality is that I barely had the nerve to stand on the street and take a picture. Be brave, sixosix reader. Go knock on the door and report for us!

 


  see previous photos

The Cross House
1500 block of Chestnut

Someone really needs to get over all their dead parakeets.

 


  see previous photos

The Leaning Tower of Niles
6300 Touhy Avenue

I'm a pretty cynical guy. So, as amazed as I had been every time I've ever driven by the Leaning Tower of Niles – a smaller replica of the famous building in Pisa, Italy, sandwiched between a YMCA and a Ford dealership – I've always started into my rant about Americans having no culture and looking to replicate something from a country that does to break up the monotony of their SUV-driven-suburban-soccer-mom-strip-mall world. Thus I was completely aghast when I discovered this structure was built in 1934, before the advent of the American Cultural Wasteland. Thank you, Baby Boomers. And therefore I put my Hat of Cynicism back on its rack and bow before thee, almighty Leaning Tower of Niles. You have my full respect.

 


  see previous photos

Tromp'e' loi Building
The corner of Morgan and Van Buren

(Enter room full of architects, designers, and capitalists …)

“You know what would really save us costs?”
“What?”
“If instead of designing and building a really interesting building, we had someone paint the whole building to make it appear like it's something great!”
(the crowd ooohs and ahhhs)

“Oh, you know what would be just super? If we painted the Sears Tower on the west side of the building so people think they're looking right through it!”
“My God that's a smashing idea, Rupert! This will be incredible, no one will notice! All will be fooled by our trickery!”
(many high fives and slaps on the back)

Nice try, boys. This building is an atrocity, and thus has made our list.



  see previous photos

The Gold Pyramid
37921 N. Dilleys Road, Wadsworth , Illinois

This building is a little outside of the realm of Chicagoland, but when we heard of its existence, we immediately tacked this architectural oddity onto our list. If you want to learn more about the bazaars and all the wonders of Egypt you could buy within this compound of weird, do visit their Web site. I'm here to tell you that as architecturally shocking as this building might be, it's really kinda creepy. I visited on a Saturday afternoon, and the gates, which are strung between two yellow cement walls filled with hieroglyphics, were locked and I could only peer through them, past the dilapidated gift shop, past the acres of driveway gravel that I can only imagine were once a parking lot to hold all those who would make their pilgrimage to this Waco-wannabe, and past the enormous statue of a pharaoh's sarcophagus, to see a pyramid dot the horizon.

I'm exaggerating a bit, but this thing was closed when I arrived. I had just driven the hour and a half from Chicago just to see it, and I was peeved. Nonetheless, we all must still tip our hats to brave souls who decided that rural northern Illinois was a good place to put a pyramid of gold, regardless of what all the Pabst-drinking, pickup-truck driving yokels hooted as they drove by, showering the stop sign with bullets.



  see previous photos

St Joseph's Ukranian Catholic Church
5000 North Cumberland Avenue

•  You shall not take the Lord's name in vain.
•  You shall not worship false idols. (cough, giantgoldenphalluses, cough)

title: feature - architectural artifacts

pages.html:
“Chicago is a city with an attitude problem,” he says. “It's the second city, and many people think along those lines: ‘Maybe if we build a shiny new building, then people will look at us.' You idiots, you had gorgeous buildings, now you have Niketown.” If you listen to Stuart Grannen, the future of commercial architecture in Chicago is grim. As the owner/operator of Architectural Artifacts, a high-end dealer of almost anything related to architecture – specifically that of the 19th and 20th centuries – Grannen is expected to be somewhat cynical of modern structural design. It's not the cynicism that makes this interesting, but its source. In speaking to him, you never get the sense that he is happy with his displeasure, as cynics so often are. It's readily apparent that he would like nothing more than to observe and enjoy as many beautiful buildings as possible, regardless of their date of construction.

“It's kind of like a beautiful woman,” he says, attempting to explain his fascination with architecture. “You see all kinds of beautiful women, but you also want something more, something classical and intelligent, something of quality. It's not just how ornate these buildings were, but the quality of the work.” From doors and mantelpieces to 20-foot concrete pillars and terra cotta gargoyles, Grannen saves anything he finds interesting from buildings that are to be demolished, even that which he knows he won't be able to sell for profit. Walking with him through his store, you can sense his passion for the architecture of the past, as well as his hope that he's contributing to its preservation.

It's not unfair to ask if what Grannen does is truly preserving art, or if he actually is cheapening its legacy by selling pieces of it to those who can afford such luxury. Initially, my thoughts followed a similar pattern. The idea of removing the choice pieces from a building seems antithetical to the ideas of preservation and restoration. Aren't the architectural wonders of the past best appreciated by allowing them to remain as they were at their inception, standing untouched, beautifully anachronistic? It very well may be that these days have passed. When constructing a new building, “there isn't the public appreciation or the tax breaks that there once were,” Grannen says. “I understand why someone wants to build an economically viable building. But, it's all about the almighty dollar now.” But the question remains: How can Grannen criticize the pursuit of the dollar when his business is so profitable? His business takes pieces of buildings and sells them, which makes his critique of those who build thinking only of the bottom line seem hypocritical.

Surprisingly, he doesn't run from these questions, nor does he seem at all rankled by their undertones. “I acknowledge that there is a tenuous line between art and profit in what I do,” he says. “But I'm always willing to sacrifice profit for some piece that I just can't allow to be destroyed.” But it doesn't work both ways: “I won't sacrifice art for profit,” he says. Grannen notes that neither he nor his company has anything to do with the decision to destroy the buildings, bristling at the suggestion that he is destroying art. “Without me, it would all go in the dump,” he says, rightfully so. “If another person were to ask a wrecking company, they'd be refused. We're the ones who risk our lives and spend our time keeping these things out of the dump.”

go to page 2

The amount of time to rescue these objects can range from a few hours to a few weeks, and the actual process is very simple: “We just climb up there and chip away,” Grannen says. He and his employees salvage pieces from 50-75 buildings each year, and it's never an easy project. He shows me the grating from an elevator from the Granada Theater – which was torn down in 1990 after standing in Rogers Park for more than 60 years – while explaining the perils of working around with a wrecking crew . “We work before, during, and after they're done,” he says. “They almost got us with the [wrecking] ball while we worked in the building. They don't care at all.”

The majority of the buildings on which Grannen works are in the Chicago area, though his network of contacts extends all over the country and into Europe. Whenever a building with any sort of historical significance is slated for demolition, Grannen is ready to travel, no matter the distance. While the majority of the buildings are in Chicago, the majority of his sales are outside, usually on either coast. “There just isn't the same appreciation here,” Grannen says.

Still, the question remains: Is this preservation? To some extent, the answer to such a question is going be based on the individual who's doing the answering. To think only in terms of simple preservation – the restoration of only a building's defects, without changing any vital parts, keeping the structure free-standing and not threatening its surroundings – is probably too narrow-minded. The world that we inhabit, quite simply, is out of space. The cities in which we live are already sprawling. Leaving every building with any aesthetic value standing would only result in endless, empty cities, with preserved buildings impeding progress. Perhaps the only way to preserve as much of the past as possible is to follow the lead of companies like Architectural Artifacts, doling out remnants of the past to anyone who might appreciate them.

There certainly isn't enough museum space to hold everything in Grannen's collection – his renovated sales floor will eventually span over 80,000 square feet. So the question ultimately becomes one inseparable from the definition of art, one wildly debated for centuries, and one not likely to be answered here. Is it productive in any way for art and architecture to be gracing the garden of a million-dollar home? Not for some, perhaps, but for others, the simple fact that the memorable aspects of these buildings are viewed somewhere, even if only by a select few, does more to maintain the legacy than their outright destruction and disposal.

While Chicago is known for its outstanding architecture, it very well may be that these achievements are slowly being destroyed, by wrecking ball and by the artless new construction. “When I first moved here, seventeen years ago, Michigan Avenue was a gem; now it's a strip mall,” Grannen says, without the smile on his face that one might hope to see. “Very little modern commercial architecture will become historic architecture. The buildings are strictly dollar-driven.”

return to page 1
go to page 3

In his attempt to preserve the architecture that gave Chicago its reputation, Grannen is currently constructing a 15,000-square foot museum of pieces from Chicago buildings, with plans to open in the fall of 2004. Featuring everything from Frank Lloyd Wright to Louis Sullivan, Grannen hopes the museum will give a glimpse of the beauty of Chicago's past. None of the pieces in the museum will be available for sale, as all are from Grannen's personal collection. His attempts to preserve the rich history of architecture extend beyond his museum to his daily activities. While some customers hope to buy pieces from Grannen and then drastically change the piece's character, Grannen won't allow it, if he's able to prevent it.

“If some couple tells me that they want to paint a gorgeous mantelpiece white, I'll suggest that they don't,” he says. “If they say ‘that's what we're going to do,' I won't sell it to them. I just can't do it.” When asked about the customers who completely reconfigure pieces, such as those who might destroy a pillar to make the base for a coffee table, Grannen shakes his head in disapproval, but acknowledges the thought behind the act. “If they have an appreciation, and it's done right, it can provide a link to the past,” he says. “But it's not often done right.”

As for the newer projects that have graced – or will grace – the Chicago skyline, he remains mostly tight-lipped. Of the horrendous new Soldier Field, Grannen acknowledges the effort to do something new, but criticizes the results. “It looks like nothing else around it,” he says. “Chicago's history is in concrete and pillars, not the wild, spaceship buildings coming down to eat Earth.” Of the Frank Gehry-designed Millennium Park, Grannen again plays the role of the architectural purist, citing the jarring contrast between new materials, style and Chicago's history, but he'd rather hold judgment until it's completed. New construction is not all bad, however: He does give a great deal of credit to Chicago Mayor Richard Daley for his efforts in restoring the beauty of a number of Chicago's public high schools.

It very well may be that those who expect to see their favorite buildings and homes preserved will have to either face the reality that their wishes will not be fulfilled, or must learn to adapt to a new style of preservation. Certainly everyone would like to see the architectural history of the city and the demands of progress meld in such a way that all are appeased. If this is to happen, the roles of urban archeologists, like Grannen, may have to be enhanced. The pool of buildings that could achieve landmark status is slowly dwindling as the city's demands begin to outweigh the sentimentality of its residents. The difficulty will be in trying to find a balance between the possibilities. I won't suggest Grannen or others like him have solved the problem – or even that everyone will agree with this method of preservation – but I would use it as an example of an effort to bridge the gap between the architectural highlights of the past and the demands of modern life. Gorgeous buildings will continue to be torn down, and some atrocious ones will be erected – hello, Mr. Trump! – but for all those who can't get over the demise of their favorite buildings, they can now, at least, own a piece of them.

Images of Architectual Artifacts courtesy Doug Fogelson, whose exhibition "Intersections" is now showing at the Kraft Lieberman Gallery. For more information, visit www.dougfogelson.com.

title: asphalt

pages.html:
Hi there! My name is Joe. I'm practicing leading architecture tours because I'll be taking the Cook County Tour Guide test in a few weeks. Yes, that's why it's free – because I'm not licensed just yet. What's my dream? Well, hopefully once I get enough experience I will be hired one of the boat tours on the Chicago River … that's where the money is on the tour guide circuit.

At least this is what I was telling people.

Visiting a big city is always fun. You get a book that tells you all the cool places to go, or you surf the web for days and days to figure out what you're supposed to see in whichever city it is that you are visiting. That sounds like par for a trip to an unfamiliar city, right?

Wrong.

I'm not saying that tours like that aren't fun; I live in Chicago, and I still take the Chicago River architecture tour at least once a summer. It fills me up with useless knowledge about this great city, like how every bridge over the river has a different style of watch-house overlooking it, each designed for a particular decade of style, or how there's that building on Wacker Drive that allegedly had a speakeasy way up on the top floor during the prohibition.

But these tours are cookie-cutter. The bus and walking tours lead the sightseers to places that everybody is supposed to visit: the Sears Tower, the Hancock Tower, Michigan Avenue, the Water Tower. The boat tours are limited to the Chicago River.

What about the sights in Bucktown? Or Lincoln Park? Or Pilsen? Or any of the city's 50 wards? Most of the time, they're neglected.

I decided I was going to “host” a free architecture tour of Chicago. It took me three days, but I made an awesome Free Architecture Tour sign, and waited for a beautiful day. I was going to lead the tour in my kick-ass Jeep, which is actually a piece of crap, and drop the top so the “customers” could look up.

When I was on my way down to the spot I had chosen to recruit people, I was pretty pumped up. It was Friday, 75 degrees and sunny, and the tourists were crawling the streets like ants on a dropped lollypop.

I parked my carriage, stood on the corner with my sign and waited. And waited and waited and waited and waited. Nobody showed interest in the least. People were reading the sign, but always kept walking. I decided that I needed to be a little more aggressive, so I began tapping my sign – which is a move I learned in Vegas from the people who give out the “escort” cards – and yapping at passersby:

“Free tour. You interested? Wanna see all the sights in Chicago you've only heard about?”

go to page 2

People still weren't responding. They totally ignored me after they read my sign. The only verbal “no” I got was from a very good-looking French couple. I decided to switch locations. As I walked down the sidewalk, a gentleman who was on his cell phone held up a finger at me, an indication that he was interested.

He finished his call and asked me what the deal was. I gave him my pitch and asked him where he was from. He had just moved here from Dallas, and wanted to go on the tour so he could learn more about Chicago. “A perfect candidate,” I thought to myself, as I tried to sell the tour as best as I could. Then he asked how it would be conducted.

“Oh, in my Jeep. Top down of course,” I replied cleverly.

This is when I lost the guy. He looked at me funny, wished me luck, and he was gone. I guess he didn't feel comfortable riding around a new city in a car with a total stranger.

A few minutes later, I was approached by a lady from Argentina.

“When do the boat tours start?” she asked.

“Umm … this isn't a boat tour. I'm not affiliated with them,” I answered, “Yet.”

“Oh. Well, do you know when they start, because I really want to take one of those.”

I told her that I didn't know, and then since I had her attention, I gave her my pitch. I told her about the Cook County Tour Guide test, and then explained my theory on visiting anywhere new.

It was all going fine, and she was an incredibly sweet lady until I said that the tours were conducted from my vehicle. She looked at me like I had just shot her horse. Denied again.

What was the deal here? Why weren't people willing to take a little risk? Yes, I am a stranger, but it's not like I'm kidnapping them. Even if I was, they probably had cell phones that they could use to alert the proper authorities. These people were visiting Chicago and missing out on some of the best-kept secrets that only locals know about.

When I came up with this idea, I decided that the tour was going to be the route I drive when I need to think, which I take very often: south on Lakeshore, over to Michigan Avenue, up to Chicago, up Rush to Division, over to Wells, up to Lincoln, over on Armitage to Sheffield, up to Wrigley, then back south on Clark street, past Lincoln Park and the zoo and finally ending up where I started.

No, they wouldn't get to see every part of the city, but there are a million and one sights along that route. What they would see is my Chicago. They would be visiting places and hearing anecdotes about memorable things that happened to me, or learning why I like to go to a certain spot, or seeing places where I think the view of the city is breathtaking. They probably wouldn't even care that this was all being conducted by a stranger from his jalopy of a car.

Think about it: if you were visiting New York , wouldn't it be much more fun and interesting to get a tour from a local? I would much rather do that then pay $25 for a tour of places everybody already knows about.

Frustrated and about to give up, I was approached by a guy who asked me what the catch was. “No catch,” I told him. I gave him my pitch to no avail. He was a local who just wanted to know why a kid was on the street with a homemade sign, trying to give a homemade tour.

“You're just trying to pick up girls,” he chuckled. He got me, because I started to laugh out loud. I denied it, but then he told me that he liked my approach and would try it sometime. Then he went on his way.

At the end of the day, I had given absolutely no Free Chicago Architecture tours. I was kind of disappointed; not so much that nobody was willing to get in my car with me, but because all of these visitors were missing out on a fun and informative, yet very different view of the city.

Hopefully the next time I'm visiting a place I don't know much about, I will see a crazy young man tapping his Free Tour of the City sign. I think that's a tour I'd love to take.
