title: hopscotch
blurb: hop your way through seemingly unrelated tidbits of knowledge (throwing stones unecessary).

pages.html:
On May 13, 1917 , a luminous apparition of the Virgin Mary appeared to three peasant children and delivered a prophecy . The children gave predictions of World War II, the spread of communism and a third prophecy, which the children wrote down and gave to the Vatican . In 2000 the Vatican finally revealed the third secret: a description of the 1981 assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II.

In 1777 while encamped in Valley Forge , George Washington had a vision that has been recorded and now sits in the Library of Congress. More than 4,000 words long, the vision contains the future of America, with lines such as, “Son of the Republic, look and learn, I cast my eyes upon America and beheld villages and towns and cities springing up one after another until the whole land from the Atlantic to the Pacific was dotted with them .”

Many people believe these lines written in 1654 by Nostradamus predicted 9/11:

In the City of God there will be a great thunder,
Two brothers torn apart by Chaos, while the fortress endures, the great leader will succumb. The third big war will begin when the big city is burning

Did you know that you can fold the new $5, $10, $50 and $100 bills and they show the World Trade Center attack in sequence? Add in the $20 and you have the complete sequence.

Famous T.V. psychic Miss Cleo was arrested in February 2003 for deceptively misrepresenting in her advertising that a reading would be provided at no cost. Her psychic creadabilty was unchallenged by the FTC and remains intact. Thank God.

The first clear reference to Tarot cards is from a collection of sermons found in the Steele Manuscript. The sermon is thought to date from approximately 1450-1470 and is a diatribe against games of chance. It gives a detailed description of the Tarot trumps , not only numbering them but naming them as well. .

John Edwards is believed to talk to dead relatives of participants on his TV show Crossing Over. Some believe his talent lies in his ability to do cold readings, which is a sleight-of-tongue technique fast-talking artists or so-called readers use. Cold reading has many methods whereby the reader can get out of a blatantly wrong guess with extreme speed. So fast that, unless you listen very carefully or are able to review a transcript of what was actually said during the reading, few would ever notice.

The Romans believed in the practice of augury , in which birds were dissected and analyzed. The future was predicted by the layout, size and condition of the birds' internal organs.




Edgar Cayce gave more than 14,000 prophetic readings between 1901 and 1945 covering more than 10,000 topics. When individuals came to him with a question, he would place himself into an induced sleep state in order to see the future. For many years the information dealt mainly with medical problems. Eventually the scope of his readings expanded to include such topics as meditation, dreams, reincarnation, and prophecy. The transcripts have provided the basis for over 300 popular books about Cayce's work.

The Voynich Manuscript has been dubbed “The Most Mysterious Manuscript in the World.” Wilfrid M. Voynich discovered it in 1912 amongst a collection of ancient manuscripts. It is written in either a code or an unknown language and to this day has been untranslatable. Theories abound that the manuscript contains medical information on eternal life.

pages.html:
It was inevitable. It had to happen, and I knew I would bear witness to the end.

It was one of those moments that seems to be a win-win situation, but 50 years from now will require Terminator-esque corrections. Cyborgs from the future – who look amazingly like Italian it-girl Mariacarla Boscono – will be sent back in time to change that one moment in order to save humanity: They will keep Karl Lagerfeld from joining the ranks of H&M.

Oh the horror. Imagine legions of 14-year-old girls wearing skinny, super-cute jeans flopping fold-up fans, dark glasses hiding their dead, dead eyes. I'll always remember where I was when I discovered Lagerfeld would be collaborating with the behemoth that is H&M – I was planning a trip to the Drake for a day of wine and shopping when my heart was stopped cold by a Chanel-logo arrow.

What comes next will be bleak. It will be a future that inspires madness and ruffles. Lagerfeld's diet will become requisite and the world will finally be teeny, tiny and thin. All that excess skin will be made into wallets and belts.

I beg of you, make it a quick death.

For those whose eyes aren't open wide enough to see this vision of seventh-circle hell, allow me to show you. With Lagerfeld's designs, H&M will have the ability to rule the world. They'll make more money in the first year of this collaboration than all the big houses combined. Fare thee well, Gucci. H&M will be in every fashion spread in every magazine all over the world. Little Lindsay Lohan wannabes will join the NKA and flounce around with their cheeks sucked in, fans in hand. Uniformity will be in the form of tweed minis and gorgeous denim. Every man, woman and child will be required to dress to the specifications of H&M.

How can we stop this sea of chic chicklets from taking over? I offer up a brave, shocking, even morally depraved alternative. Shop now and put H&M out of business. Fight against falling in love with old lovable Karl's cuts and details. Shop at the smaller places, those fighting the good fight.

My brave fashion fighters, join me as we shop to save the world. I have, as your fearless leader, found the bright brave boutiques that will be our salvation.

The first stop on the underground Concorde is Smack, located at1650 Division Street. Smack's brilliance is in its camouflage techniques. They load the windows with cute, girlie clothes only to have the cooler pieces tucked away inside. Seersucker suits, tank tops and pretty skirts will throw any H&M spy off-course. Delve into the back and you'll find the sale rack, loaded with gorgeous fur vests and wraps and skirts that are easily worth a pretty fortune. The one pièce de résistance for the resistance? Ties. Yes, ties. Wide, patterned and in colors only Mr. Kotter could wear, these ties are fab. Don't turn your nose up just, yet my comrades – these ties have crystal appliqués of phrases dear to our hearts (fag hag, anyone?). Take that, Karl!

The next meeting point is down the street – 1740 W. Division Street – at one of the best empire-fighting shops around. Yes, Noir, the always-awesome store that not nearly enough people frequent. Noir is calculating, also hiding the best pieces in the back. Let the H&Mers rifle through the pink minis and white cargo pants. I want to hide behind the smock dresses and cut out blouses (In mauve! Not pink, but mauve!) that hang in the nether regions of the store. Where else can you find stilettos that are cheap but last longer than anything from H&M ever has?

Next up is an old, old store that many walk past, not realizing the bounty that lays inside. Studio 90, at 5239 N. Clark Street, repels any NKA recruits with offerings for the more mature woman. But if you venture in, you'll be rewarded with a sight that will have you singing in the rain. Wellies! The absolutely perfect way to slosh around in the rain. Studio 90's supply was dwindling (any size 9 gals out there, hurry your big feet over for one of the last few pairs) but they promise to get more in post-summer. The big rubbery boots come in black and lovely stripes a la Paul Smith. These shoes are also perfect for stomping on the cheap shoes of the NKA.

The final stop in this, our first battle, is Xcito, located at 2858 N. Clark Street. Xcito is a bastion of originality with pant suits that could be worn in Bombay, khaki jackets with cuts that fit perfectly at the waist and more dresses and skirts with cut-outs and detailing that are making me smile as I write this. Take that, you uniformed teeny boppers!

My fashion fighters, unite in this dark and troubling time, and help keep the evil empire from fully rising. Otherwise, can someone get any DNA from Ms. Boscono?

title: editor's note

pages.html:
I expected just a simple movie at the Grant Park Film Festival, but I got more than I bargained for.

The first week the festival was running would have been relatively normal were it not for the picture that appears above. People apparently don't like it when you obstruct their view to get glamour shots. But the whole affair was in the pursuit of journalism, so we pressed on.

The second week was even stranger. Let's start with the fact that I was watching Hitchcock's The Birds and there were some late-night gulls swooping around for the first few minutes of the movie– this is an outdoor event, remember – but to truly get that roughing-it-in-the-middle-of-the-city feel, I had to be treated to some rain, of course.

I was still walking towards the park after getting off the train when I get hit with the first drops. The sky didn't look promising, but Metromix promised the movies would continue “as long as lightning, strong winds or other severe conditions are not present.” Wet and near-miserable it was, but hazardous it wasn't. A few steps later, I get a call from the friends I was meeting:

They: “Where are you?”
Me ( annoyed because, well, I'm standing in the rain ): “Standing in the rain.”
They: “Are you coming?” ( unintelligible noise ) “We've made a tent.”
Me: “Out of what? Your backpack?”
They: “No, the blanket.”

Necessary background: The blanket was pretty standard for picnic affairs – in fact, it served just that purpose on the previous week's rain-less evening in Grant Park – meaning it's not made of waterproof anything, but from scratchy wool. In a heavy rain, it would be more hassle than help as a covering. This was not a Good Idea.

Me: “That blanket belongs to my roommate, and it's definitely not waterproof.”
They: “What?” ( unintelligible noise ) “Are you coming?”
Me: ( sigh ) “I'm on my way.”

I made it to the open area and, unlike the previous week, there were large open spaces to stretch out. Of course, you didn't want to because of the mud, but what counts is that the opportunity was there. My friends had ditched the tent idea and had spread the blanket on the ground since the downpour had stopped for a moment. Maybe this would work after all.

The question of the night was a simple one: How was it - “it” referring to both the movie and the weather – going to end? The quick answers: The movie ended well, if that's what you call a catatonic woman carried to a car after the four main characters survived an onslaught of avian rage. And the weather cooperated as well – the rest of the night, we remaining movie watchers were treated to a lightning fireworks show over the lake.

So that question was answered: Things would turn out fine, but I was pretty much soaked to the bone. But there's nothing like good company. Even in the rain. While getting freaked out by the sounds of seagulls. And while using a blanket that doesn't belong to you as a tent.

You're not a real trooper until the rain hits.

Enjoy the issue.

title: fcc
blurb: Don't waste time thinking up your own set of morals.  The FCC is busy writing a set for the whole country.

pages.html:
It's time to clean up American broadcasting. Decency standards are again in season; they show up every few years after a dormant period ,like cicadas. And like cicadas, they bring out the worst in everyone. At times like these, most of us follow the same range of emotion as we do when bugs start falling from the sky in droves: First you just get annoyed that you have to pick them off your windshield getting into the car every morning, you get angry when they start dive bombing into your glass of lemonade and nesting in your hair, but by the end of the summer you can't help laughing because the whole episode is starting to remind you of a clever sketch of absurdist theatre, so thick is the ridiculousness, as foreign bodies are falling from the sky at the frequency of the little winged mushrooms in the original Super Mario Brothers. There is nothing wrong with promoting decency standards, in theory, as there is nothing wrong with plagues of insects, in theory. It is when the current state of decency regulations borders the absurd that American citizens can't help but wonder if they are living within the confines of a video game or of a democratic nation. It is when a term as subjective as “obscenity” comes under public scrutiny, and government appointed officials are expected to write laws, equally subjective in nature, to define language that falls under such a label, that our country's decency neuroses start to seem more grotesque and exaggerated than obscenity itself.

Because our radio and television broadcasts have been deemed increasingly smutty, our government-appointed Federal Communications Commission has been given the task of regulating obscenity on local and national airwaves. The FCC's regulations, up until very recently were extremely clear-cut. There existed a list of seven “dirty words” that you could not say on the television or radio. (1) As comedian George Carlin outlined in his infamous 1978 monologue , the arbitrary nature of the notion of a cussword as “dirty” can be deconstructed by breaking the words down and positing new definitions based on semantics. But there are no longer only seven words that are dirty; according to recent FCC rulings under chairman Michael Powell, there are actually an infinite number of obscene word combinations punishable by law. Due to heightened frenzy on standards of morality since Janet Jackson flashed the country at the Super Bowl and Bono said “fucking brilliant” upon receiving his award at the Golden Globes, the FCC decency guidelines have become a little cloudy.

The new system in place is based on a series of complaints. If you hear something you think is obscene on the radio, you can file a complaint with the FCC, and the commission will evaluate the offense. Our national commission basically operates half-a-step up from a system of sanctioning grade school tattle-tales as relevant information sources. And that's exactly what the system is beginning to look like. Chicago has received national attention in the past months for the impending lawsuit between WKQX-FM 101.1 's Mancow Muller and Citizens for Community Values of Illinois' president, David Smith. Smith has used the current FCC complaint system as a vehicle to launch a personal crusade against the morning radio host, filing over 60 complaints for indecent programming. Smith takes copious notes, transcribing offensive material to include in his filed complaints. One has to wonder, however, if Mancow's show is so offensive, what is Smith doing listening to it everyday? If you're not interested in the suggestive moaning sounds of women callers on the line at 8am , maybe Mancow's Morning Madhouse isn't the program for you. Rest sound in the fact that you have good taste, but don't ask the whole country to have the same taste as you.

    next

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

1) Shit, piss, fuck, cunt, cocksucker, motherfucker and tits.

Due to the frequency of Smith's complaints, Mancow has filed a harassment lawsuit against Smith that demands $3 million and a court order issued to stop the complaints, as compensation for the $42,000 that seven of his 60+ complaints have cost the local station. Mancow, who it turns out studied to be a priest before becoming an “obscene” radio personality, is running around claiming, “ If we lose the 1 st Amendment, we lose America ,” in his statement. But the FCC has built into its complaint guidelines the clause, “Obscene speech is not protected by the 1 st Amendment”. So much for America , I guess. If it weren't readily apparent in the morning paper that we are already losing the very American ideals that we have been supposedly fighting a war for, then let Mancow's intrinsically thwarted statement serve as our first clue.

Since the 1 st Amendment does not protect “obscene” speech, let's look at the FCC's written definition of obscenity to see if we can guess (along with every stunned deejay, and terrified television and radio station) what the word means. I have footnoted words within the FCC's guidelines that may prove problematic.

To be obscene, material must meet a three-prong test:

  • An average (2) person, applying contemporary (3) community standards, must find that the material, as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest;
  • The material must depict or describe, in a patently offensive (4) way, sexual conduct specifically defined by applicable law; and
  • The material, taken as a whole, must lack serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. (5)

Because the FCC's guidelines for obscenity hinge upon its chairman's opinion on broadcasted material's “serious value”, context is everything. You might get away with all the obscenity you like if your intentions are right in the eyes of the country's new culture police. Just take, for example, the point of divergence in FCC dealings in regard to the case of Oprah Winfrey. This March an Oprah rerun aired in which guests gave graphic descriptions of teenage oral sex parties. Oprah airs in Chicago at nine in the morning, which, although the impetuous for decency standards always comes back to the children that are listening, didn't seem to prove problematic for the FCC in this case. Howard Stern, whose show has been fined numerous times for airing similarly sexually graphic transgressions at 8 a.m. , tried to demonstrate the irony of the situation by airing a clip from Oprah's controversial guest on his radio show. His station refused to let the clip air without bleeping out the language of the Oprah segment, as such content seemed to be asking for another fine for Stern.

"If they fine Oprah Winfrey for indecency, people are going to be outraged." Stern argued with the radio station's manager after he was informed of the bleeped out language, "My point is play it...Don't bleep it. This is what's going to expose the hypocrisy. If they fine me for this, they are going to have to fine Oprah. And if they fine Oprah all hell is going to break loose." The FCC has received a comparable number of complaints for this Oprah episode as they did for Bono's “fucking (6) brilliant” utterance, yet the daytime talk show host has yet to be informed of any impending FCC violations.

back to page 1 go to page 3

 

 

2) An “average” person? Oh, is that like a “normal” person?

3) Come on. Entire theoretical debates have been written trying to define “contemporary”. A highly debatable word has no business modifying the equally perplexing, “community standards” as it begs the question, “What community?” Are we one big national community, or would it be fair to assume that, say, community standards aren't the same in Chicago as they may be in L.A. or Colona , Iowa ?

4) Offensive to whom? The “contemporary” “average”?

5) Now a government appointed commission is deciding what constitutes artistic value? Let's take a giant fifty-year-step backwards to applaud contemporary McCarthyism at its finest.

6) In the case of Bono, the FCC ruled that because Bono's expletive did not refer to the act of fucking, so much as it was used as a charged adjective to modify “brilliant”, the pop icon is in the clear, but recently Chairman Michael Powell has brought the case to the commission for reconsideration.

I'm not sure if the “serious value” here is literary, artistic, scientific or political, but the FCC must figure it's one of these. So, language of serious value is protected by the 1 st Amendment, even if it's obscene. The commission, however, cannot afford to protect all literary material, as is the case with the notorious glutton for bathroom humor, James Joyce. Although Joyce's Ulysses is arguably a book of unrivaled literary merit in the last century, the FCC is not quite sure what to make of the language. After L.A. radio station KPFK 90.7 got into a tiff with the FCC over airing a play whose AIDS-inflicted protagonist used graphic language, the station asked the commission to provide advance ruling for another “future broadcast script” that it intended to air. The FCC, upon reading the script, declared it obscene and informed the station that airing the segment would result in a second legal brawl. When the FCC was informed that the “future broadcast script” was in fact a segment extracted from Joyce's Ulysses , the commission declined to comment.

Obscenity , after all, is not the only thing to worry about. The FCC is also responsible for regulating the profane and the indecent . James Joyce might fit better into one of these FCC distinctions, which, though they are offensive, are still protected by the 1 st Amendment, unlike obscenity. In short, indecent material makes “sexual or excretory references”, and profane material makes use of “reviling epithets”. Neither are said to be as repulsive as obscenity; for this reason indecent and profane material may be aired at night, when children are presumably asleep, so long as it is not aired between the hours of 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. But if profanity and indecency are both said to be protected by the 1 st Amendment, how is it then that they can legally be regulated at all? TV and radio broadcasters are livid, and with good reason. The FCC is placing thousands of dollars in fine distinctions between three synonyms that they refuse to adequately define. The FCC more recently announced a proposition that radio and television stations be required to keep recordings of completed shows, for up to three months after the show airs, a ruling which would force broadcasting stations to produce their own possibly incriminating evidence should complaints be researched.

Since this decency crusade has been launched presumably for the children, those incapable of the moral judgment necessary to turn off obscene radio and television programs themselves, it seems fitting to ask, why include a curfew clause at all? Half the time kids are ones sneaking in late-night television. Who stereotypically gets up at the crack of dawn to watch TV before school? Kids. Whose trademark nighttime posture includes falling asleep with headphones on? Kids. Furthermore, why are we so interested in making public broadcasting a fantasy island where no one swears or shits or moans, when most kids in this country hear worse language at school, on cable, or from their own parents' bedrooms. This is not to say that American children should be forced to sit down and soak in profanity, but it is still absurd to propose indecent language be siphoned into an eight hour window of broadcasting and then treated, in the morning, as if it didn't exist. For those in broadcasting, it is not accurate to claim that FCC regulations are, per se, censorship, as the FCC makes a point to state that obscene language is not protected. But the 1 st Amendment rights are clearly getting dicked around, and I mean that in both the obscene and profane sense of the word. Because the regulations are not well-defined, many TV and radio stations, even local and college stations that are subject to the same fines, are implementing a system of self-censoring, to insure that their staff does not cross the FCC's wavering line. Those in broadcasting continue to beg the commission for a little more guidance in this matter, but, as both sides of the debate know very well, the less concrete the rules are, the more subjectively each offense is treated, and the more subjectivity is involved, the easier it is for scapegoats to be hand selected.

title: mix tape

pages.html:
With all things mix-tape related, one never wants his hand to show entirely until the end of side two. Never does anyone make a mix-tape without motive.

There is that nephew that you've decided to take under your musical wing, determined that if you can turn him on to A Tribe Called Quest, KMD and the rest of The Zulu Nation , then he'll gnash his teeth in regret and dump all the Ja Rule tour posters into the donation bin. But you don't want him to know that's what you're doing. With a poorly placed track, the subtlety is broken, and the delicate subversion turns to audio mind control.

The following mix-tape is an internal one, a collection that is begging its own questions: how, when, where will it end? Each song is torn pages from a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book read straight through. Not making sense always in direct chronology, but after a few songs the series of endless paths to be taken is clear. In some cases, the songs on this tape pose a question of music itself and the implied inquiry of where it is heading, like the selections from The Slits and OOIOO, whereas those by Wilco and Elecrelane ask themselves where it is that the bands themselves are going to end up, both taking large strides from the places that they began. And some songs, you get the feeling that you walked in on a conversation that they are having with themselves, there seems to be no ending and no beginning, such as the case of Fennesz and Beans. Others- Tom Waits, Ghostface Killah, The Streets, Betty Harris- tell such vivid stories that the music is left to the wayside, wondering instead about where the characters in these songs will end up. It is a tape that wonders out loud to itself, concerned for all those songs living within its walls, hoping loudly for the best, unsure how they will all end.

go to Side A song 1

“In the beginning there was rhythm,” vocalist Ari Up chants from the beginning to end of the song. Taken from the last of their Peel recording sessions, this Slits staple is expanded to the massive tribal stomp that the original, at the featherweight of five

minutes, truly wanted to be. Needed to be. The all-female quartet go beyond the original goal of the girls on this dubbed-up The Slits first album. The bass bounces and weaves while staying the course, drums pump a 4x4 time so consistent in its ass-shakin' ability it posseses a certain militancy, guitars cut rather than sing and a pogoing pixie chants and screams to the audience as though her songs were threats. And if ever there were poster children for that formula, The Slits were they. And better than anyone else of their ilk. In this live version of their now oft sampled song, they start to tear away from that established blueprint. Their tight structure swells and tears at its side, a milkweed bursting in a heavy wind. They circle, yelling and yelping that the face of God is rhythm, as are bouncing knees of a schoolchild on the cross-town bus. The frequency grows louder as notes are jammed into one another and the urgency in their voices surfaces. And just before the song collapses from weight and of exhaustion, screams go up loud into the studio rafters. And the emptiness of those echoes the answer to the unasked question: if rhythm is the beginning, then what's the end?

 
back to intro go to side A song 2

They sing! Finally! Fucking right! For the daunting follow up album, the girls-only troupe Electrelane, end the silence of their instrumental first album by featuring vocals on nearly every track of their sophomore venture. And while the first album was warm with blushingly delicate pop-chamber arrangements, this album and this track comes throwing punches from the outset. From the loud celebration of The Slits we slide into the cool intimacy of another girl group, though they wonder nothing of music but use the medium to wonder about themselves. Much whimsy has drained from the four, it's gone back to grassy plains, leaving them and the listener for the better. You can only be cradled for so long. At parts they can sound a dead-on female Joy Division (that only took 25 years) and at others they can sound just like your recent ex, the first time that you speak again, without tenderness or tie. And that's in this song alone. It's Verity Susman's vocals and their recently discovered legs that give this song so much. Her voice is still new and trying to find its footing, attempting many stances to see which one is best. A growth that is fascinating to watch, the missteps as enthralling as the successes, and wonder how it turns out. That stance is not on this album. The next Electrelane outing is guaranteed to see the group and the vocals at full maturity and thrust. In the meantime there are these glimmering snapshots from a band's adolescence.

 
side A song 1 go to side A song 3

Plenty of press have these guys been given and plenty of pressings of this album will continue leaving the record store shelves. And all for good reason: everything on it is great. It's not life altering, but calming because it's so non-life altering. What was started as an idea for a karaoke group turned into two guys singing over tape loops and another guy doing the programming. That evolution, so natural and quaint that it could have started as a drinking game, one that makes up new words to old songs, providing an easier approach to such a successful record but deceivingly easy one-sided take to miss the real meat of such light fare. All sounds fall behind the huge voices of the band. They trade lines; their voices dive around one another, interweave and then switch parts only to switch again. Acting as the dual voices of the songs main character who walks out of a bar and into the rising tide of the sea. He opens his mouth for air and feels the water lapping at his chest. All the while, the yearning voices tell him that he is clear of guilt, they direct him rather to think about the temporal nature of a tree. Then the water reaches the chin, shortly after the voices and the noise behind them go silent. There is only the silence of the story's ending, a vacancy that is far more powerful than any voice. Without even a whimper, sometimes the world still ends.

 
side A song 2 go to side A song 4

Elvis Costello's words will ride him to the grave. Raising the ire of music critics, he's told them that their job is the equivalent of “dancing to architecture,” which to me sounds fun. But soundscapist Fennesz steps further out of these bounds by constructing his newest album around the decay of Venice . In his mind, the fabled sinking city is in full bloom of its graceful collapse. From the center of the eerie cracks and throbbing, low hiss of this ambient world comes moaning the only vocal "song" on the entire work. Where TV on the Radio's song noted a narrator's end with no notes at all, Fennesz poses his question of the end of a city in juxtaposing soft, whispering tones with a huge voice. In the tradition of the lamentation song, collaborator, David Sylvian sways on a barstool in an empty bar smoking the last cigarette, and mourns the death of Europe . Over the filtered static of Fennesz he asks us to “say goodbye to Europe ” and invokes visions of an old country that we all tried to visit, but was never there. He tells us that the lights are dimming there and that the cabaret is about to close, that our history will dim with it, that there is one more match to strike, that it is our last chance. For what? Not sure, but it haunts me with a reservation that is born of chances that are available but will be missed regardless. It is the type of lamentable failure that William S. Borroughs will mention on side B of this mix-tape. But then I think about that building in the Loop , the one with the blue light spilling from the top of it, out of what looks a beehive, and I just want to dance.

 
side A song 3 go to side A song 5

Jamie Stewart, the center of Xiu Xiu's rotating lineup, is a terrific wonder, with his broken lyrical narration and his emotional fucking catastrophe. With terrified wonder, this song seems to require repeated listenings. Sparse hand drums hold the strumming of an acoustic guitar in a safe place, but then Stewart's wavering falsetto comes stumbling, the voice of a child who has just had a nightmare. If we were his parents, we'd sit up, fumble for the lights and look for our glasses, and we'd show true concern, for our son's voice is perverse and spoiled with hurt. He'd ignore our invitation to sleep between us and opt to sit in the middle of the floor, out of our arms reach, though wanting to be held. He'd tell us that he'd dreamt that he was dead, dead and killed by the man he loved, a bodybuilder with the most beautiful biceps in the world. His tear-slicked face would light for a moment, showing the face of the boy we know, at the description of the dream lover's thighs and arms, all tanned and taught. He'd disappear again into the lip quivering stutters at the retelling of how this man, in a spasm of passion and disgust, broke our son's neck at the point of sexual climax. After a few shutters and sobs he'd whimper that the last thing that he remembers before waking up is the man putting an urn of ashes underneath his workout bench, and the story will stop there: our little boy rocking into a sob on our bedroom floorboards, alone in his parents' presence. Stunned, we'll try to reassure him that it was only a dream, that it'll be better in the morning and that these things don't happen in the real world. Stewart will look at us through wet eyes with pity, as though we haven't understood a word he's said. He'll go back to his room shaking his head. It is not a song that has its questions in how it ends, like the two selections prior to it, but in how it began. Where do kids come up with this shit? We'll lie in our bed, but sleep won't come, our thoughts filled with the night terrors of a child.

 
back to side A song 4 go to side A song 6

It is such a cheap trick to put two songs by one artist on a mix-tape, especially one after another, but in this case, it is well warranted. These songs are also the songs of saddened children, but not the violent despair of Xiu Xiu's, but the melancholy of illustrator Edward Gorey's characters. Besides, it will take at least two songs to wash out the taste of the last song.

Mum tends to get unfair comparisons to another, more famed older sister of their native Icelandic shores, there is some merit for the shared innocence that they both blend into their eclectic folk with electric leaning songs. Here, in these two songs, Mum manages to topple Sugarcube's ice imp of with astounding measure of craft, earnestness, and the ability to make the most of understated frailty. Every second of both tracks has sound, yet still manages to elicit the image of silence. To gain this, the trio made part of the album on an abandoned tanker. And those elements come through in every song: sea spray and sway, plus abandonment.

Sailors have their songs, tales of the rollicking sea, and we love to sing them. But for every son of the sea, there, behind him, standing on the dock, is a long-tressed wife or a gray-bonneted daughter waving hard enough that their sailor see them, knowing that it might be the last time either sees each other again. These are their songs.

 
back to side A song 5 go to side A song 8

I love, absolutely love, Wilco for making this song. It lasts 15 minutes, only three of which feature the band. The first few minutes are a soft sadness in slow piano written to the listener about how predictable, how dull they are, that there really is less to them than they think. It sounds like Wilco is breaking up with the audience. Then, as a challenge, the 12 minutes of whirling filter loops and drone begin, like a rolling cloud. This is the point where most listeners will hop off the couch and skip the needle over to the last song and miss the best part and the whole point. Having a moment to both listen to a song that can never be memorized and to get a little quiet time to reflect on what has been heard is truly a great thing. Like in the case of the Elcetrelane song, this is a band that is shifting before the public's view, but more people will wonder when will it end rather than how. This drone usually comes at the end of the album; instead Wilco leaves this space open to wonder about what the last song is and whether it is worth the wait. I'd give away the answer, but I'd rather that you wait the 15 minutes. Spend your time thinking about what the perfect last song would be, how it would go.

 
back to side A song 7 go to side B song 1

Never has any man's voice been so lilting and masculine. In these mid-‘60s recordings he still sounds as though he is beyond the groundbreaking techniques that he and Brion Gysion came to discover at their hotel in Tangiers. It is early for him. There is the voice of a tired man, a man who's been up late attempting to destroy the blueprint for writing that has been followed since the invention of prose. Writing has fallen behind, he tells us, at least 50 years behind painting. He explains that by using the ideals of the montage, writing can move forward. Cut and paste, double text back on itself, use the present existing texts to reveal the future underneath it. Catch up, dammit, his voice murmurs. Even in the instruction, the weariness in his throat, he knows that this forward thinking is too much, a lamentable failure, but worth trying none the less. It doesn't seem clear whether or not he knew that he'd become the storytelling uncle to generations of faux-junkies that didn't want to move writing forward but only wanted to hear the one about the mugwumps again and again and again.

 
back to side A song 8 go to side B song 2

While it seems that no one in the writing establishment took Burroughs' ideas about tape looping very seriously, the music industry was listening with baited breath. Sixty years later, sampling, tape reverse and over-dubbing are standard fare for even the most commercial hip-hop entities. Ghostface is the one of 20-odd members that has shown not only true stay power but the mark of a true storyteller, not just the narrator to a Cadillac commercial. Where others spend songs wandering through their shoe closets like it were the soundtrack for MTV's Cribs, Ghostface is able to discuss the longing for these things with, ironically, the most human face in the rap game.

Here he is in classic breakup mode, focusing the first verse as a reflection on he and his woman's falling out, in the blue-and-white lights of a cop car. He bristles with the betrayal felt when his girl suggests that the officers look in his trunk and check him for warrants. Ghostface tells her that maybe taking him on Jerry Springer was the wrong way to win him back, and he is practically yelling as he recites the way she changed as the money came in. Jackie-O comes in, the voice of Ghostface's girl, on the next verse with apologies and justifications. Calmly, the list of her merits illustrates a loyal wife, who silently dealt with her man's infidelities and bedroom insecurities. She gently reminds the Ghostface who it was that pawned all her rings to bond him out of lockup. Like a patient mother, she tells him to stop this foolishness and get back in the door. The last verses are all sweet sighs and scrape marks on begging bent knee, guess whose knee? The Ghost with the heart of a man.

 
back to side B song 1 go to side B song 3

So he's not brilliant- simply pairing this song, which is the album's strongest, with Ghostface proves that- but musical prodigies get old. For your money, spend it on someone honest and on your level for a change. The new album, a concept piece (insert spine shiver here), works for the reason that the concept is simple and not conceptual. In this case it actually helps to keep Mike Skinner, vocalist and garage producer, focused. Though the garage-lite beats can be a little thin and a chorus occasionally grating, the narrative thread strings the listener through a day gone from bad to worse. In this cut, the next to last, there is emotion that can only be garnered from true and recent experience. It's the breakup dance again, but here is the end of a relationship that the listener has witnessed from the start, and we feel him as he tries to force the girl to meet his eyes. He goes through the motions of someone who knows that the end is nigh and that there is nothing left to lose. Sooner than walk away, he tries everything left: waist grabbing, desperation-gripped hugs, demands, the pathetic logic of promises and begging accusations. Skinner lists failed attempts so numerous that it becomes clear that he no longer hopes to get the girl back, but is settling for a punishing display of how much pain she's caused him. Everyone can wish they don't know where this is coming from. You can only hope that the next track will wrap everything together, tied up nice and silver-lined. Hope that you can relate to that one, too.

 
back to side B song 2 go to side B song 4

Thank God for Soul Jazz Records, otherwise this amazing 1967 soul cut would have never seen the light of day. Betty Harris had only one hit released on a national scale in the ‘60s. This should have been that hit. What is thought to be one of the first uses of creative feedback in a pop song, the searing tube amp sounds not like the feedback we know from Sonic Youth, but more like an heated and angry flute. The opening high-pitched buzz of the intro, coupled The Meters's drummer beating stuttering breaks, is enough to make you clench your jaw and stamp your feet. On this tape, Harris has the female comeback to The Streets sad song before it. Harris is shouting accusations from the outset, resonantly pointing a finger in the chest of the man that has traded her in like a used Buick. She fumes at the memory of the carnal things that transpired between them, conceding that he was the only man to make this good girl bad. Now that she's alone, she wonders, who will want her after what she's done. Harris tells him to enjoy his new girl because the ride is soon to end, the road breaks for everyone and it'll soon break him, just as she now is broken. Trading rage for resentment, Harris assures him that the same is coming back to him. With so much rage and heat in her voice, you wonder whether she's letting karma take its course, of that she might have a retribution strategy of her own.

 
back to side B song 3 go to side B song 5

Top artists in every field and genre are charged with pushing their craft and the publics' understanding to the absolute brink of disaster. But what happens when they actually succeed? Yoshimi P-wee has such questions before her now. As one half of the seminal Japanese noise duo The Boredoms, she and her husband managed, through a string of amazing self-produced releases, to destroy music. Or, rather what everyone had come to expect from music, even the conventions that hardcore and electronic music couldn't let go of. They happened to destroy themselves in the process as the group is restructuring itself in current hiatus; their back catalog is being re-released- sounding as relevant as ever. But when you've gone so far that you don't remember the footsteps behind you are your own, where do go? To the beginning. Like The Slits said, “to rhythm.” Enter the new primal: focusing non-congruent sound sources with ambient field recordings, producing layers of primitive rhythms. Yoshimi P-wee leads a whole female troupe back to the nature of all music: hitting one object against another, over and over and over. But once you regress so far back, the plain is so open and filled with light that you can never find your old footpath, grown over with soft grasses and Baby's Breath. Here's to being lost in the woods.

 
back to side B song 4 go to side B song 6

Magnificent deception- that is what Throbbing Gristle specialized in, not music. They thrived on hatred, not music. They were not rock, but were themselves rock and roll, but certainly- anything but- not music. Theirs was a project to trick their fans (who weren't fans so much as gluttons for punishment) into believing that they too were in on the joke, but that wasn't possible since the joke was on them. Taking advantage of the cheap prices and ready availability of drum machines and synths that had just been introduced to a wide market, Throbbing Gristle began as a project to punish, but ended up becoming the reluctant forebears of industrial music. With a track that sounds like a cheap send-up to those clever krauts, Kraftwerk, this is supposedly a running synth loop that is seemingly representing a woman chasing love. It is actually about a murderer chasing down the prey. The song assumes that since the narrator is a female, whose voice sounds sweet and high like water, that it is love she claims to chasing, rather than her love of murder. Throbbing Gristle played upon such assumptions so many times in their short time together that song itself forgot what the original joke was. Their creative base was lost and too many people were coming to their shows; Throbbing Gristle locked their doors and said the mission was complete. They've been silent for 22 years, watched the accolades pour in. Every few months another box set or live recording is released, and everyone fawns all over it. This year finds them reactivating the dormant project for a large festival, but something is sticking out of their sleeves.

 
back to side B song 5 go to side B song 7

Beans, once the backbone of genre-shaping Anti-Pop Consortium, has been the advanced kid in hip-hop class. He's the kid that cuts class to smoke because he's so far ahead with his studies that the teacher gave him a hall pass so that he wouldn't make the other kids feel so dumb (and not as in fresh). Which is why so few heads have even heard either of his two solo releases. Amazing that the forward thinking hip-hop auteur sounds sneakingly like the Throbbing Gristle track before him, made when he was about five. Over the throb of tones and clicks Beans talks rapidly of the challenges that he imposes on himself daily, confronting his own precocious nature in flow that doesn't so much flow as it does gush out of his mouth. He doesn't stop to allow pause; the abstractions of his music are nothing in comparison to the fractal images that escape his head. Only when he shuts his jaw does the quiet return. The lush tones return pulse, but they seem quieter than before, with less depth, even his own music cannot hold up against the meter of Beans' mind. He promises that there'll be rewards for following, and while he can't say what they are, they're waiting at the end. And they are, but nothing tangible, the reward comes from watching in awe as someone so brilliant shows you a little part of how their mind works.

 
back to side B song 6 go to side B song 8

He is leaving, woman, you just need to understand that. Crying ain't going to help a thing. He's a soldier and he's got to do for the country what it ain't done for him yet, be free. James Carr's singing narrator is soft and firm. You see him coming home and standing in the kitchen door, all military khaki and deployment orders. He explains, in that honey moan of his, a few depths darker than Otis Redding's, that he is doing his part. Carr pleads with her not to cry, but the tears come anyway. He tells the woman that he'd be by her side everyday, were it up to him. Brushing her slick cheek with the backside of his hand, looking into her eyes, he promises that everything will be fine. He can't stand to look as fresh tears well up and roll down both of their faces now. This is the kind of emotion that makes you love someone so much that you have to break everything in goddamn room. This is soul so fucking good it makes your chest tingle and your mouth dry. He hugs her again, and walks across their yard to the waiting military transport. You wish you could call Carr at home, and demand to know whether the solider got home again.

 
back to side B song 7 go to side B song 9

Instead of getting Carr's answer about that leaving solider, we get Tom Waits's response. He wants to take us back to that house again, a few years later.
The reason that Waits has been lauded as the definition of cool for so many generations is not that he's genre-defining and shifting, though he is, nor is it that he can play every damn instrument under the sun, though he can; it is because he is the country's best short story writer that has never published a thing. But they live in all of his songs.
In this, against a stand-up bass and macabre piano, Wait's road-rubbed voice runs down a list of items. Everything is very pedestrian: scuffed shoes and a sewn catcher's mitt, paperbacks and swallow tail coats, a communion card and tobacco tin. Through the items that fill the song we see the life of the young man who owned them. We understand that he's away in the service, but we see all that he was before duty called, we're even shown the metals that he's won. The last item is a shoebox in which everything inside of it is priced at a dollar. The boy isn't coming home to these things; he's left them behind. We've been at his wife's yard sale.

 
back to side B song 8

title: intersection section
blurb: any moron can review music or movies. it takes a special kind of genius to review an intersection.

pages.html:
Continuing the trend of late, the area covered isn't really an intersection per se, but more of a general location. I suppose there's an intersection of some sort somewhere in Jackson Park – a footpath or a road or a bridge or something else – so this is the Omnibus Jackson Park Intersection Section.

As a quick history lesson, the World's Fair of 1893 was held in Jackson Park. The Fair was one of the seminal events that made Chicago into the world-class city it is today, but the vestiges of the event are largely forgotten. So I recently read Erik Larson's Devil in the White City , under the guise of research. While I could go into its merits and non-merits as a piece of literature – OK, you've convinced me: I felt cheated by the title, as I was suckered into thinking there was a killer literally stalking the World's Fair of 1893, killing unsuspecting victims by, I don't know, asphyxiating them with an extra-large cotton candy or something. The general story set forth was about t he huge expo in Chicago at the end of the nineteenth century, and how the serial killer with the most victims in U.S. history happened to live a few miles down the road, which is hardly causal enough to really call him the “Devil” that prowled the “White City” since most of his killing was done at his custom-built boarding house– but suffice to say I learned a great deal about Chicago. Example: The world's first Ferris wheel was built here, specifically for the World's Fair by a man named – ready? – George Washington Gail Ferris Jr.

So like I said, the area isn't technically an intersection, but I covered most of Jackson Park, the huge green expanse bordered on its north side by the Museum of Science and Industry.



The shelter on the beach, or lurking death. Rating: 3.2.
The creatively named Jackson Park Beach House played host to one of the more interesting scenes I've ever witnessed in a public place: Every available square inch of grassy area surrounding the shelter was covered by a person, a tent, a cooler or a grill, but the Beach House itself was deserted. Completely empty.

I decided to get out of there, let some alien creature leap from the shadows and drag my body to its lair, leaving no trace of the struggle that occurred. Or maybe there was an outbreak of a deadly disease that affected only those standing under the open-air shelter. Whatever your conspiracy theory, I wasn't sticking around long enough to figure it out. We were getting the hell out of there.

One of the only good things that came from the shelter was the bird's-eye view it afforded of the nearby beach. I t made me think I was living in a high-priced beachfront condo for a minute. Then I noticed the lack of furnishings, the apparent oversight on the part of the architect to install a bathroom and the hard, unyielding concrete ceilings, walls and floors. And I remembered that alien and that deadly disease. It was time to leave.



The Jackson Pavilion, or playing in your Underoos. Rating: 8.7.
There's a lot that will get you in trouble – or at least some disapproving stares – that were considered normal activities ten years ago. Listening to Vanilla Ice, for example. Or watching a group of small children play in a fountain. Sad that some pastimes that were once so pure can now be considered slightly, well, off.

But the circular fountain at the Jackson Pavilion contained 20 or so kids doing what I only dream about now: dragging their mothers to a marginally interesting concrete plaza that every five minutes erupts with jets of water. The dress code didn't apply, since there were a good number of boys and girls in their Underoos, happily waiting the five minutes for the jets of water to start. This is even more remarkable when you remember how never-ending five minutes was when you were a kid – in five kid-minutes, the Cold War ended, peace in the Middle East was secured and your mom always called you to dinner just before your favorite cartoon was over. And of course there was no TV watching during mealtimes.

So we find these children staring intently into the fountain's jets from a good six inches away, wondering when the water is going to start. I couldn't help but think of one of those clown flowers that squirt when you get too close, but even when hit in the eye – “You're going to poke your eye out,” more than one mother was saying of her child's hovering above the spout – they shrieked with delight and did kid things, romping in the fountain.

go to page 2

The Museum of Science and Industry, or The Place I Went To Once. Rating: 6.6.
Anyone who has moved to in a city that isn't the place of his birth most likely skipped all the touristy elements of their new home. Don't get me wrong; I'd seen the essentials like the Art Institute and had eaten at Bubba Gump's Shrimp Co. on Navy Pier, but it wasn't until my parents visited that I ever thought to see the other museums. It's not that the Museum of Science and Industry isn't interesting, it's just, well, inconvenient. We finally had a family trip to the museum over the Easter holiday one year, and that's just not a good way to enjoy your first trip to a major tourist attraction. When the oppressive crowds were paired with my mother asking me if I've ever smoked cigarettes and what my increased rate of heart disease would then be, the day turned out swimmingly. Plus I toured a German submarine.

Bad karma notwithstanding, the building is apparently the last vestige of the World's Fair, originally constructed as the Fine Arts building. One of the many lagoons that dot the surface of Jackson Park, all so meticulously created by Frederick Law Olmsted to ensure a visual harmony between the landscape of the Fair and its gleaming white buildings, laps against the back entrance of the Museum. It's a peaceful scene, only punctuated by the sounds of people bickering at the barbecue behind me – “I wanted a brat.” “No, you said a hot dog.” “Brat.” “Hot dog.” – and my profanity from stepping in goose shit. Otherwise, it was a moment of total consciousness.


People barbecuing, or make some noise for freeballin’. Rating: 7.1.
As I said above, literally every square inch of available park surface was covered by a person, a tent, a cooler or a grill. And this was not my usual hyperbole: This was legit. There were tents erected simply to house tables of food while people lay in the sun. There were gas-powered generators to ensure the refrigerators could run and keep beverages cold. There were grills larger than my desk.

It was a liberating experience. While walking along, wishing I weren't doing research for an article and could be sitting and enjoying the weather, I noticed a bumper sticker: “HONK if you're not wearing underwear.” I had literally nothing else to say. I didn't fit the two implicit criteria here, namely 1. I wasn't driving a car, thus had no horn to honk, and 2. I was wearing underwear. I was out of my element, so I decided it was better I couldn't stay around and party with the barbecuers. They may be more than I could handle.


The statue in the roundabout, or a faked site marker. Rating: 6.9.
A golden statue that towers over what is in actuality an intersection – rather than the rest of this review, which discusses an area of Chicago park– I was in awe of such a huge statue that I forgot for a moment that I was in the middle of a road.

For those that have driven on a European road, you've been treated to the distinct pleasure that is the roundabout . Rather than a crossing of streets, you find yourself trapped on a seeming interminable circular road, trying in vain to get from the inner lane to the outer so you can get off this godforsaken European road – think National Lampoon's European Vacation for the visual – and you'll get what I mean. I'd never encountered a roundabout on this side of the Atlantic, and I found myself standing in the middle of one. To make matters worse, there was traffic coming in both directions, and it's near-impossible to see through a solid object – in this case, the statue smack in the middle of the roundabout – to see the traffic coming from one direction. So you do the next best thing: You practice a technique best reserved for bets made in a game of high-stakes Truth or Dare when you choose “dare,” and you dart across the street blindly.

For such a life-threatening risk, you're rewarded with a closer view of a statue you could have seen from five miles away. However, the inscription on the statue's base is at least slightly interesting:

THE WORLD'S COLUMBIAN EXPOSITION / AUTHORIZED BY ACT OF CONGRESS / AND GENERALLY PARTICPIATED IN / BY THE NATIONS OF THE EARTH / WAS HELD HERE IN 1893 TO CLELBRATE / THE FOUR HUNDRETH ANNIVERSARY OF THE / DISCOVERY OF AMERICA. ON THIS SITE STOOD / THE ADMINISTRATION BUILDING.

So not only did we have a short history lesson, the more perceptive readers among us will notice that statue stands where the Administration Building used to stand. By extension, then, the statue most likely isn't the original, either. So much for that whole “historical accuracy” thing.

The intersection that's actually a park, or World's Fair circa 2004.
Although you wouldn't get the idea from waltzing around Jackson Park, you'd be surprised at the amount of history contained there. Now it's just another silent testament to what made Chicago great in its long history. And don't forget to honk, because I know you're not wearing underwear.

Final rating: 7.5 (mostly for the history, though)

title: iraq
blurb: Baghdad city culture from the mouth of an Iraqi girl

pages.html:
’Now my heart is full
Now my heart is full
And I just can't explain
So I won't even try to’”
-Morrissey


“There's nothing that can describe the current feeling in the air,” explains an Iraqi woman on the topic of her city, “It's like that Morrissey song.” In our interview she references the song while trying to describe the irrationality, the emotional upheaval caused by the occupation of Baghdad .

But the truth is she has tried to describe it.

For more then a year now, the 25-year-old Iraqi woman has been keeping a document of her life. She lives near a bend in the Tigris River in the north of Baghdad and, when the electricity permits, she posts the stories of her life since the start of the war to her website under the appropriately unassuming and anonymous name of Riverbend. Born in Iraq and educated for eight years in America , she now shares her story and the story of her city with anyone who cares to read it

Americans are delivered news of daily atrocities in Iraq from our televisions, radios and newsstands. The American public has been made well aware throughout the war that what is displayed on the nightly news can be digested as information weighted by stereotypes, by government media regulations, by our own ignorance of Iraqi culture, each impeding our understanding of Baghdad as a contemporary city with identifiable traits, not unlike our own idea of a city. The difference between the recent war in Iraq and the first gulf war is Baghdad . The gulf war was fought in the desert, removed from the city center and removed from the civilians living in that major metropolis. U.S. military forces designed this war with invading and occupying Baghdad as its goal.

Riverbend follows the news from inside Baghdad . As the Arab media more readily displays graphic detail of both the war and the rocky transfer of sovereignty, Iraqis watch the aftermath of the explosions, many of which they can hear from inside their homes, on the nightly news.

“ Baghdad is calm and relatively quiet if you don't count the frequent explosions. Actually, when we don't hear explosions, it gets a bit worrying. Hearing them is a relief and you can loosen up after they occur and hope that they'll be the last of the day…I watch television and it feels like I'm watching another country. All I can think is, ‘We've become one of those countries...' You know- the ones where hostages are taken on a daily basis and governments warn their civilians of visiting or entering the country.”

What Riverbend discusses, both in her blog and our interview, is a sentiment that can be easy to fall prey to when our military occupies a country. “[ Iraq 's] become one of those countries.” Iraq , perhaps, has always been “one of those countries” to us, to the stereotypically isolated Americans who collectively learn about a country only after we've invaded it. But when Iraq is cited as such by its very inhabitants, how can we try to identify with the city of Baghdad and its inhabitants? This month, sixosix magazine brings you, through our conversations with a girl living in it, a story of Baghdad as a city, a city irrevocably influenced by the war and its recent “freedom”, but a city with customs and landmarks and stories, none the less.

If history repeats itself, which it does, Baghdad has a long history of being attacked and occupied. It is a city that in its inception was built to house an army. Baghdad was founded in 762 and for a time, it was the largest city in the Middle East before losing that honor to Constantinople . Baghdad was once home to Muslims, Christians, Jews and pagans from across the Middle East and Central Asia . It was also one of the most forward thinking cities in the world, one of the first to do away with the caste system and open up its society to people from all backgrounds and economic levels.

For over 600 years the city grew and matured at an astounding rate until 1258 when the city was sacked a nd burned by Mongols led by Hulagu, the grandson of Genghis Khan. After this occupation, which destroyed much of the cities infrastructure, the city was caught defenseless for the next 650 years while it was occupied and fought over by one invading army after another. In 1921, Baghdad became the capitol of the newly formed country of Iraq , which began to rebuild itself with the profits from oil discovered 12 years earlier. With a new found independence from the British Empire in 1932, the rise of the Baath party and Saddam Hussein in the 1960's, Baghdad was able to build itself into the modern city it is today.

Iraq is, in fact, a city of 21 st century, not the 16 th . Riverbend's frustration in confronting Baghdad 's occupation has much to do with the Western mission to redesign an antiquated city that cannot help itself. She spells out the dichotomy she too often sees in the understanding of her city:

“The Myth: Iraqis, prior to occupation, lived in little beige tents set up on the sides of little dirt roads all over Baghdad . The men and boys would ride to school on their camels, donkeys and goats. These schools were larger versions of the home units and for every 100 students, there was one turban-wearing teacher who taught the boys rudimentary math (to count the flock) and reading. Girls and women sat at home, in black burkas, making bread and taking care of 10-12 children.

“The Truth: Iraqis lived in houses with running water and electricity. Thousands of them own computers. Millions own VCRs and VCDs. Iraq has sophisticated bridges, recreational centers, clubs, restaurants, shops, universities, schools, etc. Iraqis love fast cars (especially German cars) and the Tigris is full of little motor boats that are used for everything from fishing to water-skiing.

“In other words- there was something there in the first place. We have one of the most sophisticated networks of highways in the region: you can get from Busrah, in the south, to Mosul , in the north, without once having to travel upon those little, dusty, dirt roads they show you on Fox News. We had a communications system so advanced, it took the Coalition of the Willing three rounds of bombing, on three separate nights, to damage the Ma'moun Communications Tower and silence our telephones.

The current city of Baghdad has a population of about 5.5 million people. The entire city of Chicago by comparison only has just over 2.8 million people living in it. The entire metro area of Chicago , which includes Cook, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake , McHenry, and Will counties, has just over 8 million people. The size of Baghdad is roughly 81 square miles and the city is divided in half by the Tigris River . If we took 81 square miles of Chicago it would have it borders being the lake on the east, Pulaski on the west, North Avenue on the north and 63 rd Street on the south.

Just north of the central district of Baghdad, jutting out into the Tigris River is Baghdad 's largest park, called Baghdad Island. It is a haven of both tourist attractions and green space. For Riverbend, it was “one of the few places you could go to breath” in the city. The park is about 128 acres total and to put that into perspective the newly opened Millennium Park here in Chicago is only 24.5 acres. The park was an attraction for the whole Middle East with over 50,000 visitors a day passing through. Today the park is home to the US Military forces in Baghdad and is closed to the public. The central part of Baghdad including Baghdad Island has been blockaded and shutdown, appropriately called the Green Zone by our media.

Because it is difficult to visualize an unfamiliar city, to put this into context, it would be comparable to shutting down the Loop . Doing so would not only disrupt the business that is in the area but it would also deny access to some of our most well known and enjoyed attractions: Grant Park, Buckingham Fountain and the Museum Campus.

Baghdad is a particularly modern city, but what about a modern society? Baghdad has just over 1000 public schools compared to Chicago 's 602 schools. It is an incredible school system, though many of these schools have closed down because parents no longer let their children out of the house to go to school. It is difficult for any family member, let alone children to get permission to leave the house these days. Riverbend explains the challenge of getting out of the house in an occupied city. Her trip to Karrada she compares, for our benefit, to what she imagines our Magnificent Mile to be, and though Karrada is an out door market, it sounds about right: shoppers, tourists, long lines, total chaos.

go to page 2

“I was in Karrada yesterday- a popular area in central Baghdad . It's a mercantile district where you can find everything from butchers to ice cream shops. The stores are close together and it's the ideal area to go looking for something you're not sure you'll find. I had been looking forward to the shopping trip for at least 4 days, which is how long it takes to get the routine familial permission these days.

“Karrada was quite crowded with people coming and going. Women, of course, were a startling minority. Karrada used to be full of women- mothers, daughters and wives, sometimes alone and sometimes dragging along a weary male. As we got out of the car, my confidence and enthusiasm began to wane. I was one of the few women on the street not wearing a hijab, or head-cover. I tugged gently at the sleeves of my shirt that were cuffed almost to my elbows. They slid down once more to my wrists and I was suddenly grateful that I had decided to wear a long denim skirt.

“I feel like we've stepped back 50 years. Females in Iraq used to be a lot better off than females in other parts of the Arab world (and some parts of the Western world- we had equal salaries!). We made up over 50% of the working force. I am female and Muslim. Before the occupation, I more or less dressed the way I wanted to. I lived in jeans and cotton pants and comfortable shirts. A girl wearing jeans risks being attacked, abducted or insulted by fundamentalists who have been… liberated!


“Before we got into the car to go home, E [Riverbend's brother] asked me if there was anything else I wanted to get? A part of me did want to take a more thorough look around, but another part of me was both physically and mentally exhausted with the rare outing. I just wanted to get back to the safety of our home where I didn't have to feel like some sort of strange outcast.

The news of daily bombings and assignations gives the impression of a country in chaos, while hearing stories of the way in which Baghdad 's inhabitants try to get on with their everyday lives simultaneously gives a sense of hope. No story coming out of Iraq has been more central to its hope as a country, and at the same time such a marker of its uncertainty, then the transfer of sovereignty.

This duality of progress and chaos is what Americans get from our media. These are the stories that seem worth telling. But it is these stories that make us forget that Iraq isn't just a place on our televisions. These stories over-shadow the fact that this is a real country full of people that are affected by every headline. The hope embodied in Iraqi sovereignty is the hope of the people living in Baghdad , who fight with this progress and chaos daily. Riverbend's family is a telltale example of the duality that exists living in “one of those countries”.

“One of my uncles absolutely insisted on a family reunion of sorts at his house. We packed ourselves off to his house, across Baghdad , at 4 p.m. and he promised dinner would be served promptly at 7 (which is an obscene hour to eat dinner for Iraqis, but everyone wanted to be home early).

“Dinner was served at seven. For a brief few hours, we forgot politics and occupation and sat concentrating on the steaming array of food piled before us. By the time the initial mess was cleared, it was almost 10 pm . Where was A., my cousin's husband? His parents didn't have a working telephone and any delay simply meant additional worry. I suddenly felt queasy

“At 8 a.m. the following day I was putting the kettle on in preparation for morning tea, the phone rang. It was A.'s best friend and business partner, S. He had heard from A. just a few minutes before. [A] had been abducted and was being held for a ransom of $15,000. We'd be given 3 days to get the money- a place would be agreed upon where we'd give them the money and they'd release A. later on.

“To make a long, terrible story short- we had the money by the middle of the next day. The money was handed over on the third day after his abduction. But no A. came back. I can't even begin to describe the next couple of days. If it was bad before- it suddenly became worse. We hear about abductions ALL THE TIME… but to actually experience it is something else.

“On the fifth day after A.'s abduction, we were all sitting in the living room. We suddenly heard a feeble clang of the gate- like someone was knocking, but not very hard. E. jumped up, ran to the door and called out, "Who is it?!" A moment later he ran back- it was A… he had come home.

“It has been a nightmare and I've had to examine a lot. Everything has felt so trivial and ridiculous… the blog, the electrical situation, the insomnia, the 'reconstruction', the elections, the fictional WMD… politics and politicians…and I've also realized how grateful we should be just being able to make the transition from one day to the next in a situation like ours…

Iraq is a different place indeed. Our fear of being kidnapped in Chicago is second to the city suddenly switching to a republican stronghold – unrealistic. The only things that shut down roads in Chicago are construction and block parties, not tanks. We don't have patrolmen with automatic riffles; we have meter maids. We move around the city with a sense of freedom and safety. But, clearly, the differences between our cities are not based on reflections of what Baghdad is, but what it has become.

There are areas of our cultures that overlap, even in our own backyard. One of the best parts of Chicago is the freedom to escape your roommates, or the heat, or the stale smell of beer at a party and go out onto the porch. Porches are Chicago and we use them for everything from relaxing and partying, to drying our clothes. To be honest, it sounds like Iraq .

“During this last year, a certain sort of special bond has formed between your typical Iraqi and the roof of his or her home. We run out to the roof to see where the smoke is coming from after an explosion; we gather on the roof to watch the helicopters flying over head; we reluctantly drag ourselves out to the roof to fill the water tanks when the water is low; we hang clothes to dry on the clotheslines strung out haphazardly across the roof; we sleep on the roof during the endless, powerless nights

“On one of those powerless and sleepless nights I decided I would ‘feel my way up the stairs and out onto the roof. A few moments later, my younger brother E. joined me, disheveled, disgruntled and half-asleep. We stood leaning on the low wall enclosing the roof watching the street below. I could see the tip of Abu Maan's cigarette glowing in the yard next door. I pointed to it with the words,

“Abu Maan can't sleep either…”

“E. grunted with the words, “It's probably Maan[his son]”. I stood staring at him like he was half-wild- or maybe talking in his sleep. Maan is only 13… how is he smoking? How can he be smoking?

“He's only 13.” I stated.

“Is anyone only 13 anymore?” he asked.

“I mulled the reality of this remark over. No, no one is 13 anymore. No one is 25 anymore… everyone is 85 and I think I might be 105. I was too tired to speak and, in spite of his open eyes, I suspected E. was asleep. The silence was shattered a few moments later by the sound of bullets in the distance. It was just loud enough to get your attention, but too far away to be the source of any real anxiety. I tried to determine where they were coming from.

As Riverbend watches from her rooftop and we watch from our televisions, the tumultuous creation of a sovereign Iraq is unfolding. If Iraq is to operate as a democratic nation, the crux of democracy is its people. Just as we are not defined by the actions of the American government, Iraqis cannot be defined by what we see on television. To understand America is to understand the stories of its people; to begin to understand Iraq it is important to realize that its people are telling stories. Riverbend's story is purely an illustration of the personal narratives we cannot ignore in the current dialogue and debate surrounding Iraq .

It's not about who won the 2000 Presidential election, or our feelings about Fahrenheit 9/11, or our opinions on the newly sovereign Iraq . It is about understanding that we do not know the whole story and that our media is not going to give it to us. It's about not coming to a conclusion before you have both sides of a story. The ability to identify with life in the city of Baghdad provides the necessary tools to begin to comment on the situation.

Because, who are we?

“We the people”, the instigators of the new Iraqi government, should be able to recognize that people are the foundation of government, just as our founding documents guarantee.

Baghdad is a city with its own history and culture and it will use those factors to rebuild itself; we should try to understand that the steps toward building a new Baghdad cannot be separated from considering the people who live there.

The content has remained consistently good, but the quality of proofreading (or editing, whatever you want to call it) is slipping.  Come on guys, i expect more from you.

comments.name: Fact Checker
comments.subject: Fake??
comments.text: After reading this article I went and read some of Riverbend's blog. I found it really interesting and I forwarded it on to a few friends. To make a long story short, we are now in a debate as to if Riverbend's blog is fake or not. I have found that there was the RiverSbend blog which attempted to smear the original Riverbend blog by posting pro war propaganda. Most people are calling RiverSbend the “Fake” blog and “Riverbend” the real blog. But what sort of research did 606 do to determine if Riverbend was really who she says she is? You said you interviewed her, but did you do so via email? How much of this article was from your interview and how much was from her webblog? I’ve read a good deal of her webblog and have recognized big chunks or your article coming from that. I am just trying to get my facts straight and figure I’d write in.

comments.subject: Interview
comments.text: Intervies where done over the phone as well as email. If you read her blog you will of course see large chunks from this article taken from her blog. We did not try and hide these sections as they are set apart from the rest of the text. We used interview material to add to our text and to clarify parts of her blog. But as the point was to tell part of her story, we used a lot of her story as a choice. thanks for reading.

comments.subject: but...maybe
comments.text: It is of course possible that she is a fake. As you need to take major media with a grain of salt and find out things for yourself, the same most hold true for 606. hmm salty

comments.name: Gotta wonder
