blurb: any moron can review music or movies. it takes a special kind of genius to review an intersection.

pages.html:
I've been to some interesting intersections in the name of sixosix journalism, but none could hold a candle to the study in opposites that is Weed Street on a Thursday night.

I arrived at 9:30 p.m. , which in my mind was a good time to catch the action warming up. That was not the case: It was as silent as a church. I was told that in a few hours, when the scene was under full steam, the area would become the Vegas of Chicago, complete with big bars, gambling and exotic dancers. Since we're dealing with hardcore journalism here, I decided to make do with what I was given.

Ladies and gentlemen, Weed Street and the surrounding environs.


Jamba Juice and California Pizza Kitchen: Yuppies and sex acts. Rating: 9.3
The main characteristic of this intersection is its juxtaposition of differing elements – in this case, the bastions of yuppie drinking Jamba Juice and eating California Pizza Kitchen beside biker bars and topless clubs. I have to incriminate myself slightly on this one, because Jamba is one of the best possible things to have while nursing a hangover, but when paired with the Pizza Kitchen, the double whammy is almost too much. The Kitchen's latest press release on the company's Web site is that the management was just authorized to repurchase $20 million worth of common stock before going on to describe the restaurants as “a leading casual dining chain in the premium pizza segment.”

While I didn't know the premium pizza segment was such a cutthroat market, I was more angered by the fact that I couldn't have a pizza at that point in the evening. You would think the place could make a killing from the hordes of late-night bar patrons, but I'm no market researcher.

The final nail in the coffin of strangeness was the, let's say, exchange of money for pleasures of the flesh around the corner. I pointed out a good shot to the photographer with me, and in the process of setting up, she walked past a parked 1984 Chevy Astro Van. As she did so, a head popped up from under the driver's seat, ostensibly in the act of giving a something that rhymes with “snow bob.”

When I asked the photographer if she was noticed, she replied with, “I think they were both a little busy.”

Naturally. I still wanted a pizza, though.


Venus de Milo reproductions outside VIPs: Of course. Rating: 4.3
While I didn't expect anything extremely high-class from the area, especially after the scene just described above, I was pleasantly surprised by VIPs, the strip – oops! Gentleman's – club, with its fine renditions of the Venus de Milo lining its façade. Fulfilling all stereotypes, luxury cars lined the front parking spots: Lexus. Mercedes. Jaguar. Hyundai.

Looks like someone was slumming it that night.

From my vantage point slightly up the street, it looked as if I was in some surreal, alternate-universe version of Sin City, all lit by a neon glow of the palm trees in front of North Beach, a bar / indoor sand volleyball court / indoor basketball court arena all in one. There's just something to be said about standing on a sidewalk, watching a rat scurry across the street, and then walking into a bar lit on the outside by green palm trees. There's nothing that says American commercial excess like that.

As a side note, the only other establishment I've seen with décor like that sells spinning rims.

The bouncers outside VIPs were surprisingly open to the sixosix photographer. Maybe we looked legit. Maybe they wanted the free publicity. Or maybe they just didn't care what slightly disheveled, non-strip-club-patron-looking people were up to.

go to page 2

The Menomonee Center: Don’t forget about the children. Rating: 7.4
I continued down the street, fascinated by the sign of the off-track betting facility – of which the “B” in “OTB” was flickering, making it appear to read “off-track. Off-track. Off-track betting. Off-track” over and over – and came across a sheet of looseleaf paper posted to the door of the Menomonee Center . As far as I can tell, the Menomonee Center on Weed is a satellite location of the Menomonee Club, an outreach program for children.

The strange mix of opposites found at the intersection continued. Bars and topless clubs, fine. But a center that, according to its Web site, “has been improving urban life for children on Chicago 's North Side for almost 60 years”? Somehow, I'm having a problem understanding that one. I suppose this is the school-of-hard-knocks teaching approach wherein small children are expected to learn quickly about right and wrong, about making good choices amid a myriad of potential bad ones.

The note read “clubbers practice at [address] enter in south parking lot.” The word “lot” was underlined, making me think it had extra significance. Those kids were really going to learn a valuable lesson, the most likely option of which is how to go clubbing, which will better serve them at the other establishments in the general vicinity.

For sheer fly-in-the-face-of-logic reasoning, I'm going to have to give this section an inflated score.


“Work play dine shop”: The Weed Street Big Brother is watching. Rating: 5.4
As if serving as the gateway to Weed Street fun, a sign over the intersection of Weed and Clybourn Avenue admonished me to “work play dine shop,” hopefully not all in the same trip. Apparently the directions were for the monosyllabic only. I did two of four, which wasn't bad for a whirlwind tour late at night: I was working on this piece, and I most certainly played. However, it's bad form to tell me to dine and shop, yet not have any restaurants or stores open to do so. Points off for that – nevermind what time of the day it was.

The closest I came to fulfilling the four of my criteria was at Hogs and Honeys, where the atmosphere was dirty, the bartenders attractively disheveled and the drinks, well, full of alcohol, I guess. Bonus: The bar's marketing director was playing Golden Tee, waiting for the night to start . The strange part about Hogs was that, while I was dressed for work and carrying a shoulder bag, I didn't feel out of place. It was that kind of joint: one of those places brokers and investment bankers go to blow off steam, throw a few back and watch attractive girls dressed up for the night ride a mechanical bull. Since I was the only person in there with a pen and a pad of paper, I had to ask the bartenders about the whole scene, in the name of journalism, of course.

Her reply was simple: “I've seen some crazy shit. The strippers come in around midnight .” Sounds like the “play” part of the intersection's motto is firmly under control.


Nicholas Auto Body: A sound business model. Rating: 3.4
There's a school of business thought that says the home-based approach is critical in gaining a rapport with customers. The van for Nicholas Auto Body, however, took that to a new level with its obviously hand-painted back window of an old-school van – we're talking faux wood trim, a ride my younger brother would call a “woody” – and writing so small it's near-impossible to read.

For one minute, let's suspend the belief that dictates a company excel in its own field, such as seeing an impeccably dressed fashion designer or an IT company with a stellar Web site, and wonder what would happen were the converse to be true. Could you possibly have a horribly dressed designer? Would you trust a company that deals in computers and technology if it had a badly managed site? The answer, Nicholas Auto Body, is usually no. Call me shallow, but for some reason, were I to see a dinged-up woody van from the mid-‘80s pull into my driveway to do body work on my car, I may suddenly decide I didn't need the assistance after all.

In closing, Weed Street and the general environs.
The whole place was a study in opposites: children's center vs. strip clubs. Garish green neon palm trees and trendy upscale eateries. I can see why this is the Vegas of Chicago – the only thing missing is a casino. Off-track betting will have to do.

title: mix tape
blurb: play and work, thursday night; friday morning

pages.html:
The order is everything. It doesn't even look right on the page: “play and work,” the eye quickly wants to reverse it as soon as it's scanned. Everyone knows that we work and then we play; we file our report sheets and total quotas and check in with the supervisor and sweep up the cigarette butts for the next shift, then we relax. Work is for the betterment of all, the greater good is served through the smallest of acts, and when the whole is attended, the individual within the labor structure also benefits. Play is for the self, what that self does to reinvigorate the sense of individuality and reinvent itself from outside of the work force so that the self can return to the labor pool Monday morning with a refreshed sense of self-awareness and thereby once again better serve the whole. You're welcome; I just saved you four years studying the Frankfurt School's theories of capitalist economical structure in relation to the leisure industry. All to explain that you work and then you take that money and go by things, namely, strong drinks for young dumb things. Our revolution is Thursday evening.

If you go out and tear the throat out of a Sunday night you are referred to as “rummy.” Now if you are one of tens of thousands that begin the weekend bender a night early, so much so that the possibility of getting any work slid into the outbox is near an act of God, you are “typical.” The great majority. And these songs are for you, those who can't stand to wait another day for your reward, you who peel the scotch tape ever so gently back from the folds of your closet-hidden birthday presents; you have turned the five day work week into four and two-fifths day.

The mix is play and work. It is the good before the bad, that reward just so that you can get through the next day. A reward so strong and loud, causing even the glass in your hand to sweat, that it more often than not makes the next day impossible to suffer through. Side one are the songs that are people; from the Peaches minimal fuck techno to the brazen screaming of the Gossip, you know all of these songs, they drink where you drink, and often with you. At times you are these songs. Side two is the collective everyone from the night before, all those different song-people, putting on the similar suit and dragging through the same endless last workday. All of them smelling like last night and begging the digital desk clock to inch forward faster.

go to Side A song 1

For Peaches, and for the rest of the 96 percent of the population not defined as genetically pleasing to the eye, bravado is the only and best weapon. She has staked her entire career on the fact that because she tells us that we want to kiss her in the pants, over and over again, we will. She's right: We do. Her voice's insistent repetition coupled with the minimal, but driving, beats of early techno do not lull, but call into the audience a dare, a less-than-preverbal snake charmer. The formula is so simple that it could save all that bookshelf space in the self-help section: positive self-actualization.

This is the anthem for us, having just gotten out of the shower. Don't dry off; just stand wet and nude in front of the fogged glass above the sink. Listen to the chorus as Peaches coos, “I'm the kinda bitch that you want to get with,” and repeats. Watch as beads of water slide and highlight different curves of flesh while catching and pooling in other hallows of our body. As the song builds through insistence, it is no longer Peaches that we want to get with, it's us. Throwing so many varied outfits on our bed, still sing the empowering line though the song hasn't changed from the beginning 12 bars. We are that bitch – maybe not thin, we note, as taking the towel from around us, watching to see which parts are giggling more than others – but the one that others will want to be with, or at least make conversation with. Beats get louder, rougher, as we simply decide on something to wear, not the best outfit but that doesn't matter, and the voice is now slightly sneering. It is our voice, more forceful now that our shoulders have rolled back and our neck longer with the chin tilted upwards and out. And that voice is only sneering at the thought there might be someone out in this world that wouldn't want to be with us. Walking down the street towards the open black expanse of Thursday night, we think of that fictional person, we're going to find them and tell them and show them. We are the kinda bitch that you want to get with.

The song is the kind of person that everyone wants to be and wants everyone else to be as well. A strong member in NYC's early 1980's avant-garde downtown scene (think Basquiat, Zorn, Glass, etc.), cellist Arthur Russell was the one in the advanced classes not wanting to rest on the accomplishments that landed him there but wanted to use his talent to bridge out. Doing so, he took on the bane of the music world – disco. He wanted to take it, grafting music theory and the free form spontaneity of jazz improvisation to it, and give it back to the masses and the academics so that they could all dance and think together. This song is one of his many attempts to do that, it is not surprising that so few have heard of it. The song title and chorus, “Is it all over my face,” more innocent than salacious, refers to the pleasure of being caught dancing, just enjoying rhythm and endless possibilities of each note.

We love to see this song at the beginning of the night, right when we hand over our ID and make through the crowd and for the bar, there it is, illuminated by its own halo of self-contentment. Our friends stare with us, quipping that nobody dances in this bar or to this song or at this early in the night and who dances alone and like that, but we know who does. In our mind, it is us, dancing like this little disco song, trying to lead the way for others to follow or possibly just watch and enjoy.

We pull our eyes away from Arthur Russell's little-song-that-could and back to the pressing matters of making the week fall away one drink at a time, and still remember the Peaches mantra that we started the evening with. There is a song over at the bar looking at us, not really up or down or kindly, but just looking straight at us. We end up standing next to this song, staring back at it.

James Murphy, owner and producer of DFA Records and here the sole member of LCD Soudsystem, bounces out this perfect piece of pretentious dance-punk mockery. At least we hope that he's kidding. The sound is a flawless dance floor pumped-fist-in-the-air synth-driven funk, but it's the lyrics that we agree to sit in the booth with. It looks like fun, but it seems to have had something that it needs to tell. The song seems to think that the music it's dressed in is hardly the point; the song wants to sing. Its voice is lingering and familiar as The Rainbo's ever-present thin lyrics of stale cigarette smoke: “All these kids don't remember … I came here when … I know them … Did you ever go to [insert long dead West Side bar] when it was still open … I remember them when they still had a keyboardist … the first time …” It is like we walked in on the time of this song's life flashing before its eyes. Like a dying man, the lyrics and 24 bars of name-dropping want us to know that it was here, that it was there when what it cared about happened, that it happened, finally. But once it happened, then what? What songs like this always try to do, find some one to relive all the good times that never happened by telling them to someone new. This song is the Virgil of the cantina, but all it does is manage to keep anything new from happening by convincing itself and anyone foolish enough to listen that the past is the only thing that ever happened. We want songs about what's happening.

We excuse ourselves from one table to another booth, another bar, in cabs and up streets. We have to be back at work in nine hours, but that is not what is to be thought of. Only this song is in the front of our mind, it's hoarse whisper in our ear since we stumbled into this place. It doesn't care where we work or the fact that we have to be back there whenever; it doesn't want to know who we know and it isn't introducing us to its friends. All it wants is us right now – right now. And we're up against the speakers with it.

Gramme put out this EP and then pretty much disappeared. Maybe it was too early for their distorted funk leanings or their broken snare and high hat drum claps, or the tiny voiced front-woman's dirty librarian demure. Of the six songs presented, a wrong note isn't hit once, though this, the second track stands out as the best of them. Filled with enough breaks and thudding bass to make the kids uprock but enough sexy enthusiasm to make them want to get down. On top of the clamor are the sultry, if not the slightest bit intoxicated, vocals that win us over, that get us in the corner with them. They come at us like an over-enthusiastic child, bounding, asking as if we trust them even though this is the first time we've met and before we answer the song wants us to follow it, take its hand. It tells us, with faint blurry eyes that it wants us, it wants to push our hair back behind our ears to take our face in both its hands and look at us. And when it does, not only does it see us, but we see the song for what it is, something usually restrained and disciplined, but that now, at one a.m., is unstrung and with out care, like it was a hardcore song until it ran into that Arthur Russell song from the beginning of the night. Now this song loves everyone it sees, which is good, because the song is looking us up and down.

There are those that go home after a few drinks in the thick of night, to get a solid seven hours of sleep before riding out Friday smoothly. We are not such people, we'd like to be, but it's that song before dragging us down the street, swerving and occasionally falling into us in laughing fits and trying to stand up straight. That song says it knows where an after-party show is, right down this way. At the doorway of a nice brownstone that we've never seen before, we're introduced to another song, this one taking money for empty plastic cups that promise to be filled with something once we walk through the door. This song hugs everyone like it knows everyone, even though we'd swear that it couldn't be much older than nineteen.

This song, however, is almost 40, but you'd never guess by listening to it. The Pleasure Seekers were a short-lived, all-girl garage group that only cut two 45s but made the absolute most of their time together. This song is very clear in its intent, between another drink and you; the song will have a double. This simple truth would be a sad giving-up if it came from the likes of Tom Waits, but coming from the screaming mouths of four blond teenage girls from Michigan it's, well, the cute kind of alcoholism.

The Pleasure Seekers' song punches us in the shoulder while we stand there wondering if we want to cross the threshold to see what the five-dollar plastic cup has promised and where that song we came in with has run off to. The song's 19-year-old eyes ask, “Are you in or out?” in such a way that forces us through the door, down a stairwell where shadows are talking to silhouettes and the smell of sweat on skin on skin is palpable. Right before we push through the door, we turn to look at the young song. It looks back at us then points at its empty cup and then to its chest, we smile and nod while it makes the universal gesture for “drinky-drinky” and we see all that wet youth shine of its brown eyes. The example of youth makes buying the next round regret-free. We're in.

Through the door of 1,000 basements in America there are bands playing songs just like this one. They are too good to want to share with anyone, and certainly not with the rest of the country. The Gossip represents the perfect neighborhood band: loud and trashy with out smacking of shtick and pretense, house rockin' and soulful without borrowed nostalgia or pandering theatrics. Cool, we walk in to the thick of the basement throng, feeling the heat of a hundred dancing kids as we push to the front to catch a glimpse of the band, and the cool center is exactly what this band is.

The song is all about the crush, played by this band of three, two women and one man (no bass). The song is directed at us and the one we came with, and to all the other couples that are now sectioning themselves off in musty gray corners of the basement brushing cobwebs from their hair and sweat from their brows and necks. Starting with cupped hands to one another's ear and moving to arms around the waist, we try to say all the things this stomping song is already doing for us in the only way that rock can – blatant and brazen. But as clumsy loud discussions on natural attraction lead to violent hip-rolling kisses up against the cinder block wall, so does floor-stomp rock lead to the Chicago Police Department pulling the plug on the PA and saying that they're only asking once for everyone to get the hell out. Now. The one thing more rock n' roll than a rock band is a hundred drunk kids stumbling over each other trying to get out of a busted house party on a Thursday night.

It's near 4:30 in the morning and we've dropped our keys twice trying to get them in the door. This song is us, loaded and confused but still floating from kissing a stranger. God, where are they? we wonder, knowing that we probably lost them when the cops busted up the party. And all the other people and/or songs that we'd met tonight: Where are they? Our thoughts of these random connections that meant so much in all of those temporal moments are interrupted by the ringing static and shrill buzzing that remains from all the noise, all the music at once and so loud. We sit down rather than attempt the three-flight stair crawl.

This song is the evening being played at once and out of focus. Need New Body forms one of the largest collectives of sloppy-rock-cum-space-jazz that actually maintains the fun of these two things. Unlike other groups that have attempted the bridge between the two, NNB retains what is important: the messy affair that the creation of either one is. Starting with quick snare drum snaps and a rolling bass, it could easily be the beginning of a cut-tempo “My Sharona” before the runaway screeches of feedback come in followed by aggressive handclaps. Like the rest of the songs this evening, this too has a simple, repeatable chorus, “He / hits it off / hangs out / makes friends / and is never seen again,” a strange and familiar idea, like skipping a heartbeat when you sneeze, but it occurs nightly just the same. Sometimes it's an out of town kid that throws back more than they handle and ends up walking into the lake, only to be seen again on the shores of Gary, Indiana. Other times it's more random: Meet someone, talk all night and then the west-running Chicago 66 bus picks them up and they are only blocks away and gone forever. It just works like that sometimes, we think, as we've made it to the second landing, then the third and finally through our door. And sometimes that is us, we think, for all the others that we've met and enjoyed a Thursday evening with, we too have gotten on the bus or up the el train steps. There is nothing wrong with leaving when every one of us in this city is in continuous stages of abandoning each other. This song makes that seem all right, just like every song ought to.

After three hours of drunken coma – not to be mistaken as tangible sleep – this song by NYC's abusive noise trio, Sightings, is what waking up is and sounds like. It seems that there might be the pieces of an 8/4 rock song in there, but one can never tell when it is buried under screaming and beyond-decibel fuzz, fuzz even so distorted that there seems to be no original source or any comparable sound. It is only loud. And the loud is coming from everywhere. Is it the alarm-clock-how-long-has-it-been-going-off-why-is-there-pounding-on-the-front-door-and-the-phone-why-is-anyone-calling-me-this-early-holy-shit-how-did-get­-to-be-this-late-fuck-how-do-I-turn-off-this-goddamn-alarm? This is not a hangover. This is drunk without the inflated sense of security, this is Eugene O'Neal-style dementia coupled with a splitting headache. The mind attempts the massive task of reorganization of the entire constructs of reality. The alarm is going off because we set it two hours ago. It has been going off for quite awhile. Someone is pounding on the door because we left a trail of our mail starting with the phone bill on the first floor leading all the way to the crumpled Jewel SuperSaver waded up in front of our door, where our keys are still jammed. The lady downstairs just wanted to see if we're all right, and though we assure her we're fine, doubt is still registered on her face when we close the door. The song keeps going; it doesn't get louder or faster, but only because thankfully we live in a dimension that won't physically allow it to. The phone stops ringing as we stand under the showerhead, not getting clean but only wet, and we realize that the car pool has left without us. Grabbing keys from the front door and swishing the mouthwash in lieu of proper hygiene we hope that we had a good time last night. Climbing the steps to the train the song finally just stops, now our soft head contends with the sounds of a Friday morning and the distant rumbling of a late train.

Hangovers are when most spiritual deals are broken, as in: “Please God don't let me puke in front of all of these people this early in the morning, I swear I'll do whatever you want.” We're willing to give up anything that we were probably going to give up anyway, such as killing raccoons for sport. This song by The Louvin Brothers is the gentle balm that the bargaining soul needs. This song is the whimper after the fury. The brothers were fundamental to their righteous black-bible belts. Which is why this parable of a drunkard missing his mother's death is so touching, or, at least, palatable early in the morning. The slide guitar is restrained of its typical shrill twang, at moments it even seems haunting. The brothers tell a straightforward tale of failure, regret and redemption, so soft are their voices that they must have had the hungover in mind while singing it. It is a simple song sung by proudly simple folk for the morally enfeebled, which is us. The message is simple: get drunk, mother dies, have splitting hangover, ask sky for forgiveness, Jesus cries and clean slate. Done, so long as we don't puke.

The last song, and its intention to be the patron song for all false prayers of the hungover, pale to Blind Willie Johnson's quick blues clomp and the vision that it invokes. The rawness of his holler and the ferocity at which he does so forces the listener to believe that not only is he running to the city of refuge, but that he has done so myriad times for more miles than any one could imagine.

This song is dedicated to the legion of middle age black women that we see riding the Red line into the Loop every morning, all of them intently focused on their large black bibles. Sun crests over the cityscape and streams over their floral printed dress, lighting their tired, soft cheeks and the pages of their good books to a luminescent glow. Their faces hint of a slight smiling at various portions of a book whose ending they know, and know so well that they realize it is worth reading over again until the sun erases all the dark lines of building and the silhouettes of people until there is nothing left but movement and light. The sight of such self-contained stillness in public transit soothes the pain of a hangover into a straight line of longing. Our head against the scratch-bombed train window, the sunshine no longer pains us, but we wonder what it was we were looking for last night. If people can ascend to angels, these are they, and if those transcendents sing songs, this is the one.

At our desk on a Friday morning, everyone knows it's pure theater. No one can do a stitch of paperwork and e-mails can barely be checked, although the coffee pot can be drained at infinity. The trick is to punch the plastic keys of the keyboard louder and quicker than ever, even though it is only with one hand and eyes are closed and the better part of the morning will be spent calling around to check if everyone feels as bad. Though born of laziness, this is really a subtle act of subversion. In 1929 Bessie Brown, a stage singer, recorded this jazzed-up funeral march about sharecropping cotton fields. It was her last recording session with the Brunswick label, and decided to drop away from her previous pop-romance material to get a few things off her chest. At the time, minstrel shows still held sold-out performances, audiences nostalgic for the “southern days of grandeur,” grand for white people anyway. Knowing that there was a demand for field songs, Brown wrote this derisive tune about how the hands sing so the boss thinks them happy when in fact the singers know there'll be no rest until old age. She does so with such an upbeat punch that she herself could be a minstrel. The fact that she is clearly a black woman, restrained to mostly singing ballads or “jungle” numbers, makes this number drip with accusation. The white theater folk pay to see an old-timey show and have Brown standing before them, in 1929, telling them: You are thieves and you're working me into the grave. Then the snappy chorus: “All my life / I've been making it / All my life / White folks takin' it.” No matter where we work, whom we work for or what race we are, white folks are still taking all of our money. That's why we take two-hour lunches and don't eat anything.

If the last song was the theater of working, then this is the wellspring of such material. Recorded by the great collector of rural and traditional music of the Americas throughout the ‘40s and ‘50s, Alan Lomax made these haunted recordings and interviews in the late forties in the guts of the South. This was at the point when chain gangs and labor prisons where the only kind punishments next to death that the South was offering to offenders. Through the interviews on these recordings, it is clear that much of the continued southern rebuilding was done by the black men that were reputed to be free and to whom the South were openly hostile. When one prisoner was asked by Lomax what crime landed him back in the cotton fields much like ones he sharecropped as a child, the man responds that “all [he'd] done was stay in Mississippi one day too long.” The field hollers range from beautiful to violent, but every one of them is empowered by the singer's force, the need to use the voice and the story to ascend. It's something that we, as we sit at this desk with the phone on mute, could never imagine. The repetitious use of the phrase “early in the morning” followed by a laundry list of pains – from heartbreak to jailbreak to the sharp teeth of bloodhounds – inspires growing anger with each round. The only rhythm binding their wail is the breaking of rocks with their hammers so that the South may rise again. Our jobs are not so bad, even though some jerk ate the yogurt in the refrigerator that was clearly marked as ours.

A pleasant minimalist dance track to get through the rest of the workday. It's Friday and we're a few hours to the finish line of the week's worst day –why not actually attempt to work? All the little clips and gurgles that give this song it texture? That's the sound of fat being sucked out of the thighs of the rich. Matmos decided to dedicate this album of the surgery sounds to their fathers, both doctors. Using a wealth of sounds sampled from the cosmetic surgery practices with the tools themselves, the duo creates a disturbingly accessible dance record. The sound of rhinoplasty aside, the song furthers Matmos's point that underneath the most banal job there is music hidden, waiting for the surface to be scratched away and for someone to want to find it. It's the kind of inspiration that gets us to do 35 minutes of actual labor. And then we collect our check.

title: things you should do, but don't
blurb: It's like Miss Manners, after a few pulls off some Mad Dog.

pages.html:
In life, it seems that there are two kinds of rules. There are those that are set forth by the legislature for the intent of protecting a person from himself and those with whom he may come into contact. These rules – laws – are often under-appreciated and seen as boring and constrictive, but only they have the distinct ability to make some kids with bad hair and worse hygiene say "fuck the man," which is always funny. The other type of rule is created and modified by the same populace it attempts to govern. Condensed, rules of this type are often known as etiquette. Etiquette is an ever-changing, always-suspect form of law that is, quite simply, an attempt by those who have social power to govern those who do not.

Remember when Ashton Kutcher still had people believing that he might have a shred of talent? At that point in time, he had social power. He flexed it, too. Simply because of him, a ridiculous number of white kids with excess spending money spent far too much on hats better placed on a farm or in a truck cab than suburban shopping malls. I've already written my thank-you card to Ashton. This is not meant to sound as though etiquette and social rules don't have any import. They serve an important purpose in life, in that they attempt to set a minimum standard of conduct for commonly occurring situations that involve sharing space with strangers. Etiquette, despite the fact that it often carries a negative or haughty connotation, is to be respected and observed. While it seems cool for some reason for someone to proclaim that they are always themselves, or that they act how they desire to act regardless of the people who surround them or the situation that they're in, this is simply untrue, and probably signifies that the individual making such a pronouncement is even more apt to change their personality or behavior in light of their surroundings. Such a pronouncement is surpassed only by sports cars and Hummers in how transparent they truly are. There are few situations, in particular, that immediately seem most applicable to show how everyone is subject to etiquette, and to show the benefits of our subjectivity.

Imagine, for a second, this exclamation: "Sweet ass!" When, if ever, is this appropriate? In what setting might someone employ such a statement with the expectation of a positive reception? Certainly, a single sex setting seems best suited for such a statement. Do you remember the "10:30, Diet Coke Break" commercial from a few years back that featured the office women congregating at the window to leer at the muscular, sweaty, shirtless construction worker? Yeah, me too, and he was a hunk. In this instance, the women might make such a comment because they felt it, or might make it because they feel they are expected to by the other women. But, imagine a mixed party, such as one of those incredibly awful situations where you're expected to act as though your boyfriend or girlfriend's friends are also your friends, while your friends are actually out somewhere else, laughing at your predicament. If a man were to make such a comment about a woman at one of these times, could he expect a reaction similar to the one expected by the Diet Coke woman? Probably not, even if that woman happened to be his girlfriend. But even within same-sex groups, there is no steadfast rule. Consider a typical (read: stereotypical) sports bar. During a Coors Light commercial, "sweet ass!" would probably earn some acclaim from the crowd, or at least a nodded agreement. You'd be proudly displaying that yes, you are a jackass, but you'd be accepted by the majority nonetheless. Now, the same exclamation, at the same sports bar, only this time, in reference to Nomar Garciaparra while he turns a double play? You'd be no less of a jackass, yet would probably suffer a considerably less accepting reaction from the crowd, right or wrong.
The point I'm attempting to make is that environment dictates behavior: always, and without exception. For 20- and 30-somethings, the most applicable situation, as always, is a bar. For those who are intent on being viewed as a jackass regardless of their behavior, we'll add "dance clubs" to the list as well. To begin, what do you wear when you leave your apartment? Is it an-I'm-coming-home-alone, probably-with-Jaeger-stains-on-my-T-shirt-and-jeans night? Just you and your boys, like last week and the week before that one? If I'm answering, then yes. Are you going out to pick up chicks? Are you slicking back the hair, polishing the gold chain, forgetting to button the top two or three buttons on that sweet silver shirt that lifts the responsibility of announcing that you are indeed, an asshole, away from you? That's dope, brah. Is it a shorts, white socks and gym shoes night? Not planning on getting laid, eh? Or, is it one of those just-me-and-my-girls, we're-sick-of-guys-not-treating-us-right-so-we're-going-to-make-no-effort-whatsoever-to-attract-them nights? That's fine, but a hat doesn't hide anything, and we all know that you're still looking, only this time you're hoping to find that guy who doesn't care that you've made no effort to make yourself presentable, because he sees beauty in the soul. Keep looking, killer, but don't hold your breath. Is it a black pants night tonight? From what I can tell, it usually is, and I'm not complaining. There are very few people who don't put thought into what they plan on wearing when they leave their homes, and those few people who don't are fairly easy to spot, which is not meant to be read in positive way.

next

Simply by leaving your home, you're allowing other people to see you. In seeing you, they're going to judge you. That's the agreement involved in entering the public sphere. All in all, this unspoken agreement is an incredibly good thing, for two specific reasons: entertainment and sanity. Regarding entertainment, I'm referring to the enjoyment derived in watching those who either don't recognize the existence of such an agreement or choose to ignore their responsibility within it. I can offer this simple analogy to elucidate: What's the most fun thing at Great America? That's right, the trash. Jean shorts, huge hoop earrings, socks and sandals, and T-shirts with the wearer's name freshly "tagged" across the front with an airbrush, almost every example of what not to do is perfectly presented for your entertainment. This, truly, is the only reason anyone would stand in a three-hour line for a two-minute-ride not named Houston. Regarding sanity, would anyone really want to go to Great America every day, constantly surrounded, with no escape? It is the rules of etiquette that keep us sane. For all the great laughs we might get out of that kid with Korn T-shirt and black jean shorts, who doesn't realize that what was a shitty trend in its prime is years buried, these laughs would come less easily as they became more frequent. It ceases to be a joke when you have no one with whom to share the story. Enjoyment would become exasperation if you were the one being ridiculed for not wearing jean shorts.
Specific situaions are also governed by the laws of etiquette, thankfully. How does the night that you enter a bar affect the way that you act? Or, how does which bar you enter effect the way you act? Regardless of whether or not you do it consciously, you affect a specific air about yourself that seems most applicable to the bar you're about to enter. A sports bar is far different than a dance club, and going to either on Sunday night is different than going on Saturday night. To wit, while a white tee might be completely within the bounds of propriety for a sports bar on a Tuesday, it may not send the same message on Saturday night. On Tuesday night, it's probably fair to say that there is no dress code. On the weekend, there's always a dress code, only it may not be enforced by the bar, but by its patrons. Imagine that you notice that cute girl in the black pants and blue shirt staring at you? Is she staring at you because you're attractive, or because it seems to her that you're lost? Her looks may be inviting you to talk to her, but also may be a subtle method of explaining that no one actually watches Baseball Tonight on the bar television on Friday – at least, not at her bar. If you and your girlfriends are dancing at a neighborhood bar on a Sunday or Monday night, the guys at the bar aren't admiring your moves, but silently wishing that you'd die, quickly. There are certain standards for each bar that tend to differ on each night, and respecting them is a must. No one likes the loud girl, and no one likes the loud guy. While wearing a sports jersey to a dance club will get you ostracized, wearing a jersey to a sports bar will only confirm to the rest of the patrons that you, like them, have never gotten laid, and might ease your integration into the situation. Does this reek of conformism? It should. Individuality has been misunderstood, at least in the context of outward expression. You do not compromise your individuality by pausing as you prepare yourself for an evening out to ask yourself if what you plan on wearing will fit in with those with whom you'll soon be sharing space. You compromise your individuality only with a consistent effort to subvert that which is truly unique about you. If your clothes are what makes you unique, I'm not quite sure what to say. Except that, simply by existing, you commit a crime on humanity.

In dating, there are innumerable rules of etiquette. No one acts the same way on a first date as they do on a date three years in to a relationship. Do you order exactly what you want on your first date, never thinking about how after you've enjoyed your endless salad bar and breadsticks, she'll never look at you quite the same way? Or, for those of you who are wealthy enough to think beyond Olive Garden as a classy date, do you act the same way at your fancy restaurants? Do you assume the same posture at the table, or speak as freely as you might later on in your time spent together? After how many dates is it OK to talk about how hot her friend is?

Now, let's imagine what it might be like if there were no rules of etiquette. The world would be far different, and far scarier. If you find it hard to imagine what it might be like, simply take the Skyway to I-90, and exit at Portage. Etiquette is, in many ways, the only thing that allows people with different views on life to occupy the same space. If people refuse to respect and maintain the rules that have been reached only through years of subtle tweaking, there is no common ground on which two people who have absolutely nothing in common can stand together without developing a sense of hatred for each other.

pages.html:
Have you ever wanted to be someone else? When you were growing up, everyone had that person they thought had every quality they ever wanted in a human being. For some, it's their father and for others, it might be a celebrity. In a brief period of my life growing up I also had one. That person was Alex P. Keaton from Family Ties . I don't quite know why I identified with him, but for a small part of my life, he was the most amazing human being that ever existed.

Maybe it was his quick wit or his entrepreneurial attitude, or maybe I just wanting to be a big brother to someone named Ming. I wanted to be Alex P. Keaton. I remember never being quite as emotional before the age of 10 as I was when I watched the last episode of Family Ties . I even went as far as telling people at school my real name was Alex Ryan Marshall.

If you ask anyone who know me, that is absolutely true. I can remember signing homework as Alex R. Marshall. Teachers would ask why I used a different name on my homework and I would fully explain that I casually went by my middle name. Still, to this day, can't figure out why I thought my story was so air-tight considering my mother was a teacher at the same school.

We had a lot in common. I figure the only way to show this is a point-by-point comparison of Ryan Marshall and Alex P. Keaton:

Keaton Marshall
  1. Got straight As and went to Oxford
  2. Graduated second in his class
  3. Excellent stock portfolio

  4. Managed Jennifer's all-girl band
  5. Hippie parents
  6. Republican
  7. Friend named Skippy
  8. Dated a psychologist
  9. Overachiever in everything he does
  1. Got an A in math

  2. Graduated

  3. Saved $200 once to buy a Nintendo
  4. Used to work at a Domino's managed by a girl named Jenny
  5. Non-hippie parents
  6. Utilitarian
  7. Dog named Sparky
  8. Dated a stripper
  9. Achieved just over the bare minimum


You see, we should have been related. Blablabla funny ending.

title: intersection section

pages.html:
The idea behind covering an intersection as gaudy and tacky as State and Rush Streets was to capture that which makes the area so unique; namely, the people and the neon signs. Only the neon half of the equation was present, complicating matters somewhat. The photographer and I showed up at that middling time between the end of the business day and the beginning of the nightlife, freeing us to judge the section with impunity, free of human intervention. Ah, to be arbitrary.


The terrace: Where to smoke your cigars like a good bond trader. Rating: 7.7.
As the light of day slowly faded and the bond traders all retuned home from their days of, well, trading bonds, I stood and soaked in the scenery. There's nothing quite like the glow of neon over a well-landscaped strip of greenery to set your urban heart aflame. The signs bringing such joyful light to the area belong to Gibson's, Carmine's and Frog Bar. The patrons smoking their cigars just added to the ambience: There's very little as American Dream-esque as slightly pudgy white-collar workers surrounded by twiggy blondes and fried appetizers at an outdoor table. It restores my faith in America , to be honest. In a world that lacks absolutes, some stereotypical aspects of the culture don't change.

While I was pondering the Gold Coast's rendition of Chicago 's motto, Urbs in horto, the Rush Street bus pulled up and a high school-age girl stepped off. The event would normally have been unremarkable, but there was a glint from her cell phone that broke my reverie. I've never seen a blinged-out phone, much less a high school girl with a blinged-out phone. There's another ideal for which I should be striving: How to get a phone that would be the envy of Paris Hilton.


Of psychics, Tarot readings and the Jared diet. Rating: 8.7.
There's nothing like cooperation, as we all learned at a very young age from Sesame Street . However, most of us limit the sentiment to getting along with others, to better cooperate with co-workers in order to see a radical, revolutionary coup take over the office. We don't typically apply it to inanimate objects, say, store signs. But it is somewhat refreshing to see the stereotypically corporate sandwich chain Subway link arms and sing “Kumbaya” with Mrs. Devon who, according to her sign, does “readings.” There has to be some underhanded plot to all this. Maybe Mrs. Devon knows some dirt about Jared – that he's really a fictitious figure, or that he's recently ballooned, Oprah-style, to more than his original weight – that would make a national chain eatery share sign space.

A more investigative reporter would have picked up a Subway turkey club and headed directly upstairs for some hardcore palm reading. That reporter would have asked the infamous Mrs. Devon exactly what he had just eaten and would have been told – because psychics are never wrong – that dinner consisted of pesto linguine at Carmine's. Granted, that's making a huge assumption, because I'm sure the omnipotent seer above Subway would have been able to poke holes in that plot and would have known I was doing this for kicks, not for journalistic integrity. I took the easy way out and made up the above exchange, so I'm giving Mrs. Devon quite the benefit of the doubt with her rating.

go to page 2

Von Dutch: Empowering the likes of Aston Kutcher & Co. Rating: 3.2.
I don't know what to say about Von Dutch; I'm almost at a loss for words. I have to delve deep into the archives of my brain to recount an actual conversation from six or so months ago:

Me: What the hell is going on with Von Dutch, anyway?
Fashion editor: It's just the newest trend. I can't explain it.
Me: Well, when is it going to be over?
Fashion editor: I would give it two months, tops.

Since I was given a drop-dead date at which the Reign of Aston Kutcher & Company In Trucker Hats would end, I've been anxiously awaiting it. And finally the day has come: Name the last time you saw a sorority girl with playfully faux-punk tendencies and her over-muscled boyfriend – the cornerstone of the Von Dutch market – out and about at the hip nightclub that just opened in Chicago 's hottest up-and-coming neighborhood. The answer? Months ago. I'm happy to report the Reign has ended.

However, the Von Dutch marketing department gets a nod, as it did great work for a trend that burned hot and fast. The Chicago store's location at 1133 N. State Street was the right place at the right time, which saved this section's rating.


Giant wastes of corporate space: Slowly anti-gentrifying the Gold Coast. Rating: 5.6.
The fine art of being a critic is to seize upon those points overlooked by the causal consumer and to elevate those flaws to prime importance. For example, you can look at an otherwise flawless piece of photography and see that guy in the background making that stupid, I-know-you're-taking-this-picture face, missing the points of the entire work. If the work of art is solid enough, the point of the piece still rings true, and can take into account the chaotic nature of the world it reflects.

The boarded-up building two doors down from Carmine's is nothing like that. It's just a blighted, boarded building that's a giant waste of space.

But let's play architectural critic for a moment. Assume the intersection of Rush and State represents that Platonic ideal to which all things aspire, full of happy consumer culture that serves as the lifeblood of a major metropolitan area. Further assume the closed, wasted space of a building in the intersection can do no good, and will only bring down the values of property around it, creating a black hole of negative real estate. As an isolated phenomenon, it sure gives the area a rustic feel. I'm the architecture critic here, and it's just a cool thing to see. This aspect of the review would have scored much lower, but the closed building adds some personality.


Target-ing your voting practices with vague Anderson Cooper look-alikes. Rating: 7.7.
I have to be honest: I have a weak spot for CNN host and Details columnist Anderson Cooper. I think it happened when I read one of his articles on nail-biting – one of my vices – that made him seem, well, more human somehow. So the Target billboard above the Corner Bakery was all the more welcoming, seeing as a Cooper clone was prominently displayed holding hands with this plastic wife, hawking Target products and telling me to vote. It was all a billboard that carried the promise of all the right elements: designer home trinkets, political activism and beautiful people.

While the scene created in the ad was admirable – the entire message, apart from the selling of Target products – was to implore the viewer to get out and vote, which is a worthy cause. However, it seems odd that a retailer like Target, which has made its mark on the American psyche by offering designer goods at affordable prices, would place a billboard in one of the city's most affluent nightspots. A more prime location would seem to be Lakeview, or even parts of Lincoln Park , not a neighborhood that has a Bentley dealership two blocks down Rush. But who am I to argue? Once in a while, I suppose even the city's rich and famous like tacky Isaac Mizrahi crap that would look better in my just-out-of-college apartment.

The good, the bad and the Gold Coast.
State and Rush Streets, throughout most of Chicago , run parallel. However, in the Gold Coast, when it matters the most, some of the city's most affluent roads converge to create an area custom-created for ostentatious displays of money. And oh, is it fun.

Final rating: 7.1.

title: technology
blurb: You bought an iPod. Now what the hell do you do with it?

pages.html:
When an item has become the topic of pundits it is a sure sign that once again the eyes of human nature are too big for the stomach. One need look no further for a culprit then the nefarious counter-culture of the dreaded Book Club. Housewives, divorcees, lonely 35-year-old men living with their parents and, of course, the pundits get together across this country to discuss topics they don't understand. Take The Da Vinci Code for example, a reasonably good book, with nothing inherently wrong with it except for its horribly misguided and sickening-by-implication popularity. Now every Book Club member is instantly a scholar of the Bible and the life of Jesus Christ.

Well, Jesus Christ!

It is hard these days to travel into any type of store and not find at least one item that is connected to that damn book. Blockbuster carries DVDs to help unlock the secrets of the New Testament and I even received a mail-order card with a phone number I could call to help me through the book. For those of us who would rather club a baby seal then join a Book Club and for those of us who feel they are above being sucked into waves of consumer product hysteria, I have one question for you: Do you own an iPod?

The problem
The problem is the iPod has reached such a level of ubiquity that it is now out of control. In the beginning it was only the geeks and audiophiles – the difference between the two is minimal – who were buying the devices. Now my mother owns one. At Duke University incoming freshmen are getting a new iPod. All I got was a freakin' VD. And thus starts the wave that all popular technologies must bare: the wave of idiocy. For years, every PC (read: Microsoft) product dealt with waves of people that had no clue and usual no business using their product. Now it's Apple's turn to experience the asshats. Microsoft, we see you snickering over there.

Now assuming you own one, as everyone does, we aren't going to touch on the basics of playing music or hooking it up to your computer but we are going to learn all the other cool things you can do with an iPod other then just listen to your horrible taste in music. I'm only spiteful because my iPod was stolen not long ago and I have convinced myself the thief has replaced all of my collection with his best of Garfunkel collection. If the iPod is going to be the next Da Vinci Code , which it is, then dammit, you're going to be the ultimate pundit. 

The solution
The iPod is, first and foremost, a computer. It's neither the most powerful, nor the most user-friendly computer, but it's a computer nonetheless. This idea of an iPod being a computer is essential to understanding all the other uses for the iPod. Your home computer can be used for almost anything, and the iPod is catching up.

Simple
Let's start simply. Remember the game Breakout? Where you control the ever-heroic, umm, line that bounces balls in an effort to destroy those, umm, annoying blocks. Well, you can play it on any version of the iPod. In versions 1.0.4 and earlier go to the “about” screen and for higher versions go to the “legal” screen. Once there, hold down the select button for five seconds and the game will start immediately. Use the wheel to control the paddle. Enjoy!

Here's another one to ooh and aah your friends. We all know how annoying the black text on the iPod can be. You can change the color of the screens and text from black to blue by entering the diagnostic mode. Now, unlike you cooking in the kitchen or trying to assemble the latest Ikea addition, just follow the instructions. First reset the iPod by pressing and holding the “menu” and “play” buttons. When the Apple logo appears, press and hold the “rew,” “fwd” and “select” buttons. After you hear a little chirp, yes, like a bird, you're in diagnostic mode. From here scroll to contrast, labeled “N. DISPLAY” and you can change the black text to blue. Enjoy!

Software
So these two tips have been a bit childish, but then again, so is high school . There are a number of software programs out there other than iTunes that let you have some fun with you iPod. Lets look at these awesome creations so you can be enticed and spend hours trying to get them to work. Just kidding, they work. Most of the time.

Now for those among us who love text adventure games so much that they will not leave their home to seek out losing their virginity are in luck. You know those freaks, the ones who stare a computer game with shitty graphics trying to decide what to do when asked, “Ye be thirsty. Should ye A: drink, B: die or C: use magic potion?” contemplate their next move like it's the fucking Cuban missile crisis. There is software which allows you to create your own games in a variety of styles from quiz games to choose-your-own adventure games. There is even a site to download games that were made by other people. It's a lot like those games for the Texas Instruments calculators you used in calculus, except now you're older and can get paid while you play them at work.

The next software is for all you “forgetful paranoids”. You know those people who are paranoid to think the government, or hell, even the maid, are after your personal data, but are also too dumb to remember their debit card PIN. It's called, ironically enough, Pod Secret 1.0. With this software you can transfer important data like credit card / bank numbers, hookers' addresses and the identity of the second grassy knoll shooter and encrypt it so now one else can read it except you, all accessible from your iPod.

Now for those of us on the go, which we all must be because we own a goddamn iPod, there is GoogleGet 1.2.3 . It's a piece of simple software that allows you to download the latest Google news by topic to your iPod, which is a perfect combination of the world's two most widely-used and yet least-understood technologies. How I love these moments of technological bliss.

We hear all the time about the Bible is the most translated book in the world. I personally own it in at least 90 different languages . And I believe in fairies, too. Now you can download the Bible into your iPod for the “on the go” Jesus experience . Much to my enjoyment, it's called BiblePod.

Gadgets
iPods are cool as-is, there is no doubt about that. But Apple, along with a few other companies, are making add-ons for the device which are provide a downright religious experience.

The coolest item is the iTrip. And by cool I mean people will meet you and think to themselves, “Wow, that person is cool. If only I could be so cool. If I was that cool, other people would think I'm cool. That's the cool type of cool!” It is the only device of its kind specifically made for the iPod. When plugged in to the top of the device, it broadcasts the music from your iPod to your car stereo on a station of your choosing. There are no batteries required and the damn thing's only $35.

The second-best device ever is a bit less flashy but equally as useful, kinda like a one-legged whore. Have you ever been out with you digital camera and right when little Jimmy was about to take his first step, or Suzie finally agreed to flash you for those cheap plastic beads you run out of space on your memory card? Well I certainly have, though it might have been Jimmy's boobs and Suzie steps – it's kinda blurry. Belkin makes a product to plug in a Flash card into your iPod so you can transfer you images and free up space. No, you can't view the images on the iPod … yet.

Conclusion:
Feel free to impress everyone with you knowledge of the amazing iPod. You can even lie and tell them you always knew about these things, just like you always knew Jesus had a sister and while you're at it, why don't you tell us the location of Atlantis and who's going to win in November?

pages.html:
Pee-Wee's Big Adventure

“I'm a rebel, Dottie. A loner.”

A movie character has never spoken truer words. And, despite that edgy Brando-esque tone, the phrase finds itself in a cinematic treasure. A great director, an interesting story, pitch-perfect performances: All are found in Pee-Wee's Big Adventure, Tim Burton's first feature.

The reason the movie (which spawned a sequel) is a cult classic today, despite its pop-culture status at the time, is simple. A movie about an overgrown man-child who treks all the way to the Alamo , among other places, to reclaim his stolen bicycle, is anything but the type of enduring classic that will make a critic's list. Instead, it found a home among hipsters and kid-movie aficionados, and is quoted to this day, the above example being only one of a slew of choice lines.

Yes, the journey Pee-Wee goes on is epic, and the film is a true cult classic.

next movie

Pee-Wee's Big Adventure

“I'm a rebel, Dottie. A loner.”

A movie character has never spoken truer words. And, despite that edgy Brando-esque tone, the phrase finds itself in a cinematic treasure. A great director, an interesting story, pitch-perfect performances: All are found in Pee-Wee's Big Adventure, Tim Burton's first feature.

The reason the movie (which spawned a sequel) is a cult classic today, despite its pop-culture status at the time, is simple. A movie about an overgrown man-child who treks all the way to the Alamo , among other places, to reclaim his stolen bicycle, is anything but the type of enduring classic that will make a critic's list. Instead, it found a home among hipsters and kid-movie aficionados, and is quoted to this day, the above example being only one of a slew of choice lines.

Yes, the journey Pee-Wee goes on is epic, and the film is a true cult classic.

next movie

Monty Python and the Holy Grail

Of course, there are journeys, and then there are journeys . There are treks for bicycles, and then there are searches for grails.

Possibly the quintessential cult classic, Monty Python and the Holy Grail couldn't be more cultish, inspiring rabid fans capable of quoting virtually any line from any scene. In that sense, the film is perfect.

The free-associative wonder of the movie, of course, is the most marvelous quality. Chronicling the Monty Python gang's fights with everything from bloodthirsty rabbits to armless knights, the film never ceases to amaze.

And, moreso, it is pointed satire. Anyone familiar with English literature is sure to gain added chuckles from the various comedic set pieces. A beautiful skewering of Anglo-heroics, the stupid jokes are grounded in smart criticism. It's really exactly what you'd expect from Terry Gilliam, who went on to direct absurdist social commentary like Brazil.

next movie

Dead Alive

Speaking of expert directors and their early efforts (a recurring theme thus far), this shoestring budget gore-fest shows that even the most un-Oscar worthy film can be made by a very Oscar-worthy director. In this case, the man behind the lens was Peter Jackson.

Will the Academy ever give an award to a movie like this? Let's imagine how they would intellectualize some of its scenes, were they so inclined:

•  A priest busts out karate moves on the undead. Academy interpretation: Truly, the deviant life of the clergy is not without its merits. In this case, without the typical restrictions of secular life, individuals have the time to think of the lord and learn Tae Kwon Do.

•  An elderly woman eats her own ear. Academy interpretation: A symbolic act, Jackson shows how we as society turn a deaf ear to the elderly.

•  Our hero kills undead with a lawnmower, coating himself in blood. Academy interpretation: A smart metaphor for the blood we will cover ourselves in when we turn our tools of destruction (lawnmowers) on the environment (I realize zombies don't really parallel the environment here, but, well, it's a metaphor. Gimme some slack.)

next movie

Donnie Darko

Another shining example of cultdom, in which a movie absolutely fails at the box office but grows into a cinematic mainstay among a fervent group upon video release , is Donnie Darko.

Jake Gyllenhal leads a respectable cast, which includes his sister Maggie, Patrick Swayze, Drew Barrymore and Noah Wyle, in this head trip of a feature. It's recently been re-released, thanks to the following it found. Word on the street: Don't bother. Too much explanation, as well as the removal of Echo and the Bunnymen from the soundtrack, make for a more tired and typical movie. Instead, see the original.

By not telling us nearly enough to connect all the dots, writer/director Richard Kelly made a movie about the difficulties of being a teenager in the ‘80s. Or maybe it was about time travel. Or dead people. Or rabbits. Or dead people dressed up as rabbits.

Regardless, it's good. See it.

next movie

Bubba Ho-Tep

There are directors who got their start directing future cult classics, and then there are stars who built their careers in cult films, like Bruce Campbell.

There are a ton of the man's movies that would work on this list, most notably the Evil Dead trilogy, but this movie is somehow more … archetypal. And what better film to characterize cult film's archetypal star than such a movie?

Campbell plays a nursing-home bound man who is either a) insane, or b) Elvis. The movie never really makes it clear which it is. He teams up with another resident who is either a) also insane, or b) JFK. Granted this man is black, so it seems like he's probably the former, but he does explain why the skin-tone change. It has to do with a CIA plot.

It's a funny, funny movie. It's also kind of creepy. The two men, you see, are teaming up to stop a mummy from sucking their souls. Somewhat schizophrenically paced, the movie never had a chance at reigning the box office, though you can bet you'll find posters for the film in specialty shops (and dorm rooms) for the next 20 years at least.

next movie

Anchorman

Of course, there's hilarious and then there's hilarious.

I know Anchorman grossed, like, $80 million. And it also just came out. It's not really a “cult film.” But – and stay with me here – it will be.

This movie should never have been made. It is arguably the most absurd, ridiculous, cock-eyed story ever and, I would argue, was only a success because the middle part of America joined the east and west coasts in loving Will Ferrell after Elf came out, not to mention the media's love of other “Frat Packers” like Vince Vaughn and Luke Wilson.

I mean, come on! There's a villain named Wes Mantooth! An orgasm is symbolized in an animation sequence! A lion bites off a man's arm for no other reason than it's part of a running joke involving the loss of limbs. And our hero plays jazz flute! These are not the elements of a successful picture. It was a freak accident that it was a mainstream success.

Despite this, it will have a frothy-mouthed group of followers who memorize every exchange. (Q: “Where are you?” A: “I'm in a glass case of emotion!”)

It's hilarious and, in a decade, people who attend comic conventions will have every line of it memorized.

next movie

Rocky Horror Picture Show

Yeah, Anchorman sure is not a cult classic, like this one. You see, Anchorman is good. This movie, however, is not.

Despite some catchy tunes, “Time Warp” being my favorite, and the occasional clever double entendre, this movie is too long, and too … I don't know, Midnight Matinee.

Which, it could be argued, is exactly why it belongs on a list of cult films. I will grant it's fans that: It holds a place, however ill-achieved, in cult cinema. But, despite the fact that it is the reigning king to cult fanatics, if you haven't seen it, I give this good, solid advice: Don't. It's lame.

pages.html:
Panty Raids
Legend has it that the tradition of the panty raid began the night of March 21, 1952, at the University of Michigan, when 600 or so male students stormed a women's dormitory, confiscating lingerie. Soon male college students across the country began to participate in this custom, making it a staple of fraternity pledges everywhere.

The leisure suit
Leisure suits first originated in Europe in the 1700s, but the 1970s saw the emergence of the polyester version, sported by lounge lizards across the United States. While serving as an informal alternative to sports coats or suits, the leisure suit eventually became a cause of ridicule, with certain restaurants and businesses going so far to ban them from being worn in their establishments.

Goldfish swallowing
Goldfish swallowing started as a fad in the spring of 1939. Harvard freshman Lothrop Withington swallowed one when a classmate wagered that he wouldn't. The event received vast coverage from the local media in Boston, and soon college students throughout the country were trying to top his feat. A t its height, goldfish swallowing was all the rage, with the record allegedly exceeding 300 fish swallowed in one sitting. Unfortunately (fortunately?), the fad quickly passed as the students left their campuses and returned home for summer vacation.

The Nehru jacket
Named after Jawaharial Nehru, the first prime minister of an independent India, the Nehru jacket was well-known for its lack of lapels or a collar, and was the favored apparel of such stars as Johnny Carson, Joe Namath, the Beatles and Mike Love of the Beach Boys. The most well known Nehru connoisseur was Sammy Davis Jr., who claimed to have owned over 200 of the jackets.

Zubaz
In 1991, Dan Stock and Bob Truax wanted to develop a pair of shorts that could expand and stretch to accommodate the bulging muscles of bodybuilders. They called the shorts Zubaz, and the trend caught on. The pair received orders from J.C. Penney as well as the National Football League, so they turned to the Minnesota Corrections Institute to have female inmates stitch them together. No one seemed to care about the fact that the shorts were brightly colored, very flashy and tacky as all hell.

Telephone booth stuffing
The fad of cramming as many humans as possible in a small phone booth is often associated with college students from the west coast, but it was, in fact, started in South Africa. Twenty-five students there were able to pack in a booth and announce that they had set a world record in doing so. Soon students in England, Canada and the United States were attempting to top that mark. Some students in England went on diets, and some at MIT attempted to used geometry and calculus to determine a precise method to achieve the highest efficiency for stuffing.





Of all the things you can do to yourself, following a ridiculous trend ranks up there with the decision you made three years ago to tattoo your (now ex-) girlfriend's name on your left bicep. But don't worry, because you're in fine company. Different generations have been working to outdo each other's fads since at least the 18th century.

Bermuda shorts
British military officers originally wore Bermuda shorts, but they soared in popularity in the United States in the mid-1950s. They came to the States when tourists brought them back from Bermuda and were unfortunately worn at home, at play and in the office.

Glassless glasses
In the summer of 1965, kids on the west coast made popular the practice of wearing eyeglass frames without the lenses in an attempt to make fun of the intellectual Clark Kent look that was popular among adults of the day.

title: Revisiting the ‘80s in Aurora
blurb: Revisiting the '80s in Aurora

pages.html:
Michelle and Brandy are psyched to see the Lounge Puppets.  So psyched that they're pounding as many Bud Lights as they can before the show starts, so they'll have "a nice buzz on and two fists for pumpin.'"  I ask them if they've seen the band before and Michelle, in her best Axl Rose impression, screams, "Hell yeah!  We saw them last week in Bolingbrook and they were fuckin' awesome!"  But tonight the Lounge Puppets, a.k.a. the Midwest 's ultimate tribute to ‘80s hair bands, are getting ready to rock Aurora , Illinois .  Not just regular Aurora , but an outdoor gazebo at Walter Payton's Roundhouse in Aurora .

Now maybe it's just me, but when I think of Walter Payton the last thing that comes to mind is ‘80s hair metal.  I picture number 34, Sweetness, the greatest running back of all time, leading Da Bears to the Super Bowl.  I think of Ditka, the Fridge, and the Super Bowl Shuffle, not "Cherry Pie" or "Welcome to the Jungle."  But here we are in Walter Payton's monument to beer, burgers and football, surrounded by life-size statues of Bears tossing the pigskin and paintings of Bears playing poker and we're getting ready to rock out to Skid Row and Bon Jovi in the heart of Aurora .

Ah, Aurora.  You know the one.  The home of, sing it with me, Wayne 's World!  Wayne 's World! Party time! Excellent! Just listen close enough and you can still hear the reverberations of “Bohemian Rhapsody” bouncing off the never-ending stream of strip malls, tanning salons and bowling alleys.  And considering Aurora's two most famous (fictitious) residents are a couple of aspiring rockers with big hair and a penchant for air guitars, it should come as no surprise that an ‘80s cover band would be a big draw here. 

In fact, people are anticipating the Lounge Puppets so much that even before they take the stage – which is seriously a gazebo surrounded by lawn chairs – guys with beer guts are screaming "She's Only Seventeen" and girls with mullets are pouting "Pour Some Sugar on Me."  Michelle and Brandy, on the other hand, are interested in one thing and one thing only – Guns N' Roses – and they chant "Sweet Child" over and over and over again.  Then, with a thunderclap of the drums and a burst of fog and lights, the tribute begins.

"Shot through the heart and you're to blame / You give love a bad name!"

Instantly I am warped to 1986, and everyone around me is standing and singing "I play my part and you play your game / You give love a bad name ... bad name!"  It doesn't matter that we're gathered around a gazebo gulping down overpriced beer. We are in the ‘80s and we're paying homage to the hirsute gods of metal.  To my left there is a wedding party and the wide-eyed bride is screaming the words at her new husband.  To my right there's a row of capri-clad soccer moms singing at the top of their lungs and dancing like a bunch of slutty groupies.  Behind me there are the dudes trying to look cool, displaying the devil horns, and barely containing their giddiness.  And in front of me there's Michelle and Brandy stomping their feet and pumping their fists in the air as the band seamlessly slides from Bon Jovi into Ratt's "Round and Round."

I realize that the Lounge Puppets are less a tribute than a full-out worship at the altar of the leather-soaked, lipstick-smeared, liquor-stained gods of hair.  Their show is a "we're not worthy" to the ‘80s and all of its androgyny, debauchery and unbridled libido.  The singer, Pete Greco, is sleaze incarnate.  A leather-clad cross of Dan Cortese, Steven Seagal and your stepmom's boyfriend, he constantly has one hand on his crotch while channeling the spirits of Jon Bon Jovi, Sebastian Bach, Bret Michaels and Vince Neil all in a span of four songs.  Jason Sochacki embodies the ‘80s drummer, twirling his sticks and throwing his blond locks back with every hit of the snare.  In true over-the-top ‘80s form, he is swallowed by a kit that takes up half the stage with six toms, two bass drums – one for Lounge and one for Puppets – and a superfluous amount of cymbals.  He also controls the fog machine.  The guitarist, Bob Irvine, is the consummate shredder, taking every opportunity to spin off a solo while his Jheri-curled wig hangs on for dear life.  His leg kicks and Van Halen-esque hammer-ons perfectly suit his snakeskin axe.  And Bill Dixon, the chest-baring bassist, is the true talent of the group, rocking the bass chops and leading acoustic versions of Poison's "Every Rose Has Its Thorn" and Tesla's "Signs."  All together, they're a well-oiled, spandexed tribute machine.

Sure, the show stumbled a bit when the singer asked, "Did anyone try the jalapeno shrimp?" and it was downright hilarious when the bassist took a bathroom break in the middle of "Talk Dirty to Me."  And the stage was being rushed by bridesmaids and suburb bunnies instead of scantily-clad, Sunset-Strip groupies.  But for one Friday night in a gazebo under the stars, the ‘80s rocked a Roundhouse in Aurora.  I think Walter Payton would be proud. 

Catch the Lounge Puppets in all their hair-metal glory at Chicago City Limits on Oct. 2, North Beach on Oct. 16 and Nellie's Pub on Oct. 30.
