title: Candyman
blurb: Of Candyman, Cabrini Green and a tour bus

pages.html:
We've been asking what happens after death for ages and have usually turned to religion for the answer. Religious authorities argue that those who die peacefully or naturally usually go to a new place (heaven, hell, purgatory, again to Earth through reincarnation), or are sometimes transformed (Nirvana, moksha, unifying the entity with the entirety).

But what about murder?

What happens to men and women who are not supposed to die but are forced to die against their will? Storytellers argue that, unlike those who die peacefully, those who die malignantly and unjustly are usually trapped here on Earth, their souls, their spirits unrest. These restless spirits become the makings of ghosts.

Ghosts are made and vent their fate through haunting while always searching for peace, for rest. Some of the most haunted places in Chicago can usually trace its paranormal origins to some gruesome night of murder: a shooting, a stabbing, a fire.

How many times have you heard of a haunted hotel, nightclub, theater, ballroom or bar where some murder or mysterious killing took place? Many times, I'm sure, but doesn't that seem strange. You would think there would be more hauntings in place that had more murders, not the places where people drink and demand entertainment. What about Chicago 's more economically depressed neighborhoods were violence is a means for survival? Wouldn't there be more ghosts there and more ghost hauntings?

The logical thing to do, of course, was to take Ursula Bielski's Chicago Hauntings Ghost Tours. When I found the black and purple mini-bus on the corner of Clark and Ohio , across the street from the Rainforest Café, I found out that Ursula (author of Chicago Haunts: Ghostlore of the Windy City ) would not be leading the tour, but instead it would be her husband, David Cowan.

Cowan, a Chicago firefighter and author of Great Chicago Fires: Historic Blazes That Shaped a City , is a masterful storyteller. He wove us through the streets of Chicago as well a story in history and mystery, in murder and mayhem. There were so many sites of death, some in very well-known places, others in the obscure.

I don't want to give away the secrets, but I will tell you this: there are ghosts in the projects.

Late into the night, Cowan pulled the mini-bus into an abandon parking lot across the street from Cabrini Green. There was quiet for sometime before Cowan rose from the driver's seat to address the 17 of us on the tour:

“At the turn of the century, an African-American man, living in what would later become Cabrini Green, was known as an excellent painter. One day a rich man from the city commissioned the African-American man to paint his daughter. A short time thereafter, his daughter became pregnant. The infuriated rich man hired two thugs to kill the painter. The hitmen first cut off the painter's painting hand. Then dragged him into an open field with beehives. Then they stripped him of his clothes, coated him with honey and released the bees, which stung him to death. Afterward, the took the painter's body and burned the remains.”

We all squirmed and adjusted in our seats.

Then Cowan said, “I don't know about you, but that seems like the perfect way to make a ghost.”

After a few uncomfortable laughs Cowan continued that the dead painter became known as the Candyman and has been haunting the children of Cabrini Green ever since. In fact, a movie, released in the early ‘90s, appropriately called Candyman , was made for this reason and was shot completely on location.

In the movie, a graduate student from the University of Chicago goes to Cabrini Green to prove the Candyman ghost false. As legend has it, the Candyman haunts only those who don't believe in him and provoke him by calling his name five times in succession.

I thought Cowan was finished with the story, but instead after a chilling pause, Cowan, dead serious, whispered, “Candyman.”

There were a couple of chuckles.

And then another whisper, “Caaandyman.”

There was a voice from the back of the bus that pleaded, “Aw man, don't be playin' like that.”

The plead was ignored for another, “Caaaaaandyman.”

Silence.

“Candyman” was whispered once more.

There was a pause, a very long pause.

I felt a wave of sweat heat my neck. I couldn't believe it. This was it. I was going to die, and it was going to be in a mini-bus.

“I think four is enough for now,” Cowan said in his regular voice.

We all collectively exhaled and leaned back in our seats.
I could not help but wonder if the hauntings of the Candyman had any part in the violence in Cabrini Green over the years. Probably not. I mean, of course not, right? That's foolish, irrational, ignorant, even insensitive to think that a ghost, who was probably made up to scare kids, had anything to do the socio-economic blunder that the residents of Cabrini Green have been victims to over the last 50 years.

However, I'm curious what the future holds.

As we witness the high-rise buildings come crashing down so that rich white people can gobble them up and spit out condos, I wonder if the murdered, the restless spirits will remain. Will the abused, the oppressed, the ghosts of the Cabrini Green will haunt the new residents of the area? I'd sure like to take that tour.

title: club 606

pages.html:
When you tell people you're from Chicago you get one of two lines of questioning. The first is from people who have never lived in Chicago : They ask you about the weather, or the crime, or how many (insert sport team here) games you have attended. The second is from people more familiar with the city: Their questions are along the lines of “Oh, yeah? What part?” to which you must answer with a neighborhood.

From that statement alone you are going to be judged. Certain probabilities exist for each neighborhood. If you live in Andersonville , for instance, you might be asked about the Swedish Bakery or the Neo-Futurists. But Chicago has always been that way. People are interested in where you are from. It is a city of neighborhoods, each distinct and very rich in its distinction.

Even in times past, neighborhoods mattered a great deal. Most people could guess correctly your neighborhood by your last name or accent. The city's population exploded with immigration at the end of the 19th century, and birds of a feather all lived together. The typical Chicago resident was an immigrant living among extended family with plenty of more family in the old country. Everyone wrote home to tell tales of big city adventure. The immigrant population and the development of Chicago as a large center of business created a lot of mail. By the middle of the century, so much mail was being sent throughout the country that the post office decided to create some sort of order.

A little known controversy about that system of order is that Chicago 's root ZIP Code, 606, is dedicated to a popular strip club's address. Now that's something to write home about.

A quick ZIP history

ZIP codes didn't always exist: They were instituted in 1963 as part of a larger reorganization of the entire postal service. The post office used to be known as the Post Office Department, and the postmaster was a member of the Cabinet. With the reform came the United States Postal Service, an independent agency of the government.

With several social, economic and geographic changes in the United States since beginning of the 20th century, there was a great need to change the way mail was delivered. The vast majority of mail previous to 1930 was personal correspondence. As business grew, so did business mail and mailed marketing material. The implementation of Social Security created a growing bulk mailing of checks. The post office responded with something called the Metro System, which was broken into 85 large populated areas with distribution centers used to collect and sort the rapidly increasing amount of mail.

By 1960, a more organized plan was needed. A Presidential-appointed Advisory Board of the Post Office Department recommended that a zoning system be created to better deal with the exponentially growing amount of mail. It was dubbed the Zone Improvement Plan, or ZIP for short.

The 85 centers of population were expanded to 552, each with 50 to 150 nearby post offices. The numbering system was simple enough: A five-digit code would be given to each of the small post offices, and mail with that code would be sent directly to the appropriate post office for hand delivery. The first digit of the ZIP code designated a general geographic area, ranging from 0 in the east, and 9 in the west. The next two reflected a further delineation of the region, and the last two were local. Most of the larger cities had already developed a numerical regional system. Here in Chicago, a letter sent to John Doe, Chicago , 26 would end up at the Rogers Park post office. The designation took hold fairly quickly and Postmaster General John A. Gronouski announced the ZIP code would take effect July 1, 1963 .

By 1983, the system was expanded again to include a four-digit extension. The system is so efficient now that when the ZIP+4 number is used, the only people touching the piece of mail are the ones who pick it up and deliver it to its final destination. Machines that read the code and sort it automatically do much of the work.

On to 606

next

If you follow the zip code pattern from east to west, there is a reasonable pattern. But when you get to the Midwest, things get a little strange. Indiana zip codes start with a 4, but Iowa zip codes start with a 5. Illinois seems to be out of order with its 6. Further questions arise with the rumor that the mayor of Chicago during this time, Richard J. Daley, and his good friend, President John F. Kennedy, thought it would be funny to use 606 for Chicago as it was the name of their favorite steakhouse/strip club located at 606 South Wabash – the 606 Club.

This seems just too good to be true. But in true Chicago style, it goes deeper than that. A man by the name of Louis W. Nathan owned and operated Club 606 until 1956, when he was convicted of vote fixing. In fact, he was a party precinct captain in the city's first ward, seventh precinct, which was the south Loop . Nathan had held the post for 25 years in an area that consisted of not only his club, but of several men's hotels. For the Nov. 2, 1954, general election, Nathan and several other election officials persuaded no less than 71 men from those hotels to present themselves as registered voters, many voted several times, and in at least one case, several men voted as the same person. The result was an overwhelming number of Democratic votes.

The club itself was a place to be seen. It was sort of a supper club with nearly-naked women and live jazz, a precursor to Chicago 's Playboy Club of 1960, except Nathan didn't dress his waitresses in bunny costumes. He did load the club with hot jazz musicians of the day. Local multi-instrumentalist Ray Biondi was the leader of the house band for a long time. Up until Nathan's arrest, the club was mainly frequented by politically-connected types of the Bridgeport neighborhood sort.

Brother/neighborhood

Accusations of favoritism have plagued many a Chicago politician. Most instances revolve around old pals from the neighborhood getting lucrative city contracts to do, or not to do, various projects. Daley belonged to several social organizations that helped keep him in touch with people and shape his political agendas. Most of these organizations stressed the importance of looking out for fellow members and making members' interests part of public policy.

One in particular, the Irish Fellowship Club of Chicago, has a membership list that contains all the political elite from the last 100 years. Even in Richard J. Daley's first inaugural speech he declared the importance of serving one's roots: “I have lived all my life in a neighborhood of Chicago. All that I am I owe to the influence of my family, our neighborhood and our city.” And what's wrong with that? This pride is similar to most people who have lived in Chicago for any amount of time. It seems only natural to help out those who have helped you. But to manipulate a federal order to give props to a strip club? That does seem a little far for even the most powerful mayor in Chicago's history.

The order of things

Although it would make a really great marketing campaign to rival that of Las Vegas, having a city that choose its ZIP code based on the preferred burlesque house of its mayor does not bode well with the idea of a cultured city. Luckily, the alphabet saves our souls from moral depravity, at least sorta. The 60001 ZIP code is in Alden, Ill., a small town near the Wisconsin border, an hour and a half northwest of Chicago. 60002 is in Antioch, in the same general area. 60099 is Zion, near the lake at the Wisconsin border. The ZIP codes continue in this pattern of regionally close cities, alphabetized with some disruption by changes since the original ZIP code adoption.

This simple explanation doesn't directly clarify why Chicago starts at 606. So it could very well be a nod to Mr. Nathan and his nightclub. After all, O'Hare is exclusively 60666. It's much sexier to believe that a new powerful mayor, perhaps the largest product of the Democratic machine, in cohorts with any number of his friends and political allies, managed to bamboozle the third-largest city in the United States and declare its ZIP code be taken after the name of a strip club run by a convicted vote fixer – but it is a lot to swallow.

The importance of place

Chicago is a city of neighborhoods. Overtime the characteristics of those neighborhoods – and the people who inhabit them – change. But what does not change is the pride and excitement that comes with the territory of being from a particular place. It gives a platform to declare a favorite nearby restaurant, bar or bookstore. It also provides diverse locales for destinations both local and exotic. And in a mostly friendly way, it creates healthy rivalries.

Where you come from matters to a lot of people. If it is for personal expression, social standing, or lifestyle affiliation, people like to plant their flag. But it changes the tone when that flag is flown from a stripper's pole. Either way, it's just better than saying you live five minutes from Wrigley.

title: chaz walters

pages.html:
“No, just get a few more, would you? Yeah, that's it – one of my good side, and one of my great side. Perfect.”

I wasn't there, but I can imagine that when Chaz Walters made sweet, sweet love to the camera in the photo shoot that begat his Chicago billboard omnipresence, it probably followed a similar script, only with much more product. To be quite honest, the real estate agent has been unpredictably successful, so much so that he's been able to open his own office, Hot Property. One can only wonder what would have happened he had become a commercial airline pilot, a profession whose ranks he contemplated joining prior to his auspicious beginning in real estate. “Ladies and gentlemen, this is your captain speaking. The current temperature is 78 degrees, but it's absolutely on fire in this cockpit.”

It's easy to pick on Walters, though the ease of doing so doesn't lessen the enjoyment of the activity. By making his dreamy eyes the center of a massive billboard campaign, though, he's taken on other responsibilities. Inherent to the success of his quest to make his face synonymous with real estate in Chicago are certain responsibilities. One of these is that he'll immediately be the poster boy for all the criticism of his industry.

While some have pointed to the revitalization of many existing Chicago neighborhoods as a sign of economic strength and vitality, there exists a strong counter-argument to such an opinion. To make expensive homes into economically sound investments, the neighborhood has to support such prices by changing. When an expensive building is built in a traditionally less expensive neighborhood, it is often followed by neighborhood destabilization. Rent prices rise, more expensive buildings are built, and slowly but surely, what once was an affordable neighborhood is transformed into another Lincoln Park or Lakeview.

So, what happens to those who are moved by the new influx of capital? It seems easy to say that they can simply move to another part of the city, or even another city. But, as the “neighborhood revitalization” process continues, the choices grow fewer and less attractive. It's been suggested that this process will stop only when the city is fully and completely gentrified, a word that often carries with it an unfair connotation. Here, though, such a connotation seems just. Though it may not be the goal of developers and the city officials who subsidize their involvement to move those of lower economic classes to areas outside the city, where they can be forgotten about, that is the result. The rich move in, the businesses that cater to the rich move in, and the poor are moved out. It's a far less pretty picture than any ever taken of Walters, I'm sure.

It may not seem fair to criticize Hot Property (I get tingly every time I type it) for catering to the wealthy. But speaking from an admittedly biased perspective, it seems obvious that those who contribute to the decimation of the character of Chicago deserve the vitriol. Chicago , at one time, was a city that defied the typical structure of cities of great size in how individual neighborhoods, indistinguishable except to those who lived there, each possessed their own character, with distinct merits and faults. As the landscape of the city changes, it seems only fair to blame all those who hasten the “revitalization” of neighborhoods in such a way that the process weakens the character of the city, even if the target of such criticism happens to be able to melt hearts with a simple glance.

Yes, it's obnoxious, self-aggrandizing, and occasionally nauseating. But, there's one thing about Chaz Walters' ad campaign that cannot be denied: It's incredibly successful. So successful, in fact, that he can hardly hear you laughing at him from all the way under his immense piles of money. With average annual gross sales of around $250 million, Walters can afford to ignore the criticism, even if it may be justified.

The real estate business in Chicago is remarkably cutthroat, and the staggering number of agents that are available to sellers and buyers of home make the prospects of succeeding in the business grim. In order to be noticed, in order to stand out, an agent needs to make himself known to his prospective clients, and make sure that when the time comes that they might need his service, they remember. Years after starting his billboard campaign, Walters is remembered.

On the issue of gentrification, it not only seems unfair to pin the “problem” on Walters, it is just simply unfair. To infer that he is either somehow responsible for moving people out of their homes or is the figurehead of neighborhood revitalization is patently unjust. It's obvious that Walters tends to represent wealthier clients, and the prices of the properties he's selling reflect his clients, not his preferences.

It also doesn't seem fair to characterize neighborhood revitalization in such a negative light. There are a great deal of benefits to rehabbing older homes and building new ones. Neighborhoods mutate over time, and to bemoan this fact is both counter-productive and ignorant to the intricacies of progress. When groups of people decide to move in to a neighborhood, they hope to engage in a relationship with that neighborhood that will benefit both parties. The people will begin to take on some of the characteristics of the neighborhood, and the neighborhood will do the same. If the people prefer Borders and Whole Foods, those companies will open stores in the neighborhood. No one moves into a neighborhood with the expressed intention of slowly weeding out the long-time residents.

The aims of revitalization are far less dismal than they are often portrayed, which is to take a neighborhood in decline and make subtle changes that reverse this trend without removing the character of the neighborhood or the people who've given the neighborhood its character. It's true that this scenario doesn't always play out in the form just described, but to simply focus on the negative without even glimpsing at the positive is myopic. Neighborhoods can change, without such change being destructive, and real estate agents can make money without being referenced as the evil, beautiful genius behind the curtain.

title: monkeys
blurb: It's the year of the monkey. Too bad no one told the primates

pages.html:
The world teaches many harsh lessons, perhaps the most important of which is that life is simply not fair. The Lincoln Park Zoo has recently taken some initiative to ensure the practice of confining animals is at least a bit more modern and interesting. Among renovations to the ape house is an interactive device that allows chimpanzees to shoot bursts of air onto visitors.

The idea is that the chimps can now respond to people who pound on the glass wall of their enclosure. Sure, if given the chance, they would probably communicate a lot more than a harmless shot of air to the public. Letting apes loose upon Lincoln Park is obviously not an option, but the zoo is apparently willing to compromise: While the animals may be restricted to the ape house, they did get a remodeling and the installation of interactive equipment. It may not be revolutionary, but it's certainly an improvement. In fact, their new habitat cost $26 million. When you consider the amount of money that is allocated for public housing in Chicago , the apes really aren't getting a raw deal.

Zoo officials also hope that such interactive devices will demonstrate that apes are quite intelligent and exhibit behavior similar to humans. Certainly, this is a lesson well learned for the many children who attend the zoo, as these behavioral similarities are later reconfirmed while attending frat parties and bars like John Barleycorn, but perhaps this will create a feeling that we're not so different after all and ultimately cultivate a greater appreciation for apes.

I went to the zoo expecting to see pissed-off, confined chimps in action, emitting bursts of air on an unsuspecting public. But alas, I was wrong. Kids were pounding on the glass, but they were not subject to any retribution from the chimps. I needed further answers and fast, for standing in an ape house on a hot day surrounded by hordes of children is certainly not my preferred way to spend a Saturday afternoon. What I needed was a zoologist. I scanned the crowd and finally spotted a woman fully dressed in khaki safari wear. I had found my zoologist.

Her name was Kathy, and she informed me that she had never even personally witnessed any of the chimps press the button. Apparently, the chimps are still ignorant of the fact that pressing it will release the burst of air and, thus, they don't press it. The hope in creating the system is that the chimps will make the Pavlovian link and associate people's negative reactions, such as making faces on the glass, to the pressing of the button. Kathy added that chimps are very intelligent, but, shrugging her shoulders and smiling, she added, “They may never get it.”

Unsatisfied with her answer, I prodded further. Why might they never get it? What I wanted her to say was, “Well, because they are kept in a glass cage, hindering their ability to fully realize the concept,” she instead replied, “they just may never make the association.” I was getting the runaround from Kathy and we had obviously hit a dead end.

Elsewhere, I read that “Zoo officials hope the exhibit's realistic environments will give visitors new respect for apes and allow scientists to observe the apes acting as they would in the wild.” Of course, because Lincoln Park might as well be Africa, they're so similar. And the trees in Africa contain human installed electrical devices to facilitate interaction between confined animals and humans. The main problem is that every attempt to make their zoo habitat more like their natural one produces the very opposite of the intended effect: It makes the environment less realistic by making it even more constructed. Such devices are deemed necessary to solve the initial problem of how the zoo habitat is inauthentic. However, something cannot be made more authentic by manipulating it to a greater degree.

title: pimp your ride

pages.html:
A camera sweeps down from the sky, framing buildings, streets and cars with a ‘70s-era voice-over says, “ Chicago ! The city of broad shoulders: Home to 2.8 million people and tens of thousands of vehicles whirring through its smoothly-paved streets, up Lake Shore Drive and down Michigan Avenue .”

Really, you don't need the camera to imagine it, because anyone flying into Chicago knows what the city looks like from that bird's eye view: those teeny, toy-like skyscrapers divided up by uncommonly straight lines. And on each of those gray lines little Matchbox cars shoot north, south, east and west. America has had a thriving car culture for decades, ever since owning a sedan or station wagon became as synonymous with the idea of a family unit as children or a home.

Yet, living in Chicago, for some there is no interaction with cars whatsoever, outside of having to hurry past them as the walk signal starts blinking red. With public transportation uncommonly good, cars often don't seem worth the trouble of owning. Parking is too difficult. Insurance is too high. Thieves are too numerous. In short, cars are too much of a nuisance. And while there is little, if no, need for a car, it seems like a lot of people (other than me) have them. Sometimes, even, it seems like they are all parked between Belmont and Fullerton Avenues. Often, they're getting custom work from their loving owners.

It's no also surprise that in America, owners like to detail and customize their cars. Among other things, Americans are all about individualization and disposable income. By slapping a pair of spinning rims on that SUV, an owner gets to showcase his bankroll, as well as separate his Escalade from the rest of the pack. Souping up a ride takes care of two birds with one stone.

Now, I've always been a big fan of customizing things. In truth, I've customized things for a while. When I was much younger, I used to cover my closet doors with pictures, making customized entryways. When I was 17, I customized my Airwalks with glitter. They got me loads of women, and by “women,” I mean “slaps to the back of the head by hockey players at my high school.” Now, I live in Chicago. I no longer have Airwalks to customize. I've considered customizing my flesh with a tattoo, but that seems too permanent, too … I don't know … Tommy Lee.

So why don't I just bite the bullet and customize my car? Of course, as you may remember, I live in here and take the el. I don't have a car. Honestly, who the hell needs a car? I'll tell you who: People who don't understand the incredible ease of our nice CTA. And maybe the police. Since I am not a cop, and since I do understand the CTA (loosely, at least – I still fear the bus), I have little use for a car.

next

Apparently, though, cars are used in the city all the time. Who knew? Well, Pat Schlossberg, for one.

“Where I'm at, it's everyday working people,” she says of her car customers.

Pat owns and operates Accessories Unlimited at 4656 S. Western Ave. Dealing with the sale and installation of custom body parts, Pat knows all about the car culture in Chicago .

“I don't see a ton of re-inventing of the wheel on an older car, unless it's a classic,” she says. “Those customers are different breed entirely.”

Apparently, plenty of people in Chicago also have minor body work done on their car all the time. Why, on the day I talked with Pat, someone ordered a Cadillac grill for their Seville . Most of the traffic she gets is for pricier cars. Of course, this implies that those who own cars and do have work performed on their car have a disproportionate amount of disposable income when compared to the average Chicagoan. I would imagine they are primarily lawyers, politicians and clowns.

This idea is driven home by Pat, when she tells me that she gets “more traffic in SUV customers – Durangos , Escalades.”

Based on what I know of SUVs, I've come to understand only evil people buy them, i.e., lawyers, politicians and clowns. I'm sure I'm right about this.

I ask Pat if she thinks the CTA hurts her business, discouraging car ownership.

“No,” she says. “I'm sure there are a lot of people that take public transportation. They weren't our customers to begin with.”

Interesting. People who don't own cars – like myself – don't have work done on the cars they don't own. This is a breakthrough. And it means only one thing: I must watch MTV.

MTVs primary oeuvre is, of course, teenage fantasy. For example, the show “Pimp My Ride,” and corresponding Web site give me an outlet to all those teens watching the show that wish they had enough bank to screw around on a beater car, turning it into something worthy of P. Diddy. The site also features a “Ride Pimper” that lets users “play super-mechanic and compile the ultimate cruisin' machine.” In other words, people like me, who have no car, money or friendship with Xzibit, get to imagine what it would be like to be on the show.

[Side note: I can't help but call to attention the terminology used in the show's title, “Pimp Your Ride.” I believe they are using an improper form of the verb “pimp.” According to dictionary.com, the word means, “to procure women for the gratification of other's lusts.” At best, this means the show tries to get people to sell their cars for other individual's gratification. Grammatically speaking, a better title for the program would be “Make One's Vehicle Like That of a Pimp.” Of course that's not as catchy.]

prev next

I try to create my own vehicle using the site's Ride Pimper, but fail miserably. Either my browser isn't supporting it, or MTV's site is horrible. Well, I should say more horrible; general horribleness was presumed before even surfing that way. Regardless. After reading about Britney's big day for a while, I regroup.

You see, I am a savvy consumer. I realize that cars need insurance. This leads me to wonder what sort of monetary drain the pimpin' of my future vehicle will cost. Will added rims increase my monthly rates? What about a sweet-ass spoiler? Assuming I can afford to add grills to my non-existent ride, I'll want to protect those accessories from the shadier element in the city (the aforementioned politicians, clowns, etc.). The only way to do this is with insurance.

After some consideration, I decide to call Geico to see what this will cost me. I call Geico for three reasons:

Reason 1: They insure cars.

Reason 2: They were easy to find online.

Reason 3: They have a gecko as their spokesman.

After navigating my way through their relatively easy touchtone system, I get a Geico-person on the phone. We quickly move past the formalities, and I ask, “What sort of rate increase will there be if a soup up my car?”

“What kind of car do you have?” the Geico-person asks.

“I don't have a car. I mean, theoretically, if I had a run-down sedan, would my rates go up if I added on spoilers and stuff?”

“No,” she says. “Once you purchase the vehicle or get the exact year and make of model, we can get you a rate on it.”

The Geico-person says something about purchasing a general liability policy, which I don't really understand, having never had to deal with cars and their subsequent insurance. I have a feeling that had I spoken with the gecko on the phone, I would have gotten a clearer answer. What I'm able to glean is that, when I finally get my car and coat it in platinum (which I plan on doing), I will not have to pay more insurance than owners of the same make and model sans platinum – good news to be sure.

So what is there to conclude about cars in the city?

Well, it would seem that people in Chicago are not like me. They do own cars – SUVs even. And, at times, they choose to customize said cars, adding grills to their Caddies and rims to their Escalades. Sure, public transportation is there, but, if you can afford it, why not buy get some wheels, and make those wheels look smokin'?

Unfortunately for me at least, that will not be happening anytime soon. Platinum is hard to come by, after all.

title: mix tape

pages.html:
Pop, soda, Coke: Whatever you tell the waitress at 9 in the morning in your part of the country, it's all the same. And whatever the local colloquial phrasing calls for, it still consists of carbonated water and high-fructose corn syrup. The mixture maybe slightly sweeter if you're in the South, or possibly fizzier if you're nearer to Big Sky country out West, but the foundation remains the same, and it's still teeth-rottingly good. Just like the music that shares its name, pop is rarely good for you but is always good. And it's not what your mother would like to see you wash down a breakfast of French fries with either.

Soda pop doesn't actually mean anything. It might easily be argued that its second part – a part that is more a sound than a word, “pop” – has no meaning either. The same goes for its musical counterpart. “It's the same old pop stuff,” or “It was alright, they mostly played standard pop-fare,” is often heard, as though pop were the same as pulp (and even Faulkner wrote pulp, so did Lou Reed make pop), or as if it were synonymous with dismissible. And it isn't. Though hollow behind the wonderful shape the word “Soda Pop” forces the mouth to make, there is so much room in that hollow to invite its being filled with flavor and meaning. With a little patience and a lot of trial and error, there could be more flavors of pop than there would be memories and experiences to tie them to.

There's Coke- and outside the city limits of Memphis everything is Coke. “What type of Coke, honey?” It's something that takes some getting used to. Everything is pop music unless it says otherwise, and even then it is more so. But what type? A song is anything, a limit in the number of notes, but never in the material. A pop that tastes like the grass-stains on denim and scabbed knees of Tuesday summer night. It has to be sweet and loaded with stay-up but other than that, you can have whatever type of coke you'd like.

go to Side A song 1

side A - song 1
"Spectacle to Refute All Judgments"
by Jason Forrest
From The Unrelenting Songs Of The 1979 Post Disco Crash, released 2004 on Sonig Records.


Not so much written as it was assembled, Jason Forrest – formerly known as Donna Summers until the fear of costly legal reprisal caused him to revert to his Christian name – wants to hear all his favorite songs at once. Using laptop audio editing software as a sonic chopping block, Forrest/Summers culls the depths of summer vacation soundtracks, then smashes them headlong into one another. Couples-only roller skate disco and prog-rocking arena anthems get melded together; he plays the sadistic toy torture that's from A Toy Story and from the backyard of collective childhoods. There is not “one after another” with children like Forrest/Summers, there is “right now and at once.” With “Spectacle To Refute All Judgments,” the album's first track is its title. Using drilling drumbreaks to bind guitar solos to the organ and handclap of dance floor get down, Forrest/Summers is that kid that blew up a pile of prized Transformers not to destroy them, but to reassemble them into an unforeseen new creation, to truly transform. Around the block on Halloween, he is wearing masks on the front and back of his head, coming and going, only to change twice more throughout the evening, not out of impatience, but so he can hit the same houses – the ones giving out fifty-cent pieces and king-size Milky Ways – before bed. He is emptying pockets of sweat-softened dollar bills on the red Formica counter top at Dairy Queen for the large Mister Misty. When the slender girl, who has eyes too close to the bridge of her nose, swimming in her uniform red polo and tan cargo pants, asks him “What flavor?” he looks at her with the impatience and pity that only children can give. “All of them. Three pumps each. A Triple Suicide Misty, please.”

prev next

side A - song 2
"Therefore, I Am"
by Jim O'Rourke
from Insignificance, released 2001 on Drag City Records.


Some pop looks great, sounds great, with notes pitch-perfect and measured beat-for-beat, but it's the lyrics that turn it to sour-grapes soda. O'Rourke, a former Chicagoan and the newest member of Sonic Youth, one of the greatest improvisers and producers to show themselves this century (yeah, bring the hate mail), put out this deceptive gem of a straightforward rock album and then left town. Like the bad-seed child that is more clever than smart, O'Rourke gives these songs an almost artificial feel of accessibility to them, inviting the avant-weary listener closer and closer to the candy house. And as always, there's a witch inside. He writes lyrics so mean-spirited that the listener can't help wondering if this song is only for one person, namely (hopefully) an ex, or, moreover, every person that O'Rourke ever talked to. He is the shy, smart kid, maybe a little chubby, who moved ahead a grade early and was taken under the wing of another lonely child. Lunches are shared and backs are protected in the washroom from taunting advances and promises for future horrors when caught alone. The two are rarely alone, but to hear their secret conversations is another series of taunts. They seem to be laughing, cross-legged in deep left field, away from the threat of an errant kick ball, but only O'Rourke is laughing. The other boy is pulling handful after handful of waxy green grass and tossing the strands into the opposing breeze, and doing so with a solemn face. Little O'Rourke half-interestedly picks the wings off flies, trying to get them to fight each other crippled. And as confetti of grass blades fall around them, O'Rourke looks to his older playmate and protector, and says, “Why do I talk to you? I don't need anything to bring me down, as I'll always have you.” Recess has been over for years but there's still the taste of a lesser child's cruelty, but sweeter, balanced with perspective and artificially colored from memory.

prev next

side A - song 3
"Mariah Carey And The Arthur Doyle Handcream"
Sonic Youth
" from Sonic Youth and Erase Errata Split seven-inch, released 2003 on Narnack Records.


I wish RC would design, or engineer – however pop is made – a soda that is a commentary on Coke's world business practices. The taste would allow the drinker to see crate after crate of Diet Coke sitting off a sandy, sun-yellowed tarmac, waiting for deployment in Iraq. As in the world of soda, the feuding houses of music at times do result in the occasional death. The same is thankfully not so with off-rock bulwarks Sonic Youth, who've tried to pick more than their share of fights on the playground of pop. Or, more fairly, they've attempted through various songs and projects to understand and critique the temporal myriad pop iconoclasts. So rather than fight, they point and jeer. The latest is a fascination that both Kim Gordon and Erase Errata shared, while touring together in 2002, on the calculated collapse of Mariah Carey. So fascinated were the two groups that they decided to put out a split seven-inch on the subject of this captivation. Over the many chords and cymbal crashes, Gordon's voice retells of Carey's woes in the past several years: public breakdowns, box office poison and label trouble, all through Gordon's sneering, patronizing vocals. Just like when Sonic Youth recorded an album dedicated to Madonna, Gordon's concern with these women is not what they do in the pop world, rather it is how they are perceived by the listening community, namely, impressionable female consumer youth. Her point made, she even steps back from the jabs to give Carey some advice, performer to performer, and it could be for all of us tired from television scandal: Take a bubble bath, date an emo boy, wear underwear. Sonic Youth, the mothering cola.

Bobby Conn and the Glass Gypsies
from The Homeland, released 2004 on Thrill Jockey Records.


And if it's possible to create sodas that critique other sodas, then why not a one that really explains what is going on in the White House? Bobby Conn and his band of Glass Gypsies are just such a tall drink of fructose. In a current political climate so inhospitable even the Dave Matthews Band suddenly have opinions (but that's still about it), everyone has a protest song in their heart, and yet none of them really boogie, you know? Conn , that cosmic Chicago space fiddler, has pulled an entire band together and one concept for his newest album, and it kinda makes you want to wiggle. Here the concept is a glam opera set now with the Masonic/Illuminati conspiracy on center stage and behind it all. We're prisoners in our home, too busy playing with our income tax refunds to notice the drama being played out in the news. I know. It seems far-fetched. Set to a glam-rock soundtrack that would have diamond dogs scurrying with tails between legs, the lyrics vividly call to mind our modern day war with only slight exaggeration. The bounce of the song's tempo compliments the repeated chorus, “Relax / there'll be no warning before the next attacks / Relax / there'll be a huge refund on your income tax.” Placing himself in the conspiring sides' gilded boots makes a typically tedious critique warranted, refreshing, and hauntingly on point.

prev next

side A - song 5
"Tightly Stretched"
The Ex
" from Joggers And Smoggers, released 1989 jointly on Fist Puppet / Ex Records.


While the previous song was all sugar and tricks, were this song a soft drink, it would be carbonated black tea. And with Bobby Conn's original use of displaying political discontent in an entertainment format, entertaining soapboxing is too often like dinner theater: Neither is done very well. What if, while using the medium of music to forward social constructs, the musicians stuck to making the music and they let another take the responsibility of raising talking points? Long-running Amsterdam improv collective The Ex seem to think that's a good idea on this track from its seminal Joggers And Smoggers double LP. The constructs of the tune are loud and tight, running and leaping, opening wholes every few bars to have a female vocalist yell hoarse readings from the women's rights activist Emma Goldman. These are not interpretations or thoughts on the Goldman's essays, but are taken word-for-word. The selflessness of a band to know when another's words better serve them than their own is a rarely shown homage and ceremony to the ideals of a common good. Plus, it's a kick-ass rock song. The whole affair has too much pressure and too much carbonation, the lid is on too tightly and by the end it's exploded down the front of the listener's shirt. Hopefully other places, too.

prev next

side A - song 6
"We Tigers"
Animal Collective
Sung Tongs, released 2004 on Fatcat Records.


You don't ever have to grow up – pop has always offered you that choice. You don't have to think about the politics of the past two songs if you don't want to. You don't ever have to remember those cruel children waiting around the 3:15 flagpole of early life. The Animal Collective proves that through their hyper-active album Sung Tongs and through the hypnotic youth they display live. The message is so unattainably simple that most of us can never get it into practice: Don't grow up, be a child forever, surround yourself with similar playmates and invent your own language and field games. The stomp and playing spectral voices weave through this song and we feel like we've come upon the campfire of the Lost Boys. They dance and bound around us, kicking up dirt and paper-dry leaves. Taking our hand, they swing us in tight circles, convincing us even to brazenly leap over the licking flames from their fire pit. These boys don't have difficult political agendas, they don't know the essays of Emma Goldman and it'd surprising to find out that they know what women are. Their opinions are simply defined in their chants “Like it, like it, like it / Hate it, hate it, hate it.” It's a blessing to be young, in the woods and so caffeinated that flight is not only possible, but also an afterthought.

prev next

side A - song 7
"Carnisaur Vs. Unicorn"
Friends Forever
from Killball, released 2003 on Load Records.


There are those who drink too much pop, who gorge themselves on it. These people are tech support. But in third grade, these little energy transformers sat in the back of the classroom, illustrating page after page of elaborate gore. Typical scenes included impossibly muscular warriors clad in only the thinnest strip of animal pelt with a talon necklace and an immense laser cannon the size of a car. These characters often engaged in battles of epic proportions, matched only by Beowulf armed with duel rocket launchers and accompanied by some sort of flying tiger with the head of a shark thing. They were characters whose only goal was to destroy entire city blocks, though whose creator couldn't finish a single page in their vocabulary workbooks without illustrating a gun-laden fighter plane spraying war in every direction. Friends Forever may be the aforementioned tech support. The troupe has made a name for itself traveling and performing out of their van whenever and wherever the mood strikes them. This go-for-it attitude also landed them a their own documentary released by Plexifilm, merging their love of fast loud noise with their love of full-contact sports and their passion for Fangoria Magazine to create an album aesthetic all their own. Welcome to Killball, the ultra-gore sport of the future where teams decapitate each other and score points. The album plays through an entire championship match, moving from murderous feedback and blitzkrieg keyboard work to empty sounds with no playback, but instead a nice halftime number. This song introduces the two teams preparing to battle for the glory of being the Killball champion, Carnisaur versus Unicorn. Guess who wins.

prev next

side B - song 1
"I've Forgiven Jesus"
Morrissey
from You Are The Quarry, released 2004 on Attack Records.


Oh God, there is nothing that Morrissey can do wrong. Or right, for that matter. For Coke and Morrissey and God, they will decide when and what is too much, not us mortals. To look upon the face of Morrissey is to look on that of the Christ child. It seems that they both age at the same rate, as well as enjoy the same loyal following legions of Latino fan-boys. Coke reinvents itself every summer. But Christ had to be perfect, Coke has to apologize all the time and Morrissey, well, he's not sorry at all. The arrogance of Morrissey is his infallibility. With his most recent outing (though not what many keep hoping for) finds Him in typical form, for the best, still creating lovely pop songs, still emitting a haunting sexiness in his throat and still being indignant as a smooth faced teenager. He has song titles that read like high school journal chapters, like loud absolutes: “America Is Not The World,” (fair enough), “I'm Not Sorry,” (pretty clear there), “The World Is Full Of Crashing Bores,” (if you're Morrissey, that is), “All The Lazy Dykes,” (what?) and the pinnacle of pop declarative, “I've Forgiven Jesus.” Not even Jesus could say that he'd forgiven himself with being accused of oversized hubris. And though the bombastic is a challenge to try to hate Morrissey, in the beginning of the song we're introduced to the sweet child that Morrissey must have been. He promises that he's such a good boy, but wonders why he has so much pain, why did Christ give him so much desire and then bar all the outlets of such passion. Pleading, He cries, “Jesus, do you hate me?” Hearts fall to the floor. How could Christ be so cruel to the Morrissey child? And this is the best pop – one that which allows an offense to become implicitly forgivable – merited by the sincerity of the performer. Morrissey has forgiven Jesus. At least someone is being the bigger man here.

prev next

side B - song 2
"Cock Mobster"
MC Paul Barman
from Paullelujah!, released 2002 on Coup d' Etat Entertainment.


There are points in pop boasting, like the last Hell-bound track for instance, when one has to judge the sincerity of what's being sung. Again, in the last song, it's frighteningly sincere. For this track, well, just look at the title again. Barman is what happens when grad students are allowed to do hip-hop albums as a thesis. His rhymes are scattered and paradigm randomness, sounds torn from the pages of the NY Times, name-dropping MF Doom and John Cage at the same bar in the same four bars. But then, some boasts do tend to go too far, and, well, look at the title again. This pop song bounces and weaves, the lyrics clever and on-mark, all so that MC Paul Barman can list to us all the women he'd like to have slept with. On the illustrious roster: Lisa Loeb, Christie Alley and Isabella Rossellini. Were it not for the fact that list has no definitive aesthetic make-up, or that Barman looks like the younger cousin of Carrot Top, this song would be so over-the-top with its machismo, rendering it unlistenable. This is just slightly more charming. This is a pop for those reaching far beyond their means, for those that knowingly desire what is only illusion. To the overweight, TV-kissing boys that spent study hall making definitive, cross-referenced inventory of the movie stars they would and would not sleep with, this Coke's for you.

prev next

side B - song 3
"Shitmix2000"
Bit_Meddler
from The Cosmic Forces Of Mu, released 2001 on Planet Mu Records.


You're at Showbiz Pizza (there isn't, and never will be, a Chuck E. Cheese's to your eight-year-old mind) and you have your run of the soda fountain. One of the dangerous joys of pizza parlors in the ‘80s, the free refill, the do-it-yourself soda fountain, saw you tumbling down the slope that saw Cherry Coke, Sprite and Orange Crush being wantonly sloshed into large textured red plastic cups, sans ice. IDM laptop musician Bit_Meddler knows this time, he's stuck there, using his programming software not to create a new musical template, as others of genre did around the millennial turn did, but to smash together the songs of a junior high school dance. Besides the title, Meddler pays the songs of Vanilla Ice, Kriss Kross, C+C Music Factory and Tag Team a straightforward homage, tweaking the vocals only slightly. Together the songs all sound as though they belong together, eliminating the individuality of each artist and the embarrassment of forcing the listener to remember all the facts they remember from the backs of Yo! MTV Raps trading cards. Letting each song sing for itself for a brief time, instead of for its entirety before slipping into another, helps cut short the nostalgic baggage that is attached to such meaningless songs by the child listeners of the time. When a song is self-important, its own meaning is implicit and the listener can forget it until it is played again. However, with the vacant pop song, cloaked in its dramatic synth washes and screaming choir of black women in bicycle shorts, the temptation is to inlay the dramas of your own life as to fill the meaning that is so missing thus giving the song far more weight than it ever should have had. This is just a quick gloss-over, of course, watching nights of prime-time television, talking on the phone for hours about the sacred nothings of childhood evenings, making cassette-tape maxi-singles, kissing neighbors in empty hallways – a time that seems more important than the adult life that children think they're going to live.

You're at the soda fountain again at some cheap facsimile of Showbiz, but it has a plastic ball pit in which to dispose of your own over-sugared child. You don't look for how many mixtures that can fit in your red cup, now, you look for the unsweetened Lipton Tea spout, or at least the ice water canister.

prev next

side B - song 4
"Fallin'"
Teenage Fanclub & De La Soul
from the Judgment Night soundtrack, released 1993 on Epic Records.


This is the sugar crash from the last pop over-indulgence. It's not unlike the mix of the “Shitmix 2000” in its ideals, but it was actually created at the high point of early nineties pop guilt and insincerity that was rap-metal. This was a great soundtrack for a horrible movie that time mercifully forgot on the discard rack. There are a few pairings that have been left behind (anyone remember Therapy? and Fatal?) but the pairings of Sonic Youth and Cypress Hill, as well as Mudhoney and Sir Mix-A-Lot, do more than any downloadable mash-up could. Then there is De La Soul, backed by the loose and understated Teenage Fan Club, and suddenly all the other attachments, movie and other forced concept traps, are gone and it fells like it's raining in the sunshine. This is a song more relevant to De La Soul than the soundtrack, there is the bounce, sway and laughter of undeniable failure. At a point in their career where they had survived the pop success of songs like “Me, Myself, and I” and “Potholes In My Lawn” they were still trying to find direction and out last the “hippie hip-hop” label they'd been unfairly straddled with, but without the following they'd enjoyed some years prior. In this song, most of the time is spent laughing at themselves and how badly they'd thrown it all away. Not all lamentations are ones of teeth-gnashing sorrow, sometimes when failure is so complete and absolute, it's hilarious to think that success was ever thought to be possible and worth a celebratory song on the folly of thinking you can win.

prev next

side B - song 5
"Ghetto Pop Life"
Danger Mouse & Jemini
from Ghetto Pop Life, released 2003 on Lex Records.


On the subject of losing, Jemini, the MC of this two-turntables-and-a-microphone duo, knows well what the last song sings about. In the past several years, as hip-hop becomes as wide and dense as any other genre, complete with its own forgotten label casualties, Jemini was just one of the many. Like KMD and Del, Jemini was another MC bought up by the major labels only to have his record shelved indefinitely by the changing tastes for garage-rock and gun oil-flavored rap. This song is natural flavors, bitter soda. Brought back by the numerous independent hip hop labels that cropped up over the past six years, Jemini crafts a song that would've gotten him radio play so many years back. Starting with a swelling tabernacle choir belting about the satisfaction of women, sex and endless ammunition, then goes into a heavy drum loop. Repeating what the choir settled for the crowd, he runs line after line of ghetto rock clichés concerning robbery, weapons and women, only after each one he yells “What?” not to be tough, but as in, “is this what you wanted?” It is the song that Tab Cola would try if anyone would let it back on the store shelves again. If only there was life after the pop aftertaste. If only there were a way to target market middle-class white kids …

prev next

side A - song 1
"Spectacle to Refute All Judgments"
by Jason Forrest
From The Unrelenting Songs Of The 1979 Post Disco Crash, released 2004 on Sonig Records.


Not so much written as it was assembled, Jason Forrest – formerly known as Donna Summers until the fear of costly legal reprisal caused him to revert to his Christian name – wants to hear all his favorite songs at once. Using laptop audio editing software as a sonic chopping block, Forrest/Summers culls the depths of summer vacation soundtracks, then smashes them headlong into one another. Couples-only roller skate disco and prog-rocking arena anthems get melded together; he plays the sadistic toy torture that's from A Toy Story and from the backyard of collective childhoods. There is not “one after another” with children like Forrest/Summers, there is “right now and at once.” With “Spectacle To Refute All Judgments,” the album's first track is its title. Using drilling drumbreaks to bind guitar solos to the organ and handclap of dance floor get down, Forrest/Summers is that kid that blew up a pile of prized Transformers not to destroy them, but to reassemble them into an unforeseen new creation, to truly transform. Around the block on Halloween, he is wearing masks on the front and back of his head, coming and going, only to change twice more throughout the evening, not out of impatience, but so he can hit the same houses – the ones giving out fifty-cent pieces and king-size Milky Ways – before bed. He is emptying pockets of sweat-softened dollar bills on the red Formica counter top at Dairy Queen for the large Mister Misty. When the slender girl, who has eyes too close to the bridge of her nose, swimming in her uniform red polo and tan cargo pants, asks him “What flavor?” he looks at her with the impatience and pity that only children can give. “All of them. Three pumps each. A Triple Suicide Misty, please.”

pages.html:
An unseasonably warm September may dupe Chicago newbies, but we seasoned Second City dwellers know what lies ahead: ugly, cold, bitter-cold days and rotten, wretched freezing nights. When I pulled-up to my new Boystown digs during the blizzard of February 2001, I was certain my wool/cashmere blend car coat bought from a sale at Banana Republic would protect me. I was wrong. After suffering frostbite as a welcome-to-Chicago gift, I went shopping to find proper protection. In what I was certain was the coldest winter in the world, I could not find a single pair of gloves or a real winter coat to shield me from this cruel climate in early February.

Learn from my suffering: Shop now! By the time it becomes dreadful out and snow is seeping through your mesh-top sneakers, Target will already have been pillaged and the aisles of TJ Maxx will be barren. Make sure to follow the advice below to keep you fashionably warm as Mother Nature prepares to wield her ugly, frigid head.

Let's start with the feet. Unless you live in the Gold Coast, chances are no one will be scooping the sidewalk for your morning trudge to the el. Ladies, find some reasonable (read: flat, no heels – not even kitten heels) boots. Don't buy suede; they will be thrashed. The Camper store at 61 E. Oak Street has awesome, comfy boots. Men can find boots there as well, or any of the outdoors outfitters have a good selection. If you have $1 million, the ladies should call Paris and order a pair of luscious shearling-lined wedge boots from Balenciaga. While they have a heel of sorts, they are Balenicaga. If you have this kind of money you probably do live in the Gold Coast, or you have a driver. For the rest of us mortals, just take your good shoes in your work bag, tuck the pant legs in and deal.

You will also need a proper winter coat. Exhausted after layering underwear thermals with sweaters, cardigans, blazers and finally my coat, I discovered shearling. I went the faux-fur route, for the animals' sake. But a little hide is mighty nice when the wind chill goes negative. This season, colorful wool coats with a retro flare are popular for both sexes.

Of course you will need to accessorize, men included. Hats, gloves, scarves and, of course, the ever-curious mini clip-on ear muff preferred by those who don't want to ruffle their tresses are required. If you are crafty, or aspiring to be, pick up some knitting needles. Scarves are a good starter project and are also a good way to suggest people give you a little more space on the train. The yarn selection at the Knitting Workshop, located at 2218 N. Lincoln Ave., is exceptional. Don't forget a pair of leather gloves to keep your hands warm while packing a snowball to chuck at the bus driver who completely saw you and blew on by.

Even though you need to cover every visible part of your body when outdoors, you will have to strip off those layers once you get to your destination, therefore what's underneath is important as well. Let's face it: We are Chicagoans. Yes, we are creative, informed, inspired people, but everyday can't be a runway unless you are reading this right now in your Balenciaga boots. A burlap sack would look brilliant with those boots. My vote this season is for Kerry and tweed, a softer more forgiving cousin to burlap. It's good for him and it's good for her.

Guys if you have to show up at an office during the week, try a tweed blazer over a hoodie with denim or plain-colored flannel trousers and cool kicks. Check out Lacoste and Puma's sneakers for fall. Both make very cool options that are passable at most reasonable offices. Leather boots with a side-zip are a good way to make denim less causal. You can pick-up excellent thrift tweed at The Brown Elephant in Lakeview, located at 3651 N. Halsted Ave. Some of the best cast-offs in town can be found at this thrift store, where the neighbors are particularly finicky about fashion.

Ladies, if you get one trendy item other than a poncho – which is a good early fall piece, not to be confused with a jacket, which you'll still need – get a tweedy blazer. I'm not much for wearing suits, but the jacket from a great tweed suit can be the most practical part of your wardrobe. Blazers go from pink and prissy to more traditional in mottled browns. Shrunken and very feminine silhouettes make this season's staple modern. You can personalize your look by adding a number of broaches – 'check the Antiques at Chicago Antique Center at 3036 N. Lincoln Ave.. – trailing down the lapel. Channel Irving Penn's photograph of Nicole Kidman on the cover of Vogue a few months back. Or take inspiration from Prada and belt it with a lizard-skin-and-rhinestone-trimmed belt. Your blazer will also look great with layers. Try it with a filmy, very sheer turtleneck underneath or a chantilly lace vest. If your look is a little more rock, take a cue from Chicago-trained artists and fashion designers Libertine and screen print images on to the jacket. Political propaganda, possibly?

All that said, shop and stash these cold winter wears away. Immediately deny that the cold is coming and enjoy every last minute of fall.

title: editor's note

pages.html:
Unlike the Olympics, an every-fourth-year event that's somewhat vicariously enjoyable, a presidential election brings all sorts of horrible, gaudy nastiness. This city doesn't leave much leeway for political options. You're either for Kerry, or against Bush. Choose your poison.

It's difficult to walk down the street, or drive down the road, without seeing some sort of political activism in progress. Instead of the normal “Register to vote?” question I was asked four years ago, I'm now confronted with the somewhat less neutral “Register to vote and help get Bush out of office?”

The proliferation of stickers and signs is usually a phenomenon that can be ignored, at least after building up a tolerance, much like heroin but without the mess of narcotics. I prefer my politics to remain somewhat impersonal, but sometimes that's just a fantasy.

To set the scene: After returning home from work one day, I find a “Bush-Cheney ‘04” sticker tacked to the door of my room. I shrug and forget about it. A few days later, I come home to find another sticker on the door that reads “George Bush is a punk-ass chump.” (Disclaimer: I have no idea how the stickers got there, and the juxtaposition of both made the situation less political and more ironically funny .)

The following weekend, a few friends come back to my apartment after a night out. One of my friends sees the pro-Bush emblem, and promptly makes a noise that sounds like a cross between a sigh and a scream, as only the dramatically intoxicated can do. Not five minutes later, I see the same friend tearing past me down the hallway, making a beeline for my room. She proceeds to rip the pro-Bush sticker from the door – knocking off the anti-Bush sticker in the process – and tear it to shreds. This doesn't sit well with me, because, for some reason, I don't like seeing my belongings destroyed. This holds true even when I have no emotional attachment to said objects.

She runs to the bathroom and emerges seconds later, saying, “I put Bush where he should be. Flushed down the toilet.”

The whole incident is quickly forgotten – this is after a night at the bars, remember – and the rest of the evening/night/early morning proceeds without further mishap.

A few days later, after a weekend of wondering why my toilet has been running non-stop, I pick up the tank lid to do some quick home repair investigation. I find half a “Bush-Cheney ‘04” sticker partially blocking the flushing mechanism. She didn't flush Bush. She put him in my septic tank.

In any case, remember to vote this November and to catch this issue of sixosix. And don't worry: I'm sure Kerry will take Illinois, no matter what you or I do.

Enjoy the issue.

title: intersection section

pages.html:
The idea behind covering an intersection as gaudy and tacky as State and Rush Streets was to capture that which makes the area so unique; namely, the people and the neon signs. Only the neon half of the equation was present, complicating matters somewhat. The photographer and I showed up at that middling time between the end of the business day and the beginning of the nightlife, freeing us to judge the section with impunity, free of human intervention. Ah, to be arbitrary.


The terrace: Where to smoke your cigars like a good bond trader. Rating: 7.7.
As the light of day slowly faded and the bond traders all retuned home from their days of, well, trading bonds, I stood and soaked in the scenery. There's nothing quite like the glow of neon over a well-landscaped strip of greenery to set your urban heart aflame. The signs bringing such joyful light to the area belong to Gibson's, Carmine's and Frog Bar. The patrons smoking their cigars just added to the ambience: There's very little as American Dream-esque as slightly pudgy white-collar workers surrounded by twiggy blondes and fried appetizers at an outdoor table. It restores my faith in America , to be honest. In a world that lacks absolutes, some stereotypical aspects of the culture don't change.

While I was pondering the Gold Coast's rendition of Chicago 's motto, Urbs in horto, the Rush Street bus pulled up and a high school-age girl stepped off. The event would normally have been unremarkable, but there was a glint from her cell phone that broke my reverie. I've never seen a blinged-out phone, much less a high school girl with a blinged-out phone. There's another ideal for which I should be striving: How to get a phone that would be the envy of Paris Hilton.


Of psychics, Tarot readings and the Jared diet. Rating: 8.7.
There's nothing like cooperation, as we all learned at a very young age from Sesame Street . However, most of us limit the sentiment to getting along with others, to better cooperate with co-workers in order to see a radical, revolutionary coup take over the office. We don't typically apply it to inanimate objects, say, store signs. But it is somewhat refreshing to see the stereotypically corporate sandwich chain Subway link arms and sing “Kumbaya” with Mrs. Devon who, according to her sign, does “readings.” There has to be some underhanded plot to all this. Maybe Mrs. Devon knows some dirt about Jared – that he's really a fictitious figure, or that he's recently ballooned, Oprah-style, to more than his original weight – that would make a national chain eatery share sign space.

A more investigative reporter would have picked up a Subway turkey club and headed directly upstairs for some hardcore palm reading. That reporter would have asked the infamous Mrs. Devon exactly what he had just eaten and would have been told – because psychics are never wrong – that dinner consisted of pesto linguine at Carmine's. Granted, that's making a huge assumption, because I'm sure the omnipotent seer above Subway would have been able to poke holes in that plot and would have known I was doing this for kicks, not for journalistic integrity. I took the easy way out and made up the above exchange, so I'm giving Mrs. Devon quite the benefit of the doubt with her rating.

go to page 2

Von Dutch: Empowering the likes of Aston Kutcher & Co. Rating: 3.2.
I don't know what to say about Von Dutch; I'm almost at a loss for words. I have to delve deep into the archives of my brain to recount an actual conversation from six or so months ago:

Me: What the hell is going on with Von Dutch, anyway?
Fashion editor: It's just the newest trend. I can't explain it.
Me: Well, when is it going to be over?
Fashion editor: I would give it two months, tops.

Since I was given a drop-dead date at which the Reign of Aston Kutcher & Company In Trucker Hats would end, I've been anxiously awaiting it. And finally the day has come: Name the last time you saw a sorority girl with playfully faux-punk tendencies and her over-muscled boyfriend – the cornerstone of the Von Dutch market – out and about at the hip nightclub that just opened in Chicago 's hottest up-and-coming neighborhood. The answer? Months ago. I'm happy to report the Reign has ended.

However, the Von Dutch marketing department gets a nod, as it did great work for a trend that burned hot and fast. The Chicago store's location at 1133 N. State Street was the right place at the right time, which saved this section's rating.


Giant wastes of corporate space: Slowly anti-gentrifying the Gold Coast. Rating: 5.6.
The fine art of being a critic is to seize upon those points overlooked by the causal consumer and to elevate those flaws to prime importance. For example, you can look at an otherwise flawless piece of photography and see that guy in the background making that stupid, I-know-you're-taking-this-picture face, missing the points of the entire work. If the work of art is solid enough, the point of the piece still rings true, and can take into account the chaotic nature of the world it reflects.

The boarded-up building two doors down from Carmine's is nothing like that. It's just a blighted, boarded building that's a giant waste of space.

But let's play architectural critic for a moment. Assume the intersection of Rush and State represents that Platonic ideal to which all things aspire, full of happy consumer culture that serves as the lifeblood of a major metropolitan area. Further assume the closed, wasted space of a building in the intersection can do no good, and will only bring down the values of property around it, creating a black hole of negative real estate. As an isolated phenomenon, it sure gives the area a rustic feel. I'm the architecture critic here, and it's just a cool thing to see. This aspect of the review would have scored much lower, but the closed building adds some personality.


Target-ing your voting practices with vague Anderson Cooper look-alikes. Rating: 7.7.
I have to be honest: I have a weak spot for CNN host and Details columnist Anderson Cooper. I think it happened when I read one of his articles on nail-biting – one of my vices – that made him seem, well, more human somehow. So the Target billboard above the Corner Bakery was all the more welcoming, seeing as a Cooper clone was prominently displayed holding hands with this plastic wife, hawking Target products and telling me to vote. It was all a billboard that carried the promise of all the right elements: designer home trinkets, political activism and beautiful people.

While the scene created in the ad was admirable – the entire message, apart from the selling of Target products – was to implore the viewer to get out and vote, which is a worthy cause. However, it seems odd that a retailer like Target, which has made its mark on the American psyche by offering designer goods at affordable prices, would place a billboard in one of the city's most affluent nightspots. A more prime location would seem to be Lakeview, or even parts of Lincoln Park , not a neighborhood that has a Bentley dealership two blocks down Rush. But who am I to argue? Once in a while, I suppose even the city's rich and famous like tacky Isaac Mizrahi crap that would look better in my just-out-of-college apartment.

The good, the bad and the Gold Coast.
State and Rush Streets, throughout most of Chicago , run parallel. However, in the Gold Coast, when it matters the most, some of the city's most affluent roads converge to create an area custom-created for ostentatious displays of money. And oh, is it fun.

Final rating: 7.1.

title: marshall
blurb: everything’s better on ice

pages.html:
There has been something I have been wondering for a very long time. Why is everything better on ice? Think about it. Flavored syrup, rain, sculptures, bruises, fishing, enemies, Jagermeister, Disney's The Lion King , the list goes on. I had pondered this long enough so I decided to find out for myself. I bought myself, and two other close friends, three tickets to 100 Years of Disney – on ice.

I, myself, have never been to something “on ice.” So I was anticipating nothing less than awesome!

As I walked up to the stadium, noticing that the majority of attendees were mothers and their kids, I quickly realized I might be looked upon as a “predator.” All I wanted was to see some good Disney fun (on ice). They started the show with all the characters coming out and every kid in the house was going absolutely apeshit. I was pretty far up but from where I was, it looked like Cinderella and The Little Mermaid were very “talented.” As the show went on, they acted out all the most popular stories from Disney (on ice). Apparently Aladdin had to grow some legs because he was pulling some crazy shit (on ice)! And if I remember correctly, The Little Mermaid had fins, right? Well, at the risk of ruining someone's vision of her, that bitch had medal blades attached to her feet! I saw it! She still looked good though. I'm not going to go into much more detail about the show because when you think of what Disney's 100 Years of Disney on ice might be like, yeah, that's what its like.

Now back to the original question. Was Disney better “on ice?” Fuck yeah it was! Let's get to the root of the question. Why is everything better “on ice”? It's easy! Because water has one of the highest thermal inertias out of any natural substance and is the only substance on earth found in all of its three physical states!

title: movies
blurb: movies

pages.html:
what to watch...
When you have insomnia

Lawrence of Arabia       

When you have insomnia, do not – DO NOT – watch Insomnia . It's kind of a letdown.

I wouldn't recommend a movie that would put you to sleep – say, something in the Ken Burns school of film . The nature of insomnia being what it is, you'd probably stay awake through the boringness.

So, instead, you may as well settle in for a nice epic. And, honestly, has there even been an epic as good as Lawrence of Arabia ?

If you just thought, “Sure is. Maybe you've heard of it. A little film called Troy ?” you should be shot.

Lawrence of Arabia has it all: Sweeping desert landscapes, a gorgeous score, an excellent screenplay and a terrific cast. The film is slowly paced so, should you start to drift, you won't be brought back awake, but there are plenty of dirty battles and sadomasochistic scenes to keep you at least interested while you struggle through your long waking hours.
